sections.title: Build a carousel from its parts

sections.body: By default each slide fills the view. Set `slidesToShow` to a number of slides (`3`, `1.5`), a share of the view (`"70%"`) or `auto` to keep each slide's own width. Pass one value per breakpoint for responsive carousels, such as `{ xs: 1, sm: 2, md: 3 }`: in HTML, write `data-ok-slides-to-show`, `data-ok-slides-to-show-sm` and so on. `slideSpacing` sets the gap between slides in pixels. `slidesToScroll` moves several slides per step, or as many as fit with `auto`.
sections.html:
<section data-ok-carousel aria-roledescription="carousel" aria-label="Articles"
  data-ok-slides-to-show="1" data-ok-slides-to-show-sm="2" data-ok-slides-to-show-md="3"
  data-ok-slide-spacing="20" data-ok-slides-to-scroll="auto">…</section>
sections.react:
<Carousel
  aria-label="Articles"
  slidesToShow={{ xs: 1, sm: 2, md: 3 }}
  slideSpacing={20}
  slidesToScroll="auto"
>
  …
</Carousel>
sections.title: Size and space the slides

sections.body: `align` places the selected slides at the `start`, `center` (the default) or `end` of the view, or at a fraction of it, such as `0.1`. `containScroll` decides what happens at both ends: `trimSnaps` (the default) stops at the first and last slide without empty space, `keepSnaps` keeps a stop for every slide, and `false` leaves space so that even the first and last slides can reach their alignment. `startIndex` selects a slide when the carousel loads.
sections.html:
<section data-ok-carousel aria-roledescription="carousel" aria-label="Centered"
  data-ok-align="center" data-ok-contain-scroll="false" data-ok-start-index="1">…</section>
sections.react: <Carousel aria-label="Centered" align="center" containScroll={false} startIndex={1}>…</Carousel>
sections.title: Align and contain the slides

sections.body: Set `loop` to make the first slide follow the last one. The carousel reorders the slides visually instead of copying them, so screen readers and the Tab key still meet each slide once, in order. Loops need content at least one view and two steps long; shorter carousels stop at their ends. `dragFree` lets slides glide with momentum instead of snapping, `skipSnaps` lets a strong swipe pass several slides, `draggable` turns dragging off, and `wheelGestures` moves one slide per mouse wheel or trackpad gesture.
sections.html:
<section data-ok-carousel aria-roledescription="carousel" aria-label="Products"
  data-ok-loop data-ok-drag-free data-ok-wheel-gestures>…</section>
sections.react: <Carousel aria-label="Products" loop dragFree wheelGestures>…</Carousel>
sections.title: Loop, drag and scroll

sections.body: `effect` changes how slides move. `fade` stacks the slides and cross-fades between them. `opacity` and `scale` dim or shrink the slides away from the selected one while you scroll. `parallax` moves a layer inside each slide more slowly than the slide: mark that layer with `data-ok-carousel-parallax`, inside a box that clips it. `autoHeight` makes the carousel as tall as the selected slide.
sections.html:
…
…
sections.title: Add an effect

sections.body: `autoplay` moves to the next slide every `autoplayDelay` milliseconds, and `autoScroll` scrolls continuously at `autoScrollSpeed` pixels per frame. Both pause while the pointer is over the carousel, and stop when a swipe, a drag or keyboard focus reaches it, so people can read at their own pace. Always add a `CarouselPlayButton`: its label switches between **Play** and **Pause**. Neither starts on its own when the system asks for reduced motion. Set `playOnInit` to `false` to wait for the button.
sections.html: …
sections.react:
<Carousel aria-label="News" loop autoplay autoplayDelay={5000}>
  <CarouselPlayButton />
  …
</Carousel>
sections.title: Play slides automatically

sections.body: Arrows come in three variants: `basic` icon buttons, `floating` square buttons on both sides of the slides, and `number`, with a counter such as **2/8** between them. Dots are `circular`, `rounded` (the selected dot stretches) or `number`. Give any control a `color` from the palette, or `white` over pictures. `CarouselProgress` shows the scroll position, or the time until the next slide with `variant="autoplay"`. Thumbnails scroll to keep the selected one in view, in a row or a column (`orientation`).
sections.html:
…
…
sections.react:
<CarouselArrows variant="floating" color="primary" />
<CarouselDots variant="number" color="warning" />
<CarouselProgress variant="autoplay" color="info" />
sections.title: Style the controls

sections.body: Set `axis` to `y` for a vertical carousel and give it a height, for example with a class. The arrows turn to point up and down, and the Up and Down arrow keys move it. Right to left needs nothing: put the carousel in an element with `dir="rtl"`, and swipes, arrow keys and arrows follow the reading direction.
sections.html:
<section data-ok-carousel aria-roledescription="carousel" aria-label="Stories"
  data-ok-axis="y" class="stories">…</section>
sections.react: <Carousel aria-label="Stories" axis="y" className="stories">…</Carousel>
sections.title: Scroll vertically or right to left

sections.body: Every option works the same way in both versions: a prop in React, an attribute in HTML. Values that aren't listed fall back to the default. The first table lists the options of `Carousel`, the next ones those of the arrows, dots, progress bar and thumbnails. `breakpoints` changes behavior options per media query, such as `{ "(min-width: 900px)": { loop: true } }` (in HTML, the same JSON in `data-ok-breakpoints`).
sections.title: Options

sections.body: These props set content and callbacks. They aren't options, because HTML writes them as markup or listens to events.
sections.title: Content and behavior

sections.body:
- **`ok:carousel:select`** fires on the root when the selected slide changes, with `detail.index` and `detail.previous`. **`ok:carousel:settle`** fires when scrolling stops.
- **Other events:** `scroll` (`detail.progress`), `slidesinview` (`detail.indexes`), `reinit` (`detail.snapCount`), `autoplay` and `autoscroll` (`detail.playing`), `slidefocus` (`detail.index`), `pointerdown` and `pointerup`.
- **Instance:** `runtime.get(element, "carousel")` returns `scrollNext()`, `scrollPrev()`, `scrollTo(index)` (pass `true` as the last argument to jump without animation), `canScrollNext()`, `canScrollPrev()`, `selectedScrollSnap()`, `scrollSnapList()`, `scrollProgress()`, `slidesInView()`, `reInit()`, and `autoplay` and `autoScroll` with `play()`, `stop()`, `reset()` and `isPlaying()`.
- **React:** `apiRef` receives the same methods. Callbacks are `onSelect(index, previous)`, `onSettle(index)`, `onScroll(progress)`, `onSlidesInView(indexes)`, `onReInit(snapCount)`, `onAutoplayChange(playing)`, `onAutoScrollChange(playing)` and `onSlideFocus(index)`.
sections.title: Events and methods

sections.body: The viewport is in the tab order and answers the arrow keys, Home and End. Arrows, dots and thumbnails are buttons. Pressing Tab into a slide's content scrolls to that slide.
sections.title: Keyboard

sections.body:
- Name every carousel with `aria-label` or `aria-labelledby`. Slides are named "1 of 5" by default: pass `aria-label` on a slide to describe it instead.
- A polite live region announces the slide people move to. It stays quiet while the carousel plays on its own.
- Arrows stay focusable at the ends and say they're unavailable (`aria-disabled`), so focus never jumps to the page.
- Autoplay and auto scroll pause on hover, stop on focus and interaction, never start with reduced motion, and come with a play and pause button.
- Faded-out slides are hidden from everyone, and loops never duplicate slides.
- Dots and thumbnails are at least 24 by 24 pixels.
sections.title: Accessibility

sections.body: A chart shows values as lines, areas, columns, bars, points, slices, rings, a radar, box plots, cells, bubbles, funnels or slopes, at full size or as a sparkline. In HTML, you write the data as a table. The runtime reads the table and draws the chart as SVG next to it, with a legend and a tooltip. The table stays in the page, visually hidden, so screen readers can read every value. Without JavaScript, the table stays visible. In React, you pass the data as props, and the component renders the same chart and table.
sections.title: Overview

sections.body:
Set `type` to choose how the values are drawn:

- **`line`:** values joined by a line. `curve` sets its shape: `smooth` (the default), `straight` or `stepline`. `markerSize` adds a dot on each value.
- **`area`:** a line with the area below it filled. `fill` sets a fading `gradient` (the default) or a `solid` tint.
- **`bar`:** columns. Add `horizontal` for bars that run left to right, which suits long category names. `columnWidth` and `barHeight` set their thickness as a percentage of a category.
- **`scatter`:** points placed by two numbers. The x axis is numeric.
- **`pie` and `donut`:** one slice per category, sized by its share of the total. See "Show parts of a whole".
- **`radialBar`:** one ring per category, filled to its value. With one category, it is a gauge. See "Show progress as rings and gauges".
- **`radar`:** one axis per category around a center, and one shape per series.
- **`boxPlot` and `rangeArea`:** the spread of values in each category. See "Show ranges and distributions".
- **`heatmap` and `treemap`:** values as shaded cells. See "Show values as cells".
- **`bubble`:** points placed by two numbers and sized by a third.
- **`funnel` and `slope`:** stages that narrow, or the change between a few categories. See "Show stages and changes".

To mix types in line, area, bar, scatter, box plot, bubble and range area charts, give a series its own `type`. In HTML, set `data-ok-type` on the column header of the series.
sections.react:
<Chart
  label="Points per month"
  type="bar"
  yTitle="Points"
  categories={["Jan", "Feb", "Mar"]}
  series={[
    { name: "Team A", type: "bar", data: [22, 12, 21] },
    { name: "Team B", type: "line", data: [31, 26, 35] },
  ]}
/>
sections.title: Choose a chart type

sections.body:
Each series is a column of the table and each category is a row. A row header holds the category, and an empty cell is a gap in the line.

- **Categories:** text labels, such as months. In React, pass them in `categories`.
- **Dates:** set `xType` to `datetime` and give each row header an ISO 8601 date in `data-ok-value`, such as `2012-01-01`. In React, pass dates or ISO strings in `categories`. Axis labels then mark new years and months.
- **Numbers:** scatter charts use `xType="numeric"`. Each row header is an x value, and each cell holds a y value. In React, pass `[x, y]` pairs.

Cells may show formatted text, such as "12%". Put the raw number in `data-ok-value` when the text isn't a plain number.
sections.html: Jan 2012-12.5%
sections.react:
<Chart
  label="Cash flow"
  type="bar"
  xType="datetime"
  valueSuffix="%"
  categories={["2012-01-01", "2012-02-01", "2012-03-01"]}
  series={[{ name: "Cash flow", data: [-12.5, 3.2, 7.1] }]}
/>
sections.title: Write the data

sections.body: Series use the theme palette in order: primary dark, warning, info, error, success and then darker shades. To pick colors, use `colors` in React or `data-ok-color` on each column header in HTML. A color is a palette name, such as `info`, or a palette name and a shade, such as `primary-dark`. To color a single value, such as negative columns, give the point a `color` (React) or the cell a `data-ok-color` (HTML). Colors follow the theme and the preset, in light and dark mode.
sections.html: -41.2
sections.react: series={[{ name: "Cash flow", data: [{ y: 19.8, color: "success" }, { y: -41.2, color: "error" }] }]}
sections.title: Set colors

sections.body:
Pie and donut charts draw the first series, one slice per category. The legend lists the categories, and selecting one hides its slice. The other slices then share the whole circle.

- **Data labels:** set `dataLabels` to print the percentage of each slice on it. Slices too narrow for the text show none.
- **Total:** set `totalLabel` on a donut to show the total in its hole, such as "Total". The total is the sum of the visible slices, unless you set `total`.
- **Colors:** slices use the palette in order, or `colors`. In HTML, each cell carries its slice color in `data-ok-color`.
sections.title: Show parts of a whole

sections.body:
Radial bar charts draw one ring per category on a grey track. Values are percentages: a ring is full at 100, or at `yMax` when you set it. Values print with a percent sign unless you set `valueSuffix`.

- **Gauges:** with one category, the center shows the value and the category name. Set `startAngle` and `endAngle` in degrees, clockwise from 12 o'clock. For example, -90 and 90 draw a semicircle.
- **Dashes:** `dashArray` splits the ring into dashes of that length in pixels. `trackWidth` sets the thickness of the track as a percentage of the ring (50 by default).
- **Total:** with several rings, `totalLabel` shows a total in the center. It is the average of the rings, unless you set `total`.
- **Fill:** rings fade from a lighter tone of their color. Set `fill` to `solid` for a single color.
sections.title: Show progress as rings and gauges

sections.body:
Some charts need several values for each point. In React, pass them as an array in `y`. In HTML, give each value its own column under a second header row. The series header spans its columns, and each value header names its part in `data-ok-part`.

- **Box plots:** five values per category: the minimum, the first quartile, the median, the third quartile and the maximum (`min`, `q1`, `median`, `q3`, `max`). `boxUpperColor` and `boxLowerColor` color the boxes above and below the median.
- **Range areas:** a low and a high value (`low`, `high`). Add a `line` series for an average.
- **Bubbles:** a value and a size (`y`, `z`). In React, pass `[x, y, size]`. The area of a bubble follows its size.

The tooltip lists every value, and screen readers read each cell with its series and part, such as "Scores, Q1".
sections.title: Show ranges and distributions

sections.body:
Heatmaps and treemaps draw each value as a cell in the color of its series. A larger value gets a stronger shade, so the colors still follow the theme. Selecting a cell, or moving to it with the arrow keys, shows its value.

- **Heatmaps:** one row per series and one column per category, such as metrics over time. The first series is the bottom row.
- **Treemaps:** one group per series, with one rectangle per category sized by its value. Each series lists its own categories: in React, give each point an `x` name. In HTML, write one row per category and leave the cells of the other series empty. Names print in the cells that fit them.
sections.react:
<Chart
  label="Visits by page and device"
  type="treemap"
  series={[
    { name: "Desktops", data: [{ x: "Home", y: 60 }, { x: "Pricing", y: 41 }] },
    { name: "Mobile", data: [{ x: "Docs", y: 51 }, { x: "Blog", y: 30 }] },
  ]}
/>
sections.title: Show values as cells

sections.body:
- **Funnels:** `funnel` draws the first series as bars centered on one axis, each as long as its share of the largest value, such as the stages of a sign-up flow. For a pyramid, order the values from the smallest to the largest. `barHeight` sets the thickness (80% by default).
- **Slopes:** `slope` joins each series' values across a few categories, usually two, such as before and after. The values print beside the first and last points, and the scale fits the data.
sections.html: <figure data-ok-chart data-ok-type="funnel" … data-ok-data-labels>
sections.react: <Chart label="Sign-ups" type="funnel" dataLabels categories={steps} series={[{ name: "People", data: [1380, 990, 548, 200] }]} />
sections.title: Show stages and changes

sections.body: Set `sparkline` (`data-ok-sparkline` in HTML) to draw a chart without axes, grid or legend, such as a trend in a dashboard card or a table cell. A sparkline fills its container: give the container a height, or set `height` for the least height (40px by default). The tooltip, the keyboard and the data table still work.
sections.react: <Chart label="Visits this week" type="area" sparkline height={48} categories={days} series={visits} />
sections.title: Fit charts in cards and table cells

sections.body:
Charts redraw only what changed, so they can follow live data, such as requests per second.

- **React:** pass new `series` and `categories` arrays. To keep a sliding window, drop the oldest points yourself.
- **HTML:** call `updateSeries(series, categories)` to replace the data, or `appendData([{ data: [value] }], { categories: [label], limit })` to add points to each series in order. `limit` keeps the last points only. The runtime rewrites the data table to match, so screen readers read the same values.

Updates keep the hidden series and the category under the pointer or the keyboard, so the tooltip shows the new value.
sections.html:
<script type="module">
  import { getRuntime } from "@owlky/html";

  const chart = getRuntime().get(document.querySelector("#requests"), "chart");
  // Add the newest value and keep the last 12.
  function onData(time, requests) {
    chart.appendData([{ data: [requests] }], { categories: [time], limit: 12 });
  }
</script>
sections.title: Update data live

sections.body:
Set `zoom` (`data-ok-zoom` in HTML) to let people zoom into the x axis of line, area, column, scatter, candlestick and other charts drawn from left to right. The value axis keeps its scale, so values stay comparable while you move.

- **Mouse:** drag across the plot to zoom to that range. Hold Ctrl (or ⌘ on a Mac) and use the wheel to zoom around the pointer. A plain wheel still scrolls the page.
- **Touch:** pinch with two fingers. On a zoomed chart, drag with one finger to pan. A tap still shows the tooltip.
- **Keyboard:** `+` and `-` zoom, Shift with the Left or Right arrow pans, `0` resets. Escape hides the tooltip first, then resets the zoom.

Set `toolbar` (`data-ok-toolbar`) to add buttons for zooming in and out, resetting, panning with the mouse, and downloading the chart as SVG, PNG or CSV. Downloads start only when someone selects a button or presses a key, and a failure is announced to screen readers. In React, `zoomRange` and `onZoomRangeChange(range, reason)` control the zoom. A zoom that reaches the newest point keeps following new points, so a live dashboard stays on its latest data.
sections.react: <Chart label="Daily active users" type="area" xType="datetime" zoom toolbar categories={days} series={users} />
sections.title: Zoom, pan and export

sections.body: Give charts the same `group` (`data-ok-group` in HTML) to synchronize them, such as requests, errors and latency of one service. Moving the pointer or the keyboard over one chart shows the same category in all of them, and zooming one zooms the others. Synchronized charts should share their categories.
sections.react:
<>
  <Chart label="Requests" group="service" zoom categories={minutes} series={requests} />
  <Chart label="Errors" group="service" type="bar" categories={minutes} series={errors} />
</>
sections.title: Synchronize charts

sections.body: A brush chart is a small overview that zooms another chart. Give the main chart an `id`, then set `brushTarget` (`data-ok-brush-target` in HTML) on the overview to that id. Drag across the overview to select a range, drag the selection to move it, or drag its handles to resize it. The keys of a zoomable chart work on the overview too. The selection follows the main chart when it zooms by itself.
sections.react:
<>
  <Chart id="builds" label="Builds per day" type="area" categories={days} series={builds} />
  <Chart label="Builds, overview" type="bar" brushTarget="builds" height={120} categories={days} series={builds} />
</>
sections.title: Brush a chart

sections.body:
Annotations mark a moment, a range, a threshold or a point, such as a deploy or an incident. In React, pass `annotations`. In HTML, list them after the data table in `ul[data-ok-chart-annotations]`, one `li` each, with its label as text.

- **`x`:** a vertical line at a category, a date or a number, or a band up to `x2`.
- **`y`:** a horizontal line at a value, or a band up to `y2`.
- **`point`:** a marker at `x` and `y`.

Each annotation takes a `color` (`info` by default). The list stays readable by screen readers once the chart is drawn.
sections.react:
<Chart
  label="Error rate"
  categories={minutes}
  series={errors}
  annotations={[
    { axis: "x", x: "10:04", label: "Deploy", color: "warning" },
    { axis: "y", y: 2, label: "Threshold", color: "error" },
  ]}
/>
sections.title: Annotate charts

sections.body:
- **Candlesticks:** `candlestick` takes four values per point in `y`: open, high, low and close. Rising candles use `candleUpColor` (`success` by default), falling ones `candleDownColor` (`error`). Add a `line` series for an average.
- **Range bars:** `rangeBar` takes a start and an end value per point, such as the fastest and slowest response of a service. Set `horizontal` to draw them from left to right.
- **Timelines:** `timeline` draws tasks from their start date to their end date, one row per task. Give each point a text `x` (the task) and two dates in `y`. The axis shows minutes, hours, days, months or years, depending on the span.

In the data table, each value gets its own column under a second header row, such as Open, High, Low and Close.
sections.react:
<Chart
  label="Release plan"
  type="timeline"
  series={[{ name: "Release", data: [{ x: "Design", y: ["2026-03-02", "2026-03-13"] }] }]}
/>
sections.title: Show prices, ranges and plans

sections.body: Set `animations` (`data-ok-animations` in HTML) to grow the series in when the chart first draws, and to move bars, points and lines to their new values when the data changes. Animations never play when the system asks for reduced motion. Live charts that update often read better without them.
sections.react: <Chart label="Deploys per weekday" type="bar" animations categories={days} series={deploys} />
sections.title: Animate charts

sections.body: `locale` formats numbers and month names. The names of the values in tables and tooltips, such as Minimum or Open, come from the second header row of the HTML table. In React, pass them in `localeText`, together with the toolbar's button names and the download error. In HTML, call `setLocaleText(text)` on the instance for the toolbar.
sections.html:
<tr><th scope="col" data-ok-part="min">Nhỏ nhất</th>…</tr>
<script type="module">
  import { getRuntime } from "@owlky/html";
  getRuntime().get(element, "chart").setLocaleText({ zoomIn: "Phóng to", svg: "Tải SVG" });
</script>
sections.react: <Chart label="Thời gian phản hồi" type="boxPlot" locale="vi-VN" localeText={{ min: "Nhỏ nhất", median: "Trung vị", zoomIn: "Phóng to" }} series={series} />
sections.title: Localize texts

sections.body: Set `dataLabels` (`data-ok-data-labels` in HTML) to print values on the chart: percentages on pie and donut slices, values inside columns and bars, and values above the points of lines, areas and radars. A label is left out where it doesn't fit, such as on a short column. The tooltip and the data table still show every value. Set `dataLabelBackground` to put the labels above points on a badge, which keeps them readable over lines. For your own text, pass `dataLabelFormatter(value, series, index)` in React, or call `setFormatters({ dataLabel })` on the HTML instance. Pie and donut labels get the percentage.
sections.html: <figure data-ok-chart data-ok-type="pie" … data-ok-data-labels>
sections.react: <Chart label="Share of visits" type="pie" dataLabels categories={devices} series={visits} />
sections.title: Print values on the chart

sections.body: Set `stacked` to put the series of a category on top of each other, so the column shows their total. Without it, columns of several series stand side by side. Only the end of each column is rounded.
sections.title: Stack and compare series

sections.body: `valuePrefix` and `valueSuffix` add text around every value, such as a currency or a percent sign. `locale` sets the number format and the month names. `yMin` and `yMax` fix the value axis, and `yTitle` names it. For anything else, pass `valueFormatter(value, series)` and `labelFormatter(x)` in React, or call `setFormatters({ value, label })` on the HTML instance. The axis gets `series` -1.
sections.html: <figure data-ok-chart … data-ok-value-prefix="$" data-ok-locale="de-DE" data-ok-y-min="0" data-ok-y-max="100">
sections.react: <Chart label="Revenue" valuePrefix="$" locale="de-DE" yMin={0} yMax={100} series={series} />
sections.title: Format values and axes

sections.body: The legend shows one button per series, or one per category in pie, donut and radial bar charts. Selecting a button hides its series and fits the axis to the series that are left. Select it again to show the series. `legend` places the legend at the `top` (the default), `right` or `bottom`, or hides it with `none`. Charts with one series have no legend. On screens narrower than 600px, a right legend moves below the chart. Set `legendValues` to show each item's value next to its name: the slice or ring value, or the last value of a series. `donutSize` sets the size of a donut's hole in percent of its radius (72 by default).
sections.title: Use the legend

sections.body: A chart fills the width of its container and redraws when that width changes, so text keeps its size. `height` sets the height of the plot in pixels (320 by default). Before the width is measured, for example while the page loads, the chart is drawn 640px wide and scaled to fit.
sections.title: Size

sections.body: Every option works the same way in both versions: a prop in React, an attribute in HTML. Values that aren't listed fall back to the default.
sections.title: Options

sections.body: These props set the data and the text. They aren't options, because HTML writes them as markup or text attributes.
sections.title: Content and behavior

sections.body:
- **`ok:chart:toggle`** (cancelable) fires when a legend button is selected, with `detail.index`, `detail.hidden` and `detail.hiddenSeries`. Call `preventDefault()` to keep the series as it is.
- **`ok:chart:active`** fires with `detail.active`: the category (`{ kind: "index", index }`) or point (`{ kind: "mark", mark }`) under the pointer or the keyboard, or `null`.
- **Instance:** `runtime.get(element, "chart")` returns `{ hiddenSeries, setHiddenSeries(list), active, setActive(active), setFormatters(formatters), refresh(), updateSeries(series, categories), appendData(data, options) }`. The methods don't fire events. The chart redraws by itself when the table or an option changes. See "Update data live".
- **`ok:chart:zoom`** fires when the zoom changes, with `detail.range` (`{ min, max }` or `null`) and `detail.reason`: `user` for the chart's own gestures, keys and buttons (cancelable), `group` or `brush` when a linked chart zoomed it.
- **Phase 4 methods:** `zoomRange`, `setZoomRange(range)` (its group and brushes follow), `exportChart("svg" | "png" | "csv")` (a promise that rejects outside a user gesture) and `setLocaleText(text)`.
- **React:** `onHiddenSeriesChange(hidden)` and `onActiveChange(active)`; controlled with `hiddenSeries`, uncontrolled with `defaultHiddenSeries`. The zoom: `zoomRange` / `defaultZoomRange` and `onZoomRangeChange(range, reason)`. To export from your own button, call `exportChart(figure, format)` from `@owlky/core` with the chart's `ref`.
sections.title: Events and methods

sections.body: The plot is one tab stop. When it gets focus from the keyboard, the tooltip shows the first category. The arrow keys move through the categories, through the slices or rings of circular charts, or through the points of a scatter chart. Hidden slices are skipped. In heatmaps and treemaps, each arrow key moves to the nearest cell in its direction.
sections.title: Keyboard

sections.body:
- Give every chart a `label` (React) or a table `caption` (HTML). It names the plot and the data table.
- The data table holds every value, including hidden series. Screen readers can read it instead of the drawing, which they skip.
- The tooltip is a status region, so screen readers announce the values the keyboard moves to.
- Legend buttons report their state with `aria-pressed`. A hidden series keeps a hollow marker and crossed-out text, so the state doesn't rely on color.
- Axis labels use the secondary text color, which meets a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 in light and dark mode.
sections.title: Accessibility

sections.body:
A checkbox lets people choose any number of options from a list, or accept a single statement such as terms of use. It is a native `<input type="checkbox">`, so forms submit it, and the keyboard and assistive technology work as usual.

Put each checkbox in a **form control label**, so the text names it and clicking the text toggles it. For a setting that applies at once, use a **Switch** instead.
sections.title: Overview

sections.body: In React, use `checked` with `onChange(checked)` to control the checkbox, or `defaultChecked` to let it keep its own state. `onChange` receives the new checked state. The `ref` and every other prop, such as `name`, `value` or `aria-label`, go to the input, so form libraries can register it. In HTML, read `input.checked` and listen for the native `change` event.
sections.html:
<script type="module">
  const input = document.querySelector("[name='newsletter']");
  // Save the setting whenever the user changes it
  input.addEventListener("change", () => saveSetting("newsletter", input.checked));
</script>
sections.title: Read and set the checked state

sections.body: The color shows when the box is checked or mixed. The default is `primary`. Use `default` for the text color, or another palette color to match the context. The `small` size has a 36px target and a 20px box, for dense layouts such as tables. The default `medium` size has a 40px target and a 24px box.
sections.title: Choose a color and size

sections.body: By default, the text follows the box (`end`). Set `labelPlacement` to `start`, `top` or `bottom` to move it. The label's negative margin lines the box up with the content edge.
sections.title: Place the label

sections.body: Pass `icon` and `checkedIcon` (and `indeterminateIcon`) to replace the box. In HTML, put your SVG inside the matching `data-ok-checkbox-icon` span. Icons follow the text color, so they take the checkbox's colors. Keep them decorative with `aria-hidden`: the label names the checkbox.
sections.title: Use your own icons

sections.body:
A parent checkbox shows a dash (mixed) when only some of its children are checked. In React, compute the state with `selectAllState` from `@owlky/core` and pass `checked` and `indeterminate`. In HTML, list the children's ids in the parent's `aria-controls`: the script checks or clears all of them, and keeps the parent's state in step.

Set `data-ok-indeterminate` (or `indeterminate` in React) for a mixed state of your own. A click by the user clears it, as with native checkboxes.
sections.title: Select all with a parent checkbox

sections.body: Every option works the same way in both versions: a prop in React, an attribute in HTML. Values that aren't listed fall back to the default. The form control label has its own options.
sections.title: Options

sections.body: These props set the content and behavior. They aren't options, because HTML writes them as markup.
sections.title: Content and behavior

sections.body:
- **HTML:** the input fires the native `change` event when the user toggles it. A parent's `change` updates its children without firing their `change` events. There are no instance methods.
- **React:** `onChange(checked)` is called with the new state.

sections.body: The checkbox is a native input, so the browser provides the keyboard behavior.
sections.title: Keyboard

sections.body:
- Every checkbox needs a name: a form control label, or `aria-label` / `aria-labelledby` on the input.
- The mixed state sets the input's `indeterminate`, so screen readers announce "mixed". A parent lists its children in `aria-controls`.
- Focus is shown with a 2px ring inside the target. The target is at least 36 × 36px.
- The unchecked box uses the secondary text color, with a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1. Brand colors of checked boxes follow the design, so light colors such as `warning` are below 3:1 on white.
- Group related checkboxes under a heading or a `<fieldset>` with a `<legend>`.

sections.body: A chip is a compact element for an attribute, a filter, a choice or a small action, such as a tag on a post or an active filter. A chip can show an avatar or an icon, be clickable, and have a delete button.
sections.html: Design
sections.title: Overview

sections.body: A clickable chip is a button: pass `onClick` in React, or use a `<button data-ok-chip-action>` in HTML. Pass `onDelete` to add a delete button; Backspace or Delete on the focused chip deletes it too. In HTML, the delete button fires a cancelable `ok:chip:delete` event, then the script hides the chip. In React, remove the chip from your state in `onDelete`.
sections.title: Make a chip clickable or deletable

sections.body: The variant is `filled` (default), `outlined` or `soft`. Colors are `default` (neutral), the palette colors, `black` and `white`. The `small` size is 24px high, for dense lists such as table cells.
sections.html: …
sections.react: <Chip variant="outlined" color="info" size="small" avatar={<Avatar>M</Avatar>} label="Mia" />

sections.body: Every option works the same way in both versions: a prop in React, an attribute in HTML. Values that aren't listed fall back to the default.
sections.title: Options

sections.body: These props set the content and behavior. They aren't options, because HTML writes them as markup.
sections.title: Content and behavior

sections.body:
- **`ok:chip:delete`** (cancelable) fires when the delete button is pressed, or Backspace / Delete is pressed on the chip's button. If you don't call `preventDefault()`, the chip is then hidden.
- **Instance:** `runtime.get(element, "chip")` returns `{ delete() }`.
- **React:** `onDelete()` and `onClick(event)`.
sections.title: Events and methods

sections.body: Clickable chips and delete buttons are native buttons.
sections.title: Keyboard

sections.body:
- The label names a clickable chip. Name each delete button with what it removes, such as "Remove Paris" (React: `deleteLabel`, default "Remove").
- The chip's button and its delete button are two tab stops, so keyboard users can reach both.
- Focus is shown with a 2px outline. The delete button's target is 24 × 24px.
- Neutral chips meet a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1, and soft chips use the accessible text tone. Filled and outlined brand colors follow the design.

sections.body:
A circular progress indicator shows that something is happening. Use the **indeterminate** variant while you can't tell how long a task takes, such as loading data. Use the **determinate** variant when you know how far the task has got, such as an upload.

Each indicator is a `progressbar` for assistive technology. Give it a name that says what is loading.
sections.title: Overview

sections.body: Set `variant` to `determinate` and pass `value`, from `min` (default 0) to `max` (default 100). In HTML, the value is the `aria-valuenow` attribute: change it, and the runtime redraws the arc. Values outside the range are clamped.
sections.title: Show how far a task has got

sections.body: The default color is `primary`. Use another palette color, such as `success` or `error`, to match the context. Use `inherit` to take the text color of the surrounding element, for example inside a button.
sections.react: <CircularProgress color="inherit" aria-label="Loading" />
sections.title: Choose a color

sections.body: The default size is 40px. Set `size` to a number of pixels, or to a CSS length in `px`, `rem` or `em` so the indicator scales with the text. `thickness` sets the stroke width, as a fraction of 44 units of the size (default 3.6). Set `enableTrackSlot` to draw a faint full circle behind the arc.
sections.react:
<CircularProgress
  variant="determinate"
  value={70}
  size="3rem"
  thickness={5}
  enableTrackSlot
  aria-label="Storage used"
/>
sections.title: Change the size and thickness

sections.body: Put the value next to the indicator when people need the exact number. Keep the text outside the indicator, and point `aria-labelledby` or `aria-describedby` at it if it names the task.
sections.html: 45%
sections.react: 45%
sections.title: Show the value as text

sections.body: If a task usually finishes in less than a second, wait about a second before showing the indicator. Fast tasks then don't flash a spinner. Under heavy load on the main thread, the shrinking arc can stutter: set `disableShrink` to keep a fixed arc that only spins.
sections.react: <CircularProgress disableShrink aria-label="Loading" />
sections.title: Avoid flashing for fast tasks

sections.body: Every option works the same way in both versions: a prop in React, an attribute in HTML. Values that aren't listed or aren't valid numbers fall back to the default.
sections.title: Options

sections.body: These props name the indicator. They aren't options, because HTML writes them as markup.
sections.title: Content and behavior

sections.body:
- **HTML:** there are no events or instance methods. Change `aria-valuenow`, `aria-valuemin`, `aria-valuemax`, `data-ok-size` or `data-ok-thickness`, and the runtime redraws the indicator. It writes private CSS custom properties through the CSS object model, so it works under a strict Content Security Policy.
- **React:** render with a new `value`. The size and the arc are set with the `style` prop. On server-rendered pages with a Content Security Policy that blocks inline styles, the determinate arc and custom sizes appear once the page hydrates.
sections.title: Events and methods

sections.body: Progress indicators don't take focus and have no keyboard interaction.
sections.title: Keyboard

sections.body:
- Each indicator has `role="progressbar"`. Name it with `aria-label` or `aria-labelledby`.
- Determinate indicators report their value with `aria-valuenow`, `aria-valuemin` and `aria-valuemax`. For values that aren't percentages, such as "Step 3 of 5", add `aria-valuetext`.
- When an indicator stands for a region that is loading, set `aria-busy="true"` on that region until it's ready, and point the region's `aria-describedby` at the indicator.
- With reduced motion turned on, the arc stops shrinking and spins slowly, so activity stays visible.
- Brand colors follow the design. Light colors such as `warning` have a contrast ratio below 3:1 on white, so don't rely on the indicator alone to tell people something important.
