sections.body:
The code editor lets people write and read source code with syntax highlighting, completion, error markers, find and replace, and a diff view. It is built on Monaco, the editor of Visual Studio Code, so both versions share the same engine and markup. A frame holds the editor, a loading message and a text area with the value.

Monaco is large, so the code editor is a separate script and Monaco itself loads only when an editor appears. Load `owlky-code-editor.js` after `owlky.js`: it loads Monaco from the `monaco/` folder next to it. With a bundler, import `@owlky/html/code-editor` or use the React components, and Monaco becomes a separate chunk of your app.
sections.html: Loading...
sections.title: Overview

sections.body:
In React, use `defaultValue` for the first value, or `value` and `onChange` to control it. A new `value` replaces the content as one step that people can undo, and it doesn't call `onChange`. The editor keeps what people type even when you ignore `onChange`, because Monaco can't hold back keystrokes.

In HTML, the text area holds the value. It is the editor while JavaScript loads or when Monaco can't load, and its value follows the editor, so a `name` on it sends the code with a form. Listen to `ok:code-editor:change` and call `setValue()` on the instance to replace the value.
sections.html: Loading...
sections.title: Read and set the value

sections.body:
Each `path` is its own model: a file with its text, language, undo history and cursor. Change `path` to switch files. The editor creates a model the first time it sees a path, from `defaultValue` and `defaultLanguage`, and keeps it when you switch back. Turn off `saveViewState` to forget the cursor and scroll position of each file, and turn on `keepCurrentModel` to keep the model when the editor goes away.

In HTML, put each file's first text in a `<template data-ok-code-editor-model>` with its `data-ok-path` and `data-ok-language`, then change `data-ok-path` on the editor.
sections.html: Loading...
sections.title: Edit several files

sections.body: The diff editor shows an original and a modified text side by side, with the changes highlighted. People can edit the modified side. Set `original` and `modified`, a `language` for both or `originalLanguage` and `modifiedLanguage`, and model paths when the texts are files. Set the option `renderSideBySide` to `false` for one column, for example on narrow screens.
sections.html: Loading...
sections.title: Compare two versions

sections.body: JSON, CSS, HTML, JavaScript and TypeScript are checked as people type, and the editor underlines the problems. `onValidate` receives the current model's markers after every check, for example to list them or to block saving. In HTML, listen to `ok:code-editor:validate`. Other languages get markers only when you add them with `monaco.editor.setModelMarkers()`.
sections.html:
<script type="module">
  const editor = document.querySelector("[data-ok-code-editor]");
  editor.addEventListener("ok:code-editor:validate", (event) => {
    for (const marker of event.detail.markers) {
      console.log(marker.startLineNumber, marker.message);
    }
  });
</script>
sections.title: Show problems

sections.body:
Everything Monaco offers stays available. `beforeMount` receives the Monaco API before the editor exists, which is the place to register languages, completion providers and themes. `onMount` receives the editor itself, and `useMonaco()` returns the Monaco API anywhere in React once it has loaded. Pass Monaco's editor settings in `options`, such as `minimap`, `wordWrap` or `readOnly`; in HTML, write them as JSON in `data-ok-options`.

In HTML, listen to `ok:code-editor:beforemount` and `ok:code-editor:mount`, or register the editor yourself with `createCodeEditor({ beforeMount, onMount })`.
sections.html: …
sections.title: Use Monaco directly

sections.body:
With the default `theme` of `auto`, the editor uses Owlky's light or dark theme, whichever its scope uses through `data-ok-theme`. The colors come from your tokens and presets: the paper background, the text colors, and syntax colors that keep a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1. The editor follows when the theme or preset changes.

Monaco shows one theme on a page at a time. When editors sit in scopes with different themes, the editor that people used last decides. Set `theme` to a Monaco theme such as `vs-dark` or `hc-black`, or to a theme you define in `beforeMount`, to use it instead.
sections.html:
…
…
sections.title: Match the theme

sections.body:
Owlky never loads Monaco from another site. `owlky-code-editor.js` loads it from the `monaco/` folder next to itself. To serve that folder somewhere else, copy `@owlky/html/dist/monaco/` to your server and set `data-ok-monaco-path` on the script. The folder must be on the same origin as the page, because browsers run web workers only from there.

With a bundler, Monaco is imported from the `monaco-editor` package. If your bundler doesn't find Monaco's workers by itself, pass them to `loader.config({ getWorker })`. `loader.config()` also takes `paths.vs` for your own copy of the `monaco/` folder, a `monaco` instance you already imported, and the UI language. Call it before the first editor appears.

Until Monaco is ready, the frame shows `loading` (default "Loading..."). If Monaco can't load, the text area comes back so that people can still edit the value, and `onError` or `ok:code-editor:error` reports the reason.
sections.html:
<!-- Your own copy of the monaco/ folder, in German -->
<script src="/assets/owlky-code-editor.js" data-ok-monaco-path="/assets/monaco/" defer></script>

<script type="module">
  // With a bundler: import "@owlky/html/code-editor" instead
  import { loader } from "@owlky/html/code-editor";

  loader.config({ paths: { vs: "/assets/monaco/" }, "vs/nls": { availableLanguages: { "*": "de" } } });
</script>
sections.title: Host Monaco and set up loading

sections.body:
Owlky's own code sets styles only through the CSS object model and creates no HTML from strings. Monaco needs more than the rest of Owlky, so pages with a content security policy allow it for code editor pages:

- **Styles:** `style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'`, because Monaco writes its theme and decorations into `<style>` elements.
- **Fonts and images:** `font-src 'self' data:` and `img-src 'self' data:`, because Monaco's style sheet embeds its icon font.
- **Workers:** `worker-src 'self'`.
- **Trusted Types:** the policies `owlky-code-editor`, `defaultWorkerFactory`, `diffEditorWidget`, `diffReview`, `domLineBreaksComputer`, `editorGhostText`, `editorViewLayer`, `richScreenReaderContent`, `standaloneColorizer`, `stickyScrollViewLayer`, `tokenizeToString` and `dompurify`, with `'allow-duplicates'`. The `owlky-code-editor` policy accepts only worker files from the `monaco/` folder.
sections.html: <meta http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy" content="default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'; font-src 'self' data:; img-src 'self' data:; worker-src 'self'; require-trusted-types-for 'script'; trusted-types owlky-code-editor defaultWorkerFactory diffEditorWidget diffReview domLineBreaksComputer editorGhostText editorViewLayer richScreenReaderContent standaloneColorizer stickyScrollViewLayer tokenizeToString dompurify 'allow-duplicates'">
sections.title: Set up a content security policy

sections.body: Every option works the same way in both versions: a prop in React, an attribute in HTML. The first table is the code editor, the second the diff editor.
sections.title: Options

sections.body: These props set the content, the loading message and Monaco itself. They aren't options, because HTML writes them as markup or passes them in JavaScript.
sections.title: Content and behavior

sections.body:
- **`ok:code-editor:change`** fires after every edit, with `detail.value` and Monaco's `detail.event` (`null` when people type in the text area because Monaco couldn't load).
- **`ok:code-editor:validate`** fires when the current model's markers change, with `detail.markers`.
- **`ok:code-editor:beforemount`** and **`ok:code-editor:mount`** fire with `detail.monaco` (and `detail.editor`) before and after Monaco creates the editor. The diff editor fires `ok:diff-editor:beforemount` and `ok:diff-editor:mount`.
- **`ok:code-editor:error`** and **`ok:diff-editor:error`** fire when Monaco can't load, with `detail.error`.
- **Instance:** `runtime.get(element, "code-editor")` returns `{ status, value, setValue(value), updateOptions(options), focus(), editor, monaco }`. The diff editor's instance has `original`, `modified`, `setOriginal()`, `setModified()` and `updateOptions()`.
- **React:** `onChange(value, event)`, `onValidate(markers)`, `beforeMount(monaco)`, `onMount(editor, monaco)` and `onError(error)`.
sections.title: Events and methods

sections.body: The editor uses the keyboard shortcuts of Visual Studio Code. Tab indents the code, so it doesn't leave the editor until you switch Tab to move focus. On macOS, use Command instead of Ctrl where the table says Ctrl.
sections.title: Keyboard

sections.body:
- Name the editor with `aria-label` in React (default "Code editor"), or with an `aria-label` on the text area in HTML. Monaco uses that name for its text box.
- Tab inserts a tab character. Press **Ctrl+M** (macOS: **Ctrl+Shift+M**) to make Tab and Shift+Tab move focus out of the editor, and again to switch back. Tell people about it near the editor, or set the option `tabFocusMode`.
- Press **Alt+F1** (macOS: **Option+F1**) for Monaco's accessibility help. Screen readers are detected automatically; set the option `accessibilitySupport` to `"on"` to turn the screen reader mode on yourself.
- The loading message is a status that screen readers announce, and the text area keeps the value editable when Monaco can't load.
- Syntax colors keep a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 with the editor background in Owlky's themes.
sections.title: Accessibility

sections.body: A collapse shows or hides its content by animating its height from 0 to the height of the content. Use it for content that opens in place, such as a nested list, the details of a row or an advanced section of a form. The element carries `hidden` while it is closed, so the content is hidden even before JavaScript runs. In the example, the switch opens four collapses: two animate their height and two their width, with and without a collapsed size.
sections.html: Shipping takes two to four working days.
sections.title: Overview

sections.body:
A collapse is open while it has no `hidden` attribute. Change that state, and the collapse animates to it.

- **HTML:** give a checkbox or a switch `data-ok-collapse-toggle` with the collapse's `id`: the collapse is open while the box is checked. On a button, the attribute toggles the collapse and keeps `aria-expanded` on the button up to date. One trigger can name several collapses, separated by spaces. You can also call `show()`, `hide()` or `toggle()` on the instance, or set `hidden` yourself.
- **React:** set `in` from your state. Give the button that opens it `aria-expanded` and `aria-controls` with the collapse's `id`.
sections.html: Proxy, cache and logging settings.
sections.title: Open and close a collapse

sections.body: Set `orientation` to `horizontal` to animate the width instead of the height. Its children sit in a row and keep their width while it animates. Set `collapsedSize` to keep part of the content visible while the collapse is closed, such as the first 40px of a long text. It takes a number in pixels or a CSS length, such as `2.5rem`. Content in the visible part stays reachable, so don't hide controls there.
sections.html:
The first lines of the article stay visible while the collapse is closed.

Filters
sections.title: Collapse horizontally or to a size

sections.body: By default, a collapse animates over 300 ms (`--ok-duration-standard`) with the standard easing (`--ok-easing-standard`). Set `timeout` to a number of milliseconds, or to `auto` to derive the duration from the distance: about 300 ms for 120px and longer for tall content. Set `easing` to any CSS easing, such as `var(--ok-easing-decelerate)`. In React, `timeout` and `easing` also take `{ enter, exit }`; in HTML, add `data-ok-timeout-exit` and `data-ok-easing-exit`. When people turn on reduced motion in their system settings, a collapse opens and closes at once. Set `disablePrefersReducedMotion` only for an animation that carries meaning.
sections.html: Answers open with a duration that follows their height.
sections.title: Set the duration and the easing

sections.body: A collapse can be another element instead of a `div`, so it adds no wrapper. In React, pass the element or the component in `component`, along with that component's props. In HTML, add `data-ok-collapse` to the element itself. Lists use it for nested lists, tree views for the groups of child items, and vertical steppers for the content of each step. Put padding and borders on a child of the collapse, not on the collapse itself: they stay visible while it is closed. In React, `mountOnEnter` renders the children only once the collapse first opens, and `unmountOnExit` removes them once it has closed.
sections.html: • Starred
sections.title: Collapse another component

sections.body: Every option works the same way in both versions: a prop in React, an attribute in HTML. Values that aren't listed fall back to the default.
sections.title: Options

sections.body: These props set the content, the timing and the rendering. Some are React only, because HTML writes them as markup.
sections.title: Content and behavior

sections.body:
- **`ok:collapse:enter`**, **`ok:collapse:entering`** and **`ok:collapse:entered`** fire on the collapse as it opens: before the animation, when it starts and when it ends.
- **`ok:collapse:exit`**, **`ok:collapse:exiting`** and **`ok:collapse:exited`** fire the same way as it closes. `detail.in` tells whether it is open.
- **Instance:** `runtime.get(element, "collapse")` returns `{ in, status, show(), hide(), toggle(force?) }`. `status` is `entering`, `entered`, `exiting` or `exited`.
- **React:** `onEnter`, `onEntering`, `onEntered`, `onExit`, `onExiting` and `onExited` get the element.
sections.title: Events and methods

sections.body: A collapse has no keyboard interaction. The button or switch that opens it handles the keys: Enter and Space on a button, Space on a switch.
sections.title: Keyboard

sections.body:
- A closed collapse carries `hidden`, so screen readers skip its content and Tab doesn't reach it. A collapsed size is the exception: the visible part stays reachable.
- Give the button that opens a collapse `aria-expanded` and `aria-controls` with the collapse's `id`. The HTML trigger keeps `aria-expanded` up to date on buttons.
- The animation honors the reduced motion setting: the collapse opens and closes at once.
- When content opens below the button, focus stays on the button. Move focus into the content only when people asked for it, such as after a search.
sections.title: Accessibility

sections.body: A data grid shows rows of data in columns. People can sort a column, search and filter the rows, page through them, select rows with checkboxes, choose the columns and the row height, and download the rows as CSV. It follows the ARIA grid pattern: one Tab stop, and the arrow keys move between cells. Use the Table component instead for a static table without these features.
sections.html: …
sections.title: Overview

sections.body:
Each column has a `field` and a `headerName`. Its `type` (`string`, `number`, `date`, `dateTime`, `boolean`, `singleSelect` or `actions`) decides how it sorts, which filter operators it offers and its alignment: numbers align right.
- **Width:** `width` in pixels (100 by default), or `flex` to share the free width, with `minWidth` as a floor.
- **Values:** `valueGetter` computes a value from the row, and `valueFormatter` turns it into the text that the cell shows, the search finds and the export writes.
- **Custom cells:** `renderCell` draws anything, such as an avatar or a rating. In HTML, write that markup in the cell, and put the raw value in `data-ok-value` so sorting and filtering use it.
sections.html: 30
sections.react: { field: "age", headerName: "Age", type: "number", valueFormatter: (value) => `${value} years` }
sections.title: Describe the columns

sections.body: `showToolbar` adds a search field and buttons that open the column list, the filter panel, the row height menu and the export menu. Search matches every word you type in any column. Export downloads a CSV file or prints the grid as shown. Each feature can be turned off, for example with `disableColumnFilter`.
sections.html: …
sections.react: <DataGrid aria-label="People" rows={rows} columns={columns} showToolbar disableDensitySelector />
sections.title: Add a toolbar

sections.body: Every state works controlled or uncontrolled, as in MUI X: `sortModel`, `filterModel`, `paginationModel`, `rowSelectionModel`, `columnVisibilityModel` and `density`, each with its `on…Change` callback, or `initialState` for the starting values. Shift + click on a header adds a column to the sort.
sections.html: <!-- HTML keeps the state in the page: listen to ok:data-grid:* events (see Events and methods). -->
sections.react:
const [sortModel, setSortModel] = useState<GridSortModel>([{ field: "age", sort: "desc" }]);

<DataGrid aria-label="People" rows={rows} columns={columns} sortModel={sortModel} onSortModelChange={setSortModel} />
sections.title: Control sorting, filtering, pages and selection

sections.body: **Add filter** in the filter panel adds another condition. From the second row, choose **And** (every condition must match, the default) or **Or** (any one is enough). The remove button deletes a condition. Set `disableMultipleColumnsFiltering` to keep a single condition.
sections.html: <!-- The filter panel's Add filter button copies the first row, with an And / Or field. -->
sections.react:
<DataGrid
  aria-label="People"
  rows={rows}
  columns={columns}
  filterModel={{
    logicOperator: "or",
    items: [
      { field: "age", operator: "<", value: "20" },
      { field: "age", operator: ">", value: "60" },
    ],
  }}
/>
sections.title: Combine filters

sections.body:
- **Resize:** drag the end edge of a header, or press Alt + Left or Alt + Right on a focused header. A column never gets narrower than its `minWidth`. Set `resizable: false` on a column, or `disableColumnResize` on the grid, to turn it off.
- **Move:** drag a header onto another one, or choose **Move left** or **Move right** in the column menu. `columnOrder` and `onColumnOrderChange` control the order.
- **Pin:** choose **Pin to left** or **Pin to right** in the column menu. Pinned columns stay in view while the others scroll. Use `pinnedColumns` to pin columns from the start.
sections.html: …
sections.react:
<DataGrid
  aria-label="Employees"
  rows={rows}
  columns={columns}
  initialState={{ pinnedColumns: { left: ["firstName"], right: ["actions"] } }}
/>
sections.title: Resize, move and pin columns

sections.body: Set `editable` on a column to let people change its cells: double-click a cell, or press Enter or F2. The field matches the column type: text, a number, a date, a list for `singleSelect` or a checkbox for `boolean`. Enter saves, Escape cancels, and leaving the cell saves. With `editMode="row"`, every editable cell of the row opens together. In React, `processRowUpdate` receives the new row: return it, or return a changed row. Throw or reject to refuse it. In HTML, listen to `ok:data-grid:edit` and call `preventDefault()` to refuse.
sections.html:
<script>
  // Refuse ages above 120
  grid.addEventListener("ok:data-grid:edit", (event) => {
    if (event.detail.row.age > 120) event.preventDefault();
  });
</script>
sections.react:
<DataGrid
  aria-label="Employees"
  rows={rows}
  columns={[{ field: "age", headerName: "Age", type: "number", editable: true }]}
  processRowUpdate={async (row) => saveEmployee(row)}
/>
sections.title: Edit cells and rows

sections.body: The grid renders only the rows that are in view, plus a few above and below, so thousands of rows scroll smoothly. This works when the grid has a fixed height, such as `height: 520px` on the root: a grid that grows with its rows shows all of them. Set `disableVirtualization` to render every row of the page, for example before printing the page with the browser. To load more rows as people scroll, listen for the end of the rows. It's reported once for each number of rows, within `scrollEndThreshold` pixels (80 by default). Show `loading` while the next rows arrive.
sections.html: …
sections.title: Show large datasets

sections.body: A data source lets the server sort, filter and page the rows. The grid calls `getRows()` with the sort model, the filter model and the page, and shows the rows it returns. `rowCount` is the total number of rows on the server, for the pagination. Responses are kept in a cache, so going back to a page doesn't ask the server again. Pass `dataSourceCache={null}` to turn the cache off. Errors go to `onDataSourceError` in React and to `ok:data-grid:datasourceerror` in HTML. To handle the requests yourself, set `sortingMode`, `filterMode` and `paginationMode` to `"server"`, pass `rowCount`, and load the rows in the change callbacks. While data loads, `loadingVariant` picks a progress bar, a spinner or placeholder rows (`"skeleton"`).
sections.html:
<script type="module">
  const element = document.getElementById("customers");
  const grid = window.Owlky.get(element, "data-grid");
  grid.setDataSource({
    // params: { sortModel, filterModel, paginationModel: { page, pageSize } }
    async getRows(params) {
      const response = await fetch("/api/customers", {
        method: "POST",
        body: JSON.stringify(params),
      });
      return response.json(); // { rows, rowCount }
    },
  });
</script>
sections.title: Load rows from a server

sections.body: In HTML, the grid can build its rows from data instead of markup. Put one row inside `<template data-ok-data-grid-row>` in the grid: `setRows(rows)` copies it for each item, sets `data-ok-row-id` from `id`, and fills each cell with the value of its field as text. For cells with more than text, add `<template data-ok-data-grid-cell="<field>">`: its elements marked `data-ok-data-grid-value` receive the value. Values are always set as text, never as markup, so data from a server can't add scripts to the page.
sections.html: …
sections.title: Build HTML rows from data

sections.body: With `checkboxSelection`, people select rows with checkboxes, a click on the row, Space and Ctrl + A. Set `disableMultipleRowSelection` to allow one row at a time: selecting a row clears the others, and the header has no **Select all** checkbox. To keep some rows from being selected, return `false` from `isRowSelectable` in React, or put `data-ok-selectable="false"` on the row in HTML. Their checkbox is disabled. `checkboxSelectionVisibleOnly` makes **Select all** select the current page only. When rows go away, their ids leave the selection, unless you set `keepNonExistentRowsSelected`. Use it with server pagination, where the rows of other pages aren't loaded.
sections.html:
…
…
sections.react:
<DataGrid
  aria-label="Tasks"
  rows={tasks}
  columns={columns}
  checkboxSelection
  disableMultipleRowSelection
  isRowSelectable={({ row }) => row.status !== "Done"}
/>
sections.title: Choose how rows are selected

sections.body: A cell can cover the next columns with `colSpan` on its column: a number, or a function of the cell, such as a total that spans three columns. With `rowSpanning`, neighbouring cells of a column with the same text merge into one tall cell. Rows are 52 pixels tall by default. Change it with `rowHeight`; the density still scales it. In React, `getRowHeight` sets the height of each row: a number, or `"auto"` to let long text wrap and the row grow. `getRowSpacing` adds space above and below rows. In HTML, put `data-ok-row-height` and `data-ok-spacing-top` / `data-ok-spacing-bottom` on the rows. Columns can fit their content: double-click the edge of a header, set `autosizeOnMount`, or call `autosizeColumns()`.
sections.html:
Total
…
sections.react:
<DataGrid
  aria-label="Budget"
  rows={lines}
  columns={[
    { field: "region", headerName: "Region", colSpan: ({ row }) => (row.id === "total" ? 3 : 1) },
    { field: "team", headerName: "Team" },
    { field: "item", headerName: "Item" },
    { field: "amount", headerName: "Amount", type: "number" },
  ]}
  rowSpanning
  getRowHeight={({ model }) => (model.notes.length > 40 ? "auto" : null)}
/>
sections.title: Span cells and size rows

sections.body: React has `onRowClick`, `onRowDoubleClick`, `onCellClick`, `onCellDoubleClick`, `onCellKeyDown` and `onColumnHeaderClick`. In HTML, the same events fire on the grid as `ok:data-grid:rowclick`, `ok:data-grid:cellclick` and so on. The grid's methods are the same in both versions: pass a ref from `useGridApiRef()` as `apiRef` in React, or call `runtime.get(element, "data-grid")` in HTML. For example, `exportState()` returns the sort, filters, page, columns and density, and `restoreState()` applies them again. `restoreState()` checks what it receives, so a state from storage or a URL can't change anything else.
sections.html:
<script type="module">
  const element = document.getElementById("people");
  const grid = window.Owlky.get(element, "data-grid");
  // Save the state as people change it, and restore it on the next visit
  grid.restoreState(JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem("people-grid") ?? "{}"));
  element.addEventListener("ok:data-grid:sort", () =>
    queueMicrotask(() => localStorage.setItem("people-grid", JSON.stringify(grid.exportState()))),
  );
</script>
sections.title: React to clicks and use the grid's methods

sections.body: Check a value while people type it, and keep the cell open until it's valid. In React, return `{ error }` from the column's `preProcessEditCellProps`: `true` marks the field as invalid, and a text also shows as a message under the cell. In HTML, listen to `ok:data-grid:validate` and set `event.detail.error`. Enter and leaving the cell keep it open while the value has an error. Escape cancels. `isCellEditable` in React, or `data-ok-editable="false"` on a cell in HTML, makes single cells read-only. Typing a character on an editable cell starts editing with that character.
sections.html:
<script type="module">
  const element = document.getElementById("products");
  element.addEventListener("ok:data-grid:validate", (event) => {
    const { field, value } = event.detail;
    if (field === "price" && !(Number(value) > 0)) event.detail.error = "Enter a price above 0";
  });
</script>
sections.title: Check edited values

sections.body: The **is any of** operator keeps rows whose value is one of several values: type them separated by commas. A column's `filterOperators` replaces the operators of its type, for example with a range. Each operator returns a test for a value. In HTML, set them with `setFilterOperators(field, operators)`. Set `ignoreDiacritics` so that searches and filters ignore accents: "ha noi" finds "Hà Nội". `quickFilterLogicOperator="or"` keeps rows that match any word instead of every word. `quickFilterExcludeHiddenColumns` leaves hidden columns out of the search. To leave one column out, set its `getApplyQuickFilterFn` to `null` in React, or `data-ok-searchable="false"` on its header in HTML.
sections.html: …
sections.react:
<DataGrid
  aria-label="Places"
  rows={places}
  columns={columns}
  ignoreDiacritics
  quickFilterLogicOperator="or"
/>
sections.title: Tune filtering and search

sections.body: **Download as CSV** exports the filtered, sorted rows of every page and the shown columns. `csvOptions` changes the delimiter, the columns (`fields`, `allColumns`), the header line and the file name. **Print** prints every filtered row on its own page, without the toolbar, footer and checkboxes. `printOptions` keeps them or picks the columns. In HTML, pass the same options to `exportCsv(options)` and `print(options)`. Values in an HTML column can be formatted with `data-ok-format` on its header (`number`, `currency`, `percent`, `date` or `datetime`) and `Intl` options in `data-ok-format-options`, or with `setValueFormatter(field, format)`.
sections.html: …
sections.react:
<DataGrid
  aria-label="Products"
  rows={rows}
  columns={columns}
  showToolbar
  csvOptions={{ delimiter: ";", fileName: "products" }}
  printOptions={{ hideFooter: false }}
/>
sections.title: Export and print

sections.body: Locale packs translate every label: `enUS`, `viVN`, `frFR`, `deDE`, `esES`, `jaJP` and `zhCN`. Import the one you need. Pass it as `localeText` in React. In HTML, write the toolbar and menus in your language, and call `setLocaleText(pack)` for the text the grid writes itself, such as filter operators, empty states and the page range. With `dir="rtl"` on the page or a parent, the grid lays out right to left: columns pinned to the left stay at the start, which is the right side. The arrow keys follow the reading order. Set `toolbarVariant="icon"` to show the toolbar as icon buttons with tooltips.
sections.html:
<script type="module">
  import { viVN } from "@owlky/core";
  window.Owlky.get(document.getElementById("people"), "data-grid").setLocaleText(viVN);
</script>
sections.react:
import { viVN } from "@owlky/core";

<DataGrid aria-label="Danh sách" rows={rows} columns={columns} localeText={viVN} />
sections.title: Translate the grid and lay it out right to left

sections.body: Set `treeData` and return each row's path from `getTreeDataPath`: the names of its ancestors, then its own. Parents that a path names without a row of their own get a generated row. A group column shows the names with a button that opens and closes the children. Right and Left open and close a row when its group cell has the focus. `defaultGroupingExpansionDepth` sets how many levels are open at first. Filters keep the parents of the rows that match, and sorting orders rows among their siblings. In HTML, rows carry `aria-level` and `data-ok-parent`, and the grid fires `ok:data-grid:expand`. With a data source, `getChildrenCount` and `getGroupKey` let the grid load children when a row opens.
sections.html: …
sections.react:
<DataGrid
  aria-label="Team"
  rows={team}
  columns={columns}
  treeData
  getTreeDataPath={(row) => row.path}
  groupingColDef={{ headerName: "Name" }}
  defaultGroupingExpansionDepth={1}
/>
sections.title: Show rows as a tree

sections.body: `getDetailPanelContent` returns what shows under a row when people open it, or `null` for rows without details. A button in the first column opens and closes the panel. `getDetailPanelHeight` sets a height in pixels; by default the content decides. In HTML, put each row's content in a `<template data-ok-data-grid-detail="<row id>">` inside the grid. The grid copies it when the panel opens and fires `ok:data-grid:detailpanel`.
sections.react:
<DataGrid
  aria-label="Orders"
  rows={orders}
  columns={columns}
  getDetailPanelContent={({ row }) => <OrderLines order={row} />}
/>
sections.title: Show details under a row

sections.body: With `rowReordering`, each row gets a handle: drag it onto another row, or press Alt + Up or Alt + Down on it. A screen reader hears the new position. Moving is off while the rows are sorted or filtered. React reports moves with `onRowOrderChange`; HTML fires `ok:data-grid:roworder`, which you can cancel. `pinnedRows` keeps rows above or below the others while they scroll. Pinned rows aren't sorted, filtered or paged. In HTML, put them in `<div role="rowgroup" data-ok-data-grid-pinned-rows="top">` (or `bottom`).
sections.react:
<DataGrid
  aria-label="Agenda"
  rows={items}
  columns={columns}
  rowReordering
  onRowOrderChange={({ oldIndex, targetIndex }) => save(oldIndex, targetIndex)}
  pinnedRows={{ top: [welcome], bottom: [questions] }}
/>
sections.title: Move and pin rows

sections.body: `columnGroupingModel` puts headers over groups of columns, on as many levels as you need. A group's `description` shows as its tooltip. When a column is hidden or moved, its group splits around it. Columns can't move out of their group. `listView` shows each row as one cell, such as a card on a small screen. `listViewColumn` says which field it shows, and `renderCell` builds its content. The headers and the other cells are hidden in list view.
sections.react:
<DataGrid
  aria-label="Contacts"
  rows={contacts}
  columns={columns}
  columnGroupingModel={[
    { groupId: "person", headerName: "Person", children: [{ field: "firstName" }, { field: "lastName" }] },
    { groupId: "contact", headerName: "Contact", children: [{ field: "email" }] },
  ]}
/>
sections.title: Group column headers and show a list

sections.body: With `lazyLoading` and a data source, the grid asks for the rows that come into view, 50 at a time. Rows that haven't arrived show as placeholders. The data source answers `start` and `end`, and returns the total in `rowCount`. `lazyLoadingRequestThrottleMs` spaces the requests. Wide grids also render only the columns in view, when the columns have fixed widths. `rowBufferPx` and `columnBufferPx` set how much renders beyond the visible area. A data source's `updateRow` saves edited rows. Its answer is shown, and a failure brings the old values back. The cache keeps answers for five minutes, or for the `ttl` you pass to `createGridDataSourceCache`.
sections.html: …
sections.react: <DataGrid aria-label="Customers" rows={[]} columns={columns} dataSource={customers} lazyLoading />
sections.title: Load rows as they scroll into view

sections.body: `rowGroupingModel` lists the fields that group the rows, outermost first. The grid adds a row for each group, with the group's name, its number of rows and a button that opens it. People group and ungroup columns from the column menu. `aggregationModel` gives fields a function: `sum`, `avg` (rounded to two decimals), `min`, `max` or `size` (the number of rows). Group rows show their values, and a footer row shows the values of every filtered row. The column menu offers the functions that fit each column's type, and the header names the function in use. Sorting an aggregated column orders the groups by their values. Sorting a grouped column orders them by name. With a data source, the grid passes `groupFields` and `groupKeys`, and the server returns the groups of each level. In HTML, the models are the attributes `data-ok-row-grouping-model` and `data-ok-aggregation-model` (JSON), and the grid builds the group rows from the rows in the markup. In tree data, the grid adds a row for each parent that a path names without a row of its own.
sections.html: …
sections.react:
<DataGrid
  aria-label="Sales"
  rows={sales}
  columns={columns}
  initialState={{
    rowGrouping: { model: ["region"] },
    aggregation: { model: { units: "sum", revenue: "sum" } },
  }}
/>
sections.title: Group rows and aggregate values

sections.body: A pivot summarizes the rows in a new table. `pivotModel` names the fields whose values become rows (`rows`), the fields whose values become columns (`columns`) and the fields to aggregate with their function (`values`). Set `pivotActive` to show it. The **Pivot** button in the toolbar opens a panel with a switch and, for each column, its place and function. Filters work on the rows before the pivot. Exports keep the rows and columns of the data. In HTML, put the model in `data-ok-pivot-model` and add `data-ok-pivot-active`. The grid builds the pivot from the rows in the markup and fires `ok:data-grid:pivot`, which you can cancel.
sections.html: …
sections.react:
<DataGrid
  aria-label="Revenue by region and year"
  rows={sales}
  columns={columns}
  showToolbar
  initialState={{
    pivoting: {
      active: true,
      model: {
        rows: [{ field: "region" }],
        columns: [{ field: "year" }],
        values: [{ field: "revenue", aggFunc: "sum" }],
      },
    },
  }}
/>
sections.title: Pivot the rows

sections.body: With `cellSelection`, people select cells in ranges: press a cell and drag, press another cell with Shift, or hold Shift and use the arrow keys. Ctrl or Cmd adds a range, or toggles one cell. Ctrl + A selects every cell of the page. Ctrl + C copies the selected cells as tab-separated text, which spreadsheets read. Without selected cells it copies the selected rows, or the focused cell. Ctrl + V pastes text into editable cells, from the selection's first cell or the focused cell. One copied value fills every selected cell. Each pasted row goes through `processRowUpdate` (HTML: a cancelable `ok:data-grid:edit`). `disableClipboardPaste` turns pasting off. The grid uses the browser's own copy and paste for these keys, so it never asks for clipboard permissions.
sections.html: …
sections.react:
<DataGrid
  aria-label="Inventory"
  rows={items}
  columns={columns}
  cellSelection
  processRowUpdate={(row) => save(row)}
/>
sections.title: Select cells and use the clipboard

sections.body: `headerFilters` adds a row of fields under the column headers. Each field filters its column with the column type's first operator, and shows that operator as its label: text contains, a number equals, a date is. Booleans and choices get a list, dates get a date picker, and date times (`dateTime` columns) get a date time picker. The fields and the filter panel share one filter model. Up and Down move from a field to the cells. Date and date time filters in the filter panel use the same pickers.
sections.react: <DataGrid aria-label="Inventory" rows={items} columns={columns} headerFilters />
sections.title: Filter from the headers

sections.body: The **Export** menu downloads the filtered, sorted rows as an Excel workbook. Numbers, booleans and dates keep their type, with a date format. Text is written as text, never as a formula, because exported data may come from users. `excelOptions` sets the file name, the sheet name, the fields and whether to include the headers. In React, `apiRef.current.getDataAsExcel()` returns the file's bytes. In HTML, use `toExcel()` and `exportExcel()`, or the attribute `data-ok-excel-options` (JSON).
sections.react:
<DataGrid
  aria-label="Sales"
  rows={sales}
  columns={columns}
  showToolbar
  excelOptions={{ fileName: "sales", sheetName: "2025" }}
/>
sections.title: Export to Excel

sections.body: With `chartsIntegration`, a chart follows the grid. `chartModel` sets its `type`, its `dimension` (the field that names the categories) and its `values` (number fields drawn as series). The types are `column`, `bar`, `line`, `area`, `pie`, `donut`, `radar` and `scatter`. When the rows are grouped, the chart shows the top-level groups with the aggregated values of the rows that pass the filters. Otherwise it shows the rows of the page. A scatter chart of rows whose category is a number column places each row at that number. The **Chart** button in the toolbar opens a panel to change the type, the category, the series, the stacking, the value labels and the legend. In HTML, the chart is a Chart component inside the grid, and the grid updates it through the chart's `updateSeries()` method.
sections.react:
<DataGrid
  aria-label="Sales"
  rows={sales}
  columns={columns}
  showToolbar
  chartsIntegration
  initialState={{
    rowGrouping: { model: ["product"] },
    chartsIntegration: { model: { type: "column", values: ["revenue"] } },
  }}
/>
sections.title: Chart the rows

sections.body:
The chart model also holds the chart's configuration. Each setting applies only to the types that use it.

- **`stacked`:** stacks the series of a column, bar, line or area chart. It needs two series or more.
- **`itemLabel`:** `"value"` prints the values on the chart, such as the percentages on pie slices.
- **`legend`:** places the legend at the `top`, `right` or `bottom`, or hides it with `none`. A chart with one series has no legend.
- **`colors`:** palette names or shades, such as `"info"` or `"primary-dark"`, for the series in order. Pie and donut charts use them for the slices.
- **`height`, `curve`, `showMark`, `seriesAxisLabel`, `showToolbar` and `animations`:** the plot height in pixels, the line shape, point markers, the value axis title, a toolbar with downloads and animated updates.
- **`startAngle`, `endAngle` and `donutSize`:** the angles of pie and donut slices, and the size of the donut hole in percent.

When the grid is pivoted, a value field of the pivot draws one series per pivot column, named by its keys. Grouping, filtering, pivoting and editing redraw the chart, so it always shows what the grid shows.
sections.html: …
sections.react:
<DataGrid
  aria-label="Revenue by region and product"
  rows={sales}
  columns={columns}
  showToolbar
  chartsIntegration
  initialState={{
    pivoting: {
      active: true,
      model: {
        rows: [{ field: "region" }],
        columns: [{ field: "product" }],
        values: [{ field: "revenue", aggFunc: "sum" }],
      },
    },
    chartsIntegration: {
      model: { type: "column", values: ["revenue"], stacked: true, legend: "bottom" },
    },
  }}
/>
sections.title: Configure the chart

sections.body: Every option works the same way in both versions: a prop in React, an attribute in HTML. Values that aren't listed fall back to the default.
sections.title: Options

sections.body: These props carry the data and the state. In HTML, the data is the markup and the state lives in the page.
sections.title: Content and behavior

sections.body:
- **`ok:data-grid:sort`**, **`ok:data-grid:filter`**, **`ok:data-grid:selection`**, **`ok:data-grid:columns`**, **`ok:data-grid:density`**, **`ok:data-grid:order`** and **`ok:data-grid:pinned`** fire on the grid with the new model in `detail.model`. They're cancelable.
- **`ok:data-grid:resize`** reports `detail.field` and `detail.width`. **`ok:data-grid:edit`** reports `detail.id` and the edited values in `detail.row`, and is cancelable.
- **Instance:** `runtime.get(element, "data-grid")` returns `{ sortModel, filterModel, selection, columnVisibilityModel, columnOrder, pinnedColumns, columnWidths }` with a setter for each (`setSortModel(model)`, `setColumnWidth(field, width)` and so on; setters fire no events), `toCsv()`, `exportCsv()`, `setRows(rows)` and `setDataSource(source)` (`null` stops it).
- **`ok:data-grid:rowclick`**, **`ok:data-grid:rowdoubleclick`**, **`ok:data-grid:cellclick`**, **`ok:data-grid:celldoubleclick`** and **`ok:data-grid:columnheaderclick`** report the row id, the field and the value. **`ok:data-grid:editstart`** and **`ok:data-grid:editstop`** report the cell and the reason. **`ok:data-grid:validate`** asks for an error in `detail.error`.
- **`ok:data-grid:expand`**, **`ok:data-grid:detailpanel`** and **`ok:data-grid:roworder`** report a row opening, a panel opening and a row moving. They're cancelable. `setRowChildrenExpansion(id, open)` and `toggleDetailPanel(id)` do the same from code.
- **More methods:** `print(options)`, `autosizeColumns(options)`, `scrollToIndexes({ rowIndex, colIndex })`, `exportState()`, `restoreState(state)`, `setFilterOperators(field, operators)`, `setValueFormatter(field, format)` and `setLocaleText(labels)`. `toCsv` and `exportCsv` take CSV options.
- **`ok:data-grid:rowgrouping`**, **`ok:data-grid:aggregation`**, **`ok:data-grid:cellselection`** and **`ok:data-grid:chart`** fire with the new model in `detail.model`. **`ok:data-grid:pivot`** reports `detail.model` and `detail.active`. They're cancelable. **`ok:data-grid:clipboardcopy`** reports the copied text in `detail.data`, and the cancelable **`ok:data-grid:clipboardpaste`** the pasted cells. The instance has `rowGroupingModel`, `aggregationModel`, `pivotModel`, `pivotActive`, `cellSelectionModel` and `chartModel` with their setters, `toExcel(options)` and `exportExcel(options)`.
- **`ok:data-grid:scrollend`** reports `detail.visibleRowsCount` when people scroll to the end of the rows. **`ok:data-grid:datasourceerror`** reports `detail.error` when a data source fails.
sections.title: Events and methods

sections.body: The grid is one Tab stop. Arrow keys move between the header and the cells.
sections.title: Keyboard

sections.body:
- Give the grid a name with `aria-label` or `aria-labelledby`.
- Sortable headers carry `aria-sort`, selected rows `aria-selected`, and the grid tells its full row and column count.
- Buttons and checkboxes inside cells take part in the arrow-key navigation. Name them, such as "Edit Ana Silva".
- The menu button of each column appears on hover and focus, and always on touch screens.
- Merged cells report their span with `aria-colspan` and `aria-rowspan`. The cells they cover are hidden from assistive technologies, and the arrow keys skip them.
- An invalid edit sets `aria-invalid` on the field, and its message is announced and linked to the field with `aria-describedby`.
- Header descriptions describe their header. With the icon toolbar, each button is named by its tooltip.
- Group rows are tree rows: `aria-level`, `aria-expanded` and their position among their siblings. The grid is a `treegrid` while rows are grouped.
- Selected cells carry `aria-selected`. Header filter cells are named after their column, such as "Name filter".
- While rows load, the grid sets `aria-busy` and the loading overlay is a `status` named "Loading". The grid keeps the full row count and each row's index, also when only some rows are in the page.
sections.title: Accessibility

sections.body: Date pickers let people type a date, a time or both, or pick them from a calendar and clocks. The field splits the value into sections, such as month, day, year, hours and minutes. People edit each section with the keyboard, and screen readers announce it as a spin button. The calendar and the clocks open in a popover on devices with a mouse, and in a dialog on touch screens. A static picker shows them inline. The pickers are built from components you already know: a **TextField**, **IconButtons**, **Buttons**, **Chips**, **Tabs**, a **Popover** and a **Dialog**.
sections.html:
…label, the spinbutton sections, a hidden input and the open button…
…toolbar, calendar and actions…
sections.title: Overview

sections.body:
In React, a value is a `Date` or `null`. While the field is only partly filled, the value is an invalid date, and `onChange` reports `validationError: "invalidDate"`. In HTML, values are ISO 8601 strings, such as `2025-05-25`, in `data-ok-value` and in the events.

Set `name` to submit the value with a form. A hidden input carries the ISO date, so the server always gets the same format, whatever the locale shows.
sections.title: Read and write values

sections.body:
- **`DatePicker`:** a popover on devices with a precise pointer and a dialog on touch screens. It decides when it opens, with `desktopModeMediaQuery` (default `@media (pointer: fine)`).
- **`DesktopDatePicker`:** always a popover. Picking a day closes it.
- **`MobileDatePicker`:** always a dialog, with a toolbar and **Cancel** and **OK** buttons.
- **`StaticDatePicker`:** the toolbar, the calendar and the buttons inline, without a field.
- **`DateField`** and **`DateCalendar`:** the field or the calendar on their own.

In HTML, `data-ok-picker-variant` picks the form: `responsive`, `desktop`, `mobile` or `static`.
sections.react:
<DesktopDatePicker label="Start" />
<MobileDatePicker label="End" />
<StaticDatePicker defaultValue={new Date(2025, 4, 25)} />
sections.title: Choose desktop, mobile or static

sections.body: `views` sets what people pick, from `year`, `month` and `day`. The default is `["year", "day"]`. The header's switch button opens the year view, and picking a year moves on to the next view. `openTo` sets the first view. The field's format follows the views: `["month", "year"]` shows "May 2025", and `["day"]` shows "25". Set `format` with Day.js tokens, such as `DD/MM/YYYY`, to choose another one. Text in square brackets is literal.
sections.react:
<DatePicker label="Month and year" views={["month", "year"]} />
<DatePicker label="Day" views={["day"]} />
<DateField label="Date" format="DD.MM.YYYY" />
sections.title: Pick years, months and days

sections.body: `displayWeekNumber` adds a week number column. `showDaysOutsideCurrentMonth` fills the first and last weeks with days of the other months. `fixedWeekNumber={6}` keeps six rows, so the height never changes. `monthsPerRow`, `yearsPerRow` and `yearsOrder` lay out the month and year views. `MonthCalendar` and `YearCalendar` show those views on their own.
sections.title: Change the calendar

sections.body: `actions` sets the buttons under the calendar: `clear`, `today`, `cancel`, `accept` and `nextOrAccept`. Desktop pickers have none by default, because picking a day accepts it. `shortcuts` adds chips that set a value and close the picker. Each shortcut has a `label` and a `getValue` function. In HTML, give each shortcut chip a fixed `data-ok-value`, or call `setShortcuts()` on the instance for computed dates.
sections.react:
<StaticDatePicker
  actions={["clear", "today", "cancel", "accept"]}
  shortcuts={[
    { label: "Christmas", getValue: () => new Date(2025, 11, 25) },
    { label: "New Year", getValue: () => new Date(2026, 0, 1) },
  ]}
/>
sections.title: Add actions and shortcuts

sections.body: `minDate` and `maxDate` limit the range (by default, 1 January 1900 to 31 December 2099). `disablePast` and `disableFuture` compare with today. `shouldDisableDate`, `shouldDisableMonth` and `shouldDisableYear` disable more dates with a function. In HTML, set these functions with the instance methods of the same name, because functions have no attribute. The calendar disables the days people can't pick. The field shows an error when its value breaks a rule, and `onError` (HTML: `validationError` in the events) tells you which rule.
sections.react:
<DatePicker
  label="Appointment"
  minDate={new Date(2025, 4, 10)}
  maxDate={new Date(2025, 5, 20)}
  shouldDisableDate={(day) => day.getDay() === 0 || day.getDay() === 6}
  onError={(error) => console.warn(error)}
/>
sections.title: Validate dates

sections.body:
`TimePicker` edits a time. On devices with a mouse it opens digital clocks: one column per view, plus AM and PM. On touch screens it opens a dialog with an analog clock: press or drag the hand, and the release moves on to the minutes. `DesktopTimePicker`, `MobileTimePicker` and `StaticTimePicker` always use one form. `TimeField`, `TimeClock`, `DigitalClock` and `MultiSectionDigitalClock` work on their own too.

- **`ampm`:** a 12-hour clock with AM and PM. The default follows the locale: English uses 12 hours, Vietnamese uses 24 hours.
- **`views`:** what people pick, from `hours`, `minutes` and `seconds`. The default is `["hours", "minutes"]`, and the field's format follows the views.
- **`timeSteps`:** the distance between the digital clock's options, such as `{ minutes: 15 }`. When a day holds 24 options or fewer, the desktop form shows one list instead of columns.

Time pickers stay open after a pick, so people can change every part. **OK** accepts the time and **Cancel** restores the one from opening. In HTML, the value is an ISO time, such as `09:30:00`.
sections.html:
…the hours, minutes and AM/PM sections…
…the popover with the digital clocks, the dialog with the analog clock…
sections.title: Pick a time

sections.body: `DateTimePicker` edits a date and a time in one field. On devices with a mouse, the popover shows the calendar beside the digital clocks, and a picked day keeps the time. On touch screens, the dialog shows a toolbar, **date** and **time** tabs, the calendar and then the analog clock. **Next** moves to the next view, and **OK** accepts the value on the last one. `views` mixes date and time views, such as `["day", "hours"]`. In HTML, the value is an ISO date and time, such as `2025-05-25T09:30:00`.
sections.react:
<DateTimePicker label="Meeting" />
<MobileDateTimePicker label="Departure" views={["year", "day", "hours", "minutes"]} />
<StaticDateTimePicker orientation="landscape" />
sections.title: Pick a date and time

sections.body: `minTime` and `maxTime` limit the time of day. The date part doesn't count, unless you set `disableIgnoringDatePartForTimeValidation`. Date time pickers also take `minDateTime` and `maxDateTime`. `minutesStep` accepts only multiples of a number of minutes. `shouldDisableTime(value, view)` disables more times with a function. In HTML, call `setShouldDisableTime()` on the instance. `disablePast` and `disableFuture` compare with the current time. The clocks disable the options that break a rule, and `skipDisabled` leaves them out of the digital clocks.
sections.react:
<TimePicker
  label="Office hours"
  minTime={new Date(2025, 4, 25, 9)}
  maxTime={new Date(2025, 4, 25, 17, 30)}
  minutesStep={15}
  timeSteps={{ minutes: 15 }}
  skipDisabled
/>
sections.title: Validate times

sections.body:
`DateRangePicker` edits a start and an end date. On devices with a mouse it opens two months side by side in a popover. On touch screens it opens a dialog with one month and a toolbar that shows both ends. The first pick sets the start, the second one sets the end, and a day before the start starts again. While you move the pointer, a dashed outline previews the range. Drag the start or the end to another day to move it, with a mouse or a finger. `DesktopDateRangePicker`, `MobileDateRangePicker` and `StaticDateRangePicker` always use one form, and `DateRangeCalendar` works on its own.

- **`multiInput`:** two fields, the start and the end, instead of one. Each field's button opens the picker on its end.
- **`calendars`:** the number of months in the popover, from 1 to 3. The dialog and the inline form show one month unless you set it.
- **`rangePosition`:** the end the next pick edits, `start` or `end`. Read it with `onRangePositionChange`, or set it to edit one end.
- **`disableDragEditing`** and **`disableAutoMonthSwitching`:** turn off dragging the ends, and the jump to the end's month after a new start.

The value is a pair, `[start, end]`, and either side can be empty. An end before the start is invalid: both sides report `invalidRange`. In HTML, the value is an ISO 8601 interval, such as `2025-05-20/2025-05-25`, and the hidden input of a single field submits it.
sections.html:
…the start's and the end's sections, a hidden input and the open button…
…the popover with two months, the dialog with the toolbar and one month…
sections.title: Pick a date range

sections.body: Range shortcuts set both ends with one press, such as **Last 7 days** or **Current month**. Each shortcut has a `label` and a `getValue` function that returns the range. Compute the dates when the function runs, so the shortcuts stay right on the next day. `getValue` receives `isValid(range)`, which tells whether a range passes the picker's rules. Shortcuts that return an invalid range are disabled. A shortcut accepts its range and closes the picker. In HTML, each chip carries its range in `data-ok-value`, or you set functions with `setShortcuts()` on the instance.
sections.html:
• …Last 7 days…
  • …Reset…
sections.title: Filter a dashboard by date range

sections.body: `TimeRangePicker` edits a start and an end time, and `DateTimeRangePicker` a start and an end date with times. **Start** and **End** tabs pick the edited end. On devices with a mouse, the popover shows digital clocks, beside one month for date times. On touch screens, the dialog shows the analog clock, after the calendar for date times. Finishing the start's last view moves on to the end. **OK** accepts the range and **Cancel** restores the one from opening. The fields work on their own as `SingleInputTimeRangeField`, `MultiInputTimeRangeField`, `SingleInputDateTimeRangeField` and `MultiInputDateTimeRangeField`. In HTML, the value is an interval of ISO times, such as `09:00:00/17:30:00`.
sections.react:
<TimeRangePicker label="Opening hours" minutesStep={15} timeSteps={{ minutes: 15 }} />
<DateTimeRangePicker label="Event" disablePast />
<MultiInputDateRangeField startLabel="From" endLabel="To" />
sections.title: Pick a time or date time range

sections.body: `LocalizationProvider` sets the locale of the pickers inside, with `adapterLocale`. The locale decides the field's section order, the month and weekday names and the first day of the week. English and Vietnamese texts follow the locale on their own. Locale packs translate the other texts: `pickersFrFR`, `pickersDeDE`, `pickersEsES`, `pickersJaJP`, `pickersZhCN`, `pickersFaIR` and `pickersArSD` from `@owlky/core`. Pass a pack, or a few texts of your own, as `localeText`. A page loads only the packs it imports. In HTML, set `data-ok-locale` on the picker or on any ancestor, such as `<html>`, and pass a pack to the instance's `setLocaleText()`.
sections.html:
<!-- Every picker inside uses Vietnamese names and the day/month/year order -->
<section data-ok-locale="vi-VN">
  …date pickers…
</section>
sections.title: Translate and localize

sections.body: By default, the pickers show values in the time zone of the computer. Set `timezone` to show and edit them in another one: `"UTC"` or an IANA name such as `"America/New_York"`. The field and the clocks then show the wall time of that zone, and `onChange` returns the instant. `"default"` uses the zone of the value when your date library keeps one, such as a Luxon `DateTime`, and `"system"` always uses the computer's zone. "Today" and `disablePast` follow the zone too. In HTML, set `data-ok-timezone` on the picker or on an ancestor. Values in the markup and in events are the zone's wall times. `setValue()` also takes ISO text with an offset, such as `2025-05-25T13:30:00Z`, and the instance's `date` returns the instant.
sections.html: …date time picker markup…
sections.title: Work in another time zone

sections.body: The pickers work with native `Date` objects. If your app uses Day.js, date-fns, Luxon or Moment, give `LocalizationProvider` a `dateAdapter`: the pickers then take and return that library's dates, in values, limits, callbacks and shortcuts. Each adapter is its own entry point and takes your copy of the library, so Owlky adds no dependency: `createDayjsAdapter(dayjs)` from `@owlky/core/adapters/dayjs`, `createDateFnsAdapter({ TZDate })`, `createLuxonAdapter(DateTime)` and `createMomentAdapter(moment)`. Importing an adapter also adds its date type to TypeScript's `PickerValidDate`. Time zones need the library's own zone support, such as Day.js's `utc` and `timezone` plugins. In HTML, the markup keeps ISO values. Call `setDateAdapter(adapter)` on an instance to read `date` and call `setDate()` with the library's dates.
sections.html:
<script type="module">
  import { getRuntime } from "@owlky/html";
  import { createDayjsAdapter } from "@owlky/core/adapters/dayjs";
  import dayjs from "dayjs";

  const picker = getRuntime().get(document.getElementById("due"), "date-picker");
  picker.setDateAdapter(createDayjsAdapter(dayjs));
  picker.setDate(dayjs("2025-12-25"));
  console.log(picker.date.format("D MMMM YYYY")); // a Day.js object
</script>
sections.title: Use your date library

sections.body: Set `calendar` on `LocalizationProvider` to show the Persian (Jalali) calendar, a Hijri calendar or another calendar that the browser's `Intl` knows: `"persian"`, `"islamic-umalqura"`, `"islamic-civil"`, `"islamic-tbla"`, `"buddhist"` or `"indian"`. You can also name it in the locale, such as `"fa-IR-u-ca-persian"`, or let a Jalali or Hijri adapter bring it (`createMomentAdapter(moment, { calendar: "persian" })`). Months, years, day numbers and the field's sections follow the calendar. Values stay ISO 8601 dates, which are always Gregorian, so forms and APIs don't change. Without a calendar, the pickers use the Gregorian calendar, even for locales whose default is another one. In HTML, set `data-ok-calendar` or the locale's `-u-ca-` extension.
sections.html:
<!-- The Persian calendar, in Persian, right to left -->
<section data-ok-locale="fa-IR" data-ok-calendar="persian" dir="rtl">
  …date pickers…
</section>
sections.title: Show another calendar system

sections.body: Put the pickers in an element with `dir="rtl"`, or set it on `<html>`. The layout mirrors: the field's sections, the calendar's weekdays and the month arrows run from right to left. The Left arrow and Right arrow keys follow the reading direction, so the Left arrow moves to the next section and the next day. The analog clock keeps its face, as clocks do.
sections.html:
<html lang="ar" dir="rtl">
  …date pickers…
</html>
sections.title: Lay out right to left

sections.body:
Pickers take `slots` to replace their parts and `slotProps` to pass them props:
- **Day:** `slots.day` renders each day. Render `PickerDay` with extra content, such as a dot for days with events. `slotProps.day` can be a function of the day's state. In HTML, call `setDayRenderer((button, date) => …)` on the calendar or the picker: it runs for each day the calendar builds, on every month.
- **Toolbar, action bar and shortcuts:** `slots.toolbar`, `slots.actionBar` and `slots.shortcuts` replace them. Custom parts read and change the picker with `usePickerContext()`. `slotProps.toolbar.hidden` and `slotProps.tabs.hidden` leave the toolbar or the date and time tabs out. In HTML, write your own markup: buttons with `data-ok-picker-action` run that action, and the runtime keeps `[data-ok-picker-toolbar-title]` up to date.
- **Layout:** `slots.layout` arranges the parts. Build it with `PickerLayoutRoot` and `PickerLayoutContent`, and pass `rootRef` on, so the picker can focus the views when it opens.
- **View renderers:** `viewRenderers` choose what each view shows. `renderTimeViewClock` puts the analog clock on desktop too, and `null` leaves a view out. When every view is `null`, only the field remains. In HTML, put the clock you want in the markup: a picker without a digital clock uses the analog clock in every form.
sections.title: Customize the layout and the views

sections.body: Every option works the same way in both versions: a prop in React, an attribute in HTML. Values that aren't listed fall back to the default. Pickers pass the field and calendar options on to their field and calendar.
sections.title: Options

sections.body: These props set values, rules and texts. They aren't options, because HTML writes them as markup or sets them with instance methods.
sections.title: Content and behavior

sections.body:
- **`ok:date-picker:change`** fires on every change with `detail.value` (ISO or `null`) and `detail.validationError`. **`ok:date-picker:accept`** fires when a value is accepted.
- **`ok:date-picker:open`** and **`ok:date-picker:close`** fire with `detail.reason`, such as `button`, `escape`, `select` or `cancel`.
- **`ok:date-field:change`** and **`ok:date-calendar:change`** (cancelable) fire for a field or a calendar on its own. The calendar also fires `viewchange`, `monthchange` and `yearchange`.
- **`ok:time-clock:change`**, **`ok:digital-clock:change`** and **`ok:multi-section-digital-clock:change`** (cancelable) fire for a clock on its own, with `detail.value` (an ISO time) and `detail.selectionState`: `shallow` while dragging the hand, `partial` when another view follows, `finish` on the last one. The analog clock also fires `ok:time-clock:viewchange`.
- **`ok:date-range-picker:change`** fires with `detail.value` (an ISO interval or `null`) and `detail.validationError`, the `[start, end]` errors. It also fires `accept`, `open`, `close` and `rangepositionchange` (`detail.rangePosition`). **`ok:date-range-calendar:change`** and **`ok:multi-input-range-field:change`** (cancelable) fire for a range calendar or a multi input field on its own.
- **Instance:** `runtime.get(element, "date-picker")` returns `{ value, setValue(value), date, setDate(date), setDateAdapter(adapter), isOpen, open(), close(), setShortcuts(list), setShouldDisableDate(fn), setShouldDisableTime(fn), setDayRenderer(fn), setLocaleText(text) }`. Every picker, field, calendar and clock instance has `date`, `setDate` and `setDateAdapter`. `setValue` doesn't fire events. A range picker's instance (`"date-range-picker"`) adds `rangePosition`, `setRangePosition(position)` and `open(position)`; its `setValue` takes an ISO interval or a `[start, end]` pair.
- **React:** `onChange(value, { validationError })`, `onAccept(value)`, `onError(error, value)`, `onOpenChange(open, reason)`, `onViewChange(view)`, `onMonthChange(month)` and `onYearChange(year)`. The clocks call `onChange(value, selectionState)`. Range pickers call `onChange(range, { validationError: [start, end] })`, `onError(errors, range)` and `onRangePositionChange(position)`.
sections.title: Events and methods

sections.body: The field is one tab stop. The calendar is one tab stop too: the arrow keys move through the days, also across the months of a range calendar. The analog clock is one tab stop, and each digital clock column is one more. A multi input range field has two tab stops, one per field.
sections.title: Keyboard

sections.body:
- Give the field a `label`: it names the group of sections. Each section is a spin button with its name ("Month") and its value as text ("May").
- The open button's name says the selected date ("Choose date, selected date is May 25, 2025").
- The calendar is a grid named by its month. Today is marked with `aria-current="date"`, and disabled days can't be focused.
- The popover and the dialog are named "Select date". Escape closes them and returns focus to the open button.
- Days are 36px wide. The selected day uses white text on the primary color.
- The analog clock is a list box named by its view and the time ("Select hours. Selected time is 09:30 AM"). Each number has a name, such as "9 hours". Focus stays on the list box while the arrow keys move the hand.
- Each digital clock column is a list box named by its view ("Select minutes"). Time pickers' open buttons say the time ("Choose time, selected time is 09:30 AM"), and the date and time tabs are named "pick date" and "pick time".
- A range calendar's grids allow several selected days: every day of the range is selected, and the two ends are filled with the primary color. The open button of a single range field says the range ("Choose range, selected range is May 20, 2025 – May 25, 2025"). The dialog is named "Select date range".
- Dragging the ends is an extra: the keyboard picks the start and the end with Enter, and the toolbar or the **Start** and **End** tabs choose the edited end.
sections.title: Accessibility

sections.body: A dialog asks for a decision or shows information that needs attention, over the page. It is a native modal `<dialog>`: the page behind it is inert, Tab stays inside it, and Escape or a click outside asks it to close. Focus returns to the element that opened it.
sections.html:
Discard this draft?

You can't undo this.
sections.title: Overview

sections.body: The paper is as wide as its content, up to `maxWidth`: `xs` (444px), `sm` (600px, the default), `md` (900px), `lg` (1200px), `xl` (1536px) or `none`. Add `fullWidth` to always take that width. On phones the paper keeps 16px from the edges, and 32px from 600px up. `fullScreen` covers the whole viewport.
sections.html: <dialog id="settings" data-ok-dialog data-ok-max-width="md" data-ok-full-width data-ok-scroll="paper" aria-labelledby="settings-title">…</dialog>
sections.react: <Dialog open={open} onOpenChange={setOpen} maxWidth="md" fullWidth>…</Dialog>
sections.title: Size the dialog

sections.body: With `scroll` set to `paper` (default), the title and actions stay in view and the content scrolls. Make the content focusable (`tabindex="0"` and a name) so keyboard users can scroll it. With `body`, the whole dialog scrolls with the page. Add `dividers` to draw lines above and below the content.
sections.html: …
sections.react: <DialogContent dividers tabIndex={0} aria-label="Terms">…</DialogContent>
sections.title: Scroll long content

sections.body: By default, the paper fades and scales in briefly. Set `transition` to a Motion entrance, such as `slideInUp` or `zoomIn`, to play that animation instead. In HTML, the paper becomes a Motion that plays when the dialog opens, so the page also needs the Motion styles. With reduced motion, the dialog appears at once.
sections.html: …
sections.react: <Dialog open={open} onOpenChange={setOpen} transition="slideInUp">…</Dialog>
sections.title: Animate the entrance

sections.body: Every option works the same way in both versions: a prop in React, an attribute in HTML. Values that aren't listed fall back to the default.
sections.title: Options

sections.body: These props set the content and the state. They aren't options, because HTML writes them as markup or triggers.
sections.title: Content and behavior

sections.body:
- **`ok:dialog:beforeopen`** (cancelable) and **`ok:dialog:open`** fire on the dialog.
- **`ok:dialog:beforeclose`** (cancelable) and **`ok:dialog:close`** carry `detail.reason`: `escape`, `backdrop`, `trigger`, `api` or `native` (a `form[method=dialog]`).
- **Instance:** `runtime.get(element, "dialog")` returns `{ isOpen, open(trigger?), close(reason?) }`.
- **React:** `onOpenChange(false, reason)` with `escape`, `backdrop` or `close`. Set `open` to close it.
sections.title: Events and methods

sections.body: Focus stays inside the dialog while it is open.
sections.title: Keyboard

sections.body:
- The dialog is named by its title: React links `DialogTitle` automatically, and in HTML you point `aria-labelledby` at the title's `id`.
- When it opens, focus moves to the first focusable element (or an element with `autofocus`). When it closes, focus returns to the trigger.
- The page behind is inert, so screen readers and the keyboard stay in the dialog.
- Secondary text uses the secondary text color, with a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1.
sections.title: Accessibility

sections.body: A divider is a thin line that groups content: between sections of a menu, rows of a list or groups of buttons. It is a native `<hr>`, so assistive technology announces a separator. It needs no JavaScript.
sections.html:
<!-- Load once per page -->
<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@owlky/html@0/dist/owlky.css">

<hr data-ok-divider data-ok-variant="fullWidth" data-ok-orientation="horizontal">
sections.title: Overview

sections.body: By default the line spans its container (`fullWidth`). Use `inset` in lists whose rows start with an avatar or an icon: the line starts 72px in, under the text. Use `middle` to leave 16px on both sides.
sections.html: <hr data-ok-divider data-ok-variant="inset" data-ok-orientation="horizontal">
sections.react: <Divider variant="inset" />
sections.title: Inset or shorten the line

sections.body: Set `orientation` to `vertical` for a line between items side by side; in HTML, also write `aria-orientation="vertical"`. In a flex row, add `flexItem` so the line takes the row's height.
sections.html: <hr data-ok-divider data-ok-variant="middle" data-ok-orientation="vertical" data-ok-flex-item aria-orientation="vertical">
sections.react: <Divider orientation="vertical" variant="middle" flexItem />
sections.title: Separate items in a row

sections.body: Pass children to show text, or a chip, on the line, such as "or" between two sign-in options. Set `textAlign` to `left` or `right` to move it. With children, the divider is a `div` with `role="separator"` and the text in a `data-ok-divider-text` span.
sections.html: or
sections.react: <Divider>or</Divider>
sections.title: Put text on the line

sections.body: Every option works the same way in both versions: a prop in React, an attribute in HTML. Values that aren't listed fall back to the default.
sections.title: Options

sections.body: These props set the content. They aren't options, because HTML writes them as markup.
sections.title: Content and behavior

sections.body: Dividers have no events or methods.
sections.title: Events and methods

sections.body: Dividers don't take focus.
sections.title: Keyboard

sections.body:
- A divider is announced as a separator. Use one where the content really changes; for space alone, use margins.
- A purely decorative line between items that are already grouped can be hidden with `aria-hidden="true"`.
- Text on a divider uses the secondary text color, with a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1. The line itself is decorative and lighter.
sections.title: Accessibility

sections.body:
A drawer is a panel that slides in from an edge of the screen, for navigation, filters or details. A **temporary** drawer opens over the page as a modal: the rest of the page can't be used until it closes. **Persistent** and **permanent** drawers sit next to the page content instead.

The drawer is a native `<dialog>`, so the browser keeps focus inside it and closes it with Escape.
sections.html: …
sections.title: Overview

sections.body: Set `anchor` to `left` (the default), `right`, `top` or `bottom`. Side drawers take the full height; top and bottom drawers take the full width. A drawer never covers the whole screen: a 56px gap keeps the backdrop visible, so people can tap it to close the drawer.
sections.html: …
sections.react: <DrawerContent anchor="bottom" aria-label="Menu">…</DrawerContent>
sections.title: Choose the edge

sections.body: Escape and a click on the backdrop ask the drawer to close. Add your own close button with `DrawerClose` in React, or `data-ok-drawer-close` in HTML. Set `disableEscapeKeyDown` or `hideBackdrop` to turn those ways off.
sections.html: …
sections.react:
<DrawerContent anchor="right" aria-label="Filters">
  …
  <DrawerClose variant="contained" color="primary">
    Apply
  </DrawerClose>
</DrawerContent>
sections.title: Close the drawer

sections.body: In React, pass `open` and `onOpenChange` to `Drawer`. `onOpenChange` receives the requested state and the reason: `escape`, `backdrop` or `close`. To keep the drawer open, don't update `open`. In HTML, listen to `ok:drawer:beforeclose` and call `preventDefault()`.
sections.html:
<script type="module">
  document.addEventListener("ok:drawer:beforeclose", (event) => {
    if (event.detail.reason === "backdrop" && formHasChanges) event.preventDefault();
  });
</script>
sections.title: Control when it opens and closes

sections.body: Set `variant` to `persistent` for a drawer that people can show and hide next to the content, or `permanent` for one that is always visible. Docked drawers have no backdrop and don't trap focus. Place the drawer and the page area in a flex row (left and right) or column (top and bottom).

…

…

sections.title: Dock the drawer next to the page

sections.body: Every option works the same way in both versions: a prop in React, an attribute in HTML. Values that aren't listed fall back to the default.
sections.title: Options

sections.body: In React, the drawer is made of parts: `Drawer` holds the state, and the other parts go inside it.
sections.title: Content and behavior

sections.body:
- **`ok:drawer:beforeopen`** (cancelable) fires before the drawer opens, and **`ok:drawer:open`** after.
- **`ok:drawer:beforeclose`** (cancelable) fires before it closes, with `detail.reason`. **`ok:drawer:close`** fires after, with the reason: `escape`, `backdrop`, `trigger`, `api` or `native`.
- **Instance:** `runtime.get(element, "drawer")` returns `{ isOpen, open(trigger?), close(reason?), toggle() }`.
- **React:** `onOpenChange(open, reason)` on `Drawer`.
sections.title: Events and methods

sections.body: A temporary drawer is a modal dialog: focus stays inside it until it closes.
sections.title: Keyboard

sections.body:
- A drawer needs a name: set `aria-label`, or `aria-labelledby` pointing to its title.
- When a temporary drawer opens, focus moves into it and the rest of the page becomes inert. When it closes, focus returns to the button that opened it.
- Triggers carry `aria-haspopup="dialog"`. Docked drawers' triggers carry `aria-expanded` and `aria-controls` instead.
- If the content can scroll, put it in a **Scrollbar**: it becomes a named region that keyboard users can scroll, and it's the first thing focused when the drawer opens.
sections.title: Accessibility

sections.body:
The editor lets people write formatted text: headings, bold and italic text, lists, alignment, quotes, code, links and images. It is built on Tiptap, a framework-free editing engine, so both versions share the same behavior and markup. A toolbar sits above a text box that people type in, and the content is HTML.

The editor is a separate script so that pages without one don't download the editing engine. Load `owlky-editor.js` after `owlky.js`, or import `@owlky/html/editor` after `@owlky/html/auto`.
sections.html: The initial content is the markup inside this element.
sections.title: Overview

sections.body:
The value is an HTML string, and an empty editor has the value `""`. In React, use `value` and `onChange` to control it, or `defaultValue` to only set the initial content. A new `value` replaces the content, but the editor does not undo an edit that you ignore in `onChange`, because rich text cannot be held back key by key. In HTML, write the initial content inside the content element, listen to `ok:editor:change`, and call `setValue(html)` on the instance to replace it.

The editor keeps only what its toolbar can make, plus text transforms. Pasted or loaded HTML loses scripts, event handler attributes and unknown elements, and links only keep `http`, `https`, `mailto`, `tel` and relative URLs.

sections.title: Content and behavior

sections.body:
- **`ok:editor:change`** fires on the editor after every change, with the HTML in `detail.value`.
- **`ok:editor:fullscreen`** fires when fullscreen mode changes, with `detail.fullscreen`.
- **Instance:** `runtime.get(element, "editor")` returns `{ value, setValue(html), fullscreen, setFullscreen(on), setEditable(on), focus(), controller }`. `controller.editor` is the Tiptap editor.
- **React:** `onChange(value)` and `onFullscreenChange(fullscreen)`.
- **Trusted Types:** `setValue` and the React `value` prop parse an HTML string with the browser's `DOMParser`. Pages that enforce Trusted Types need a policy for it. Content written in the markup needs none.

sections.body:

- The link and image forms are dialogs named by their title. Escape closes them and returns focus to their button.
- Images need a text alternative: fill in **Alt text**, or leave it empty only for decoration.
- Fullscreen mode can always be left with Escape. While it is on, Tab moves between the toolbar and the text box only, so focus never reaches controls hidden behind the editor.

sections.body:
A form control groups a control with its label and helper text, and shares their states: disabled, error, required and focused. It is made of four parts:

- **FormControl:** the root. It holds the shared states, and its element is usually a `fieldset` for a group of controls.
- **FormLabel:** the label, in the secondary text color. In a `fieldset`, it is the `legend`.
- **FormGroup:** a column or a row of labelled checkboxes or switches. Radios use a **RadioGroup**.
- **FormHelperText:** a hint or an error message under the controls.

Form controls need no JavaScript. In HTML, the states are attributes on the root that the parts' styles read. In React, `FormControl` also shares them through a context. A **Text field** has its own label and helper text, so it doesn't go inside a form control.
