sections.body:
- **Required:** add `required`. The label shows an asterisk, which assistive technology skips. Set `aria-required` on a radio group, or `required` on an input, so the requirement is announced. In HTML, write the asterisk in the label.
- **Disabled:** add `disabled`. The label turns grey. On a `fieldset` root, Owlky also sets the native `disabled` attribute, which turns off every control inside. On a `div` root, set `disabled` on each control too.
- **Focused:** add `focused` to show the label in the focus color, which `color` sets. The default is the text color.

import {
  Checkbox,
  FormControl,
  FormControlLabel,
  FormGroup,
  FormLabel,
  Radio,
  RadioGroup,
} from "@owlky/react";

export function Settings() {
  return (
    <>
      <FormControl component="fieldset" required>
        <FormLabel component="legend" id="plan-label">
          Plan
        </FormLabel>
        <RadioGroup name="plan" row aria-labelledby="plan-label" aria-required="true">
          <FormControlLabel label="Free" control={<Radio value="free" />} />
          <FormControlLabel label="Pro" control={<Radio value="pro" />} />
        </RadioGroup>
      </FormControl>
      <FormControl component="fieldset" disabled>
        <FormLabel component="legend">Notifications</FormLabel>
        <FormGroup>
          <FormControlLabel label="Email" control={<Checkbox name="email" defaultChecked />} />
        </FormGroup>
      </FormControl>
    </>
  );
}

sections.body:
- Name a group of controls with a `fieldset` and its `legend`, or with `aria-labelledby` on the group pointing at the label's `id`.
- Reference the helper text from the controls or the group with `aria-describedby`, so it is read with them.
- Expose errors with `aria-invalid` and requirements with `aria-required` or `required` on the controls: the colors and the asterisk are visual only.
- Labels and helper texts use the secondary text color, and errors the error text color, with a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 in the light and dark themes. Disabled labels are dimmed, like the disabled controls.
sections.title: Accessibility

sections.body:
Owlky has six palette colors: `primary`, `secondary`, `info`, `success`, `warning` and `error`. Each color comes in five shades, from `lighter` to `darker`. The `main` shade is the color itself, and `contrast-text` is the text color to use on top of it.

Each color also has a `text` tone. Use it for colored text on the page background: it stays readable in both light and dark themes.

For neutral colors, use the `grey` scale (`50`, `100`, `200`, `300`, `400`, `500`, `600`, `700`, `800` and `900`), `common-black` and `common-white`.

The stories in the sidebar show each palette in detail. Select a swatch to copy its hex value. The `primary` color follows the **Preset** menu in the toolbar.
sections.title: Palette

sections.body:
All colors are CSS custom properties that start with `--ok-`.

- **Palette shades:** `--ok-palette-<color>-<shade>`. For example, `--ok-palette-primary-main` or `--ok-palette-grey-200`.
- **Colored text:** `--ok-palette-<color>-text`.
- **Neutral text:** `--ok-text-primary`, `--ok-text-secondary` and `--ok-text-disabled`.
- **Backgrounds:** `--ok-bg-default` for the page, `--ok-bg-paper` for cards and menus, and `--ok-bg-neutral` for subtle fills.
- **Lines:** `--ok-divider`.
- **Interaction states:** `--ok-action-hover`, `--ok-action-selected`, `--ok-action-focus`, `--ok-action-disabled` and `--ok-action-disabled-bg`.
- **Transparency:** each palette shade has a matching `-channel` variable that holds its RGB values, such as `0 167 111`.

Text, background, line and state colors change with the theme. Palette shades stay the same in every theme.
sections.title: Token reference

sections.body:
Load the Owlky stylesheet once per page. You can then use the variables in any CSS rule, in both HTML and React projects.

To make a color transparent, combine its `-channel` variable with an alpha value: `rgb(var(--ok-palette-primary-main-channel) / 0.16)`. This works in every supported browser, unlike some `color-mix()` fallbacks that drop the transparency.

sections.title: Use colors in CSS

sections.body:
Most components have a color option. In HTML, set the `data-ok-color` attribute. In React, set the `color` prop.

The available colors are `inherit`, `primary`, `secondary`, `info`, `success`, `warning`, `error`, `black` and `white`. A few components add their own values, such as `default` for Icon button. Component colors come from the palette, so they follow the active theme and preset automatically.

sections.title: Build surfaces that follow the theme

sections.body: If your project uses Tailwind CSS v4, import the Owlky theme after Tailwind. Every palette shade and theme color then becomes a utility class, such as `bg-primary`, `text-primary-dark`, `bg-grey-200`, `text-text-secondary`, `bg-paper` and `border-divider`.
sections.title: Use Tailwind CSS utilities

sections.body:
Some code needs color values directly, for example to draw a chart on a canvas. You have two options:

- **Read the CSS variable** to get the color that is on screen now. This value follows the active theme and preset.
- **Import the default values** from `@owlky/tokens`. These values are fixed: they don't change with the theme or preset.
sections.html:
<script type="module">
  // The default value (bare imports need a bundler or an import map)
  import { defaultTheme } from "@owlky/tokens";

  const brand = defaultTheme.palette.primary.main; // "#00A76F"

  // The color on screen now (follows the theme and preset)
  const styles = getComputedStyle(document.documentElement);
  const primary = styles.getPropertyValue("--ok-palette-primary-main").trim();
</script>
sections.title: Read colors in JavaScript

sections.body:
Two attributes control the colors of a page or a part of it:

- `data-ok-theme` sets the theme: `light` or `dark`.
- `data-ok-preset` changes the primary color, for example to `cyan`.

Put them on the `<html>` element to style the whole page, or on any element to style only its content. You can nest them, for example to show a light panel inside a dark page.

To change them from code, call `applyThemeSettings()`. Pass a storage, such as `localStorage`, to remember the user's choice.
sections.html:
<html data-ok-theme="dark" data-ok-preset="cyan">
  <body>
    <!-- A light panel inside the dark page -->
    <section data-ok-theme="light">…</section>
  </body>
</html>

<script type="module">
  import { applyThemeSettings } from "@owlky/html";

  applyThemeSettings({ mode: "dark", preset: "cyan" }, { storage: localStorage });
</script>
sections.title: Switch themes and presets

sections.body:
- Neutral text colors and the `text` tone of each palette color meet WCAG 2.2 level AA (a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1) on the theme backgrounds, in light and dark mode.
- Filled components use `contrast-text` on the `main` shade. Some of these brand combinations are below 4.5:1, so avoid them for long text.
- To check your own color pairs, use `contrastRatio(foreground, background)` from `@owlky/tokens`.
- To place text on any color, let `getContrastText(color, ["#FFFFFF", "#000000"])` choose between white and black. The result always has a contrast ratio of at least 4.58:1.
- Don't rely on color alone to convey meaning. Add text or an icon, as Alert does.
sections.title: Accessibility

sections.body:
All spacing in Owlky is a multiple of one unit, `--ok-spacing`. It equals `0.25rem`, which is 4px at the default font size. To get a space, multiply the unit: `calc(var(--ok-spacing) * 4)` is 16px.

Because the unit is in `rem`, spacing grows with the root font size. The **Spacing** story in the sidebar lets you try different values.

<!-- Load once per page -->
<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@owlky/html@0/dist/owlky.css">

<style>
  .toolbar {
    display: flex;
    gap: calc(var(--ok-spacing) * 2);   /* 8px */
    padding: calc(var(--ok-spacing) * 4); /* 16px */
  }
</style>
sections.title: Spacing

sections.body: The Owlky theme for Tailwind CSS v4 sets Tailwind's spacing unit to `--ok-spacing`, so every spacing utility follows it. For example, `gap-2` is 8px and `p-4` is 16px.

sections.body:
Owlky components change their layout at these screen widths:

- **sm:** 600px and wider (large phones in landscape, tablets).
- **md:** 900px and wider (small laptops).
- **lg:** 1200px and wider (desktops).
- **xl:** 1536px and wider (large desktops).

The values are also available as `--ok-breakpoint-sm` and the other `--ok-breakpoint-*` variables, for use in JavaScript. CSS media queries can't read variables, so write the pixel value in your queries.

Tailwind CSS uses different breakpoints by default (640px, 768px, 1024px). To match Owlky, use arbitrary breakpoints such as `min-[900px]:`.

<style>
  .layout {
    display: grid;
    gap: calc(var(--ok-spacing) * 6);
  }
  @media (min-width: 900px) {
    .layout {
      grid-template-columns: 280px 1fr;
    }
  }
</style>

sections.body: Page layouts use a grid of 12 equal columns. A card can span all 12 columns on phones, 6 on tablets and 4 on desktops. Use CSS grid: the browser handles the math. The **Column** story in the sidebar shows 1 to 12 columns.

sections.body:
- Let content reflow: at a width of 320px, a page must work without horizontal scrolling (WCAG 2.2, success criterion 1.4.10). Prefer `minmax(0, 1fr)` and wrapping to fixed widths.
- Keep interactive targets at least 24 × 24px, with enough space between them (success criterion 2.5.8). Owlky components already do.
- Spacing in `rem` grows with the user's font size, so text and the space around it stay in proportion.

Owlky doesn't include an icon set. Components accept any SVG icon, so you can use the library you already have, such as Iconify, Lucide or Material Symbols, or your own SVG files.

The stories in the sidebar show open-source sets from Iconify, with recommended sizes and colors.

sections.body: In HTML, place the SVG inside the component's icon part, such as `data-ok-button-icon`. In React, pass the icon as a prop, such as `startIcon`, or as the child of an icon button. Components size and color the icon for you.
sections.title: Add an icon to a component

sections.body:
Draw icons on a 24 × 24 grid and display them at one of these sizes:

- **16px:** dense interfaces and next to caption text.
- **20px:** inside buttons, inputs and menus.
- **24px:** standalone icons and icon buttons.
- **32px:** empty states and feature highlights.

Inside components, the size is set for you. For your own icons, set `width` and `height`.

sections.title: Color an icon

sections.body:
- **Decorative icons** sit next to visible text that says the same thing. Hide them from assistive technology with `aria-hidden="true"`.
- **Meaningful icons** stand alone and carry information. Give them a name with `role="img"` and `aria-label`.
- **Icon-only buttons** need a name on the button, not on the icon: set `aria-label` on the button and hide the icon.
- Make sure an icon that conveys meaning has a contrast ratio of at least 3:1 with its background (WCAG 2.2, success criterion 1.4.11).
sections.html:
<!-- Decorative: next to visible text -->
<svg aria-hidden="true" width="20" height="20" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><rect x="3" y="5" width="18" height="14" rx="2" /><path d="m3 7 9 6 9-6" /></svg> Messages

<!-- Meaningful on its own: give it a name -->
<svg role="img" aria-label="3 new messages" width="24" height="24" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><rect x="3" y="5" width="18" height="14" rx="2" /><path d="m3 7 9 6 9-6" /></svg>
sections.title: Accessibility

sections.body:
Owlky includes 16 flat illustrations for error pages, empty states, account flows and dashboards. Each one is inline SVG whose shapes name a color role, such as `main` or `paper`, instead of a color. The stylesheet turns those roles into theme colors, so every illustration follows light and dark mode, nested themes, the **Preset** menu in the toolbar and the `color` option.

- **Theme-aware:** the brand shapes use the primary palette, or another palette you choose. Neutral shapes follow the color scheme.
- **Small and private:** the pictures are data in your bundle. They need no image requests and work under a strict Content Security Policy.
- **Pay for what you use:** every illustration is its own export, so your bundle keeps only the ones you import.

The **All** story in the sidebar shows the whole set on one page. The other stories show it by category.
sections.title: Illustrations in Owlky

sections.body:
In React, import the illustration from `@owlky/core/illustrations` and pass it to `Illustration`.

In HTML, you have two options:

- **Paste the SVG:** copy the snippet from the story's **Code** panel. It needs only the stylesheet.
- **Name the picture:** write an empty `<svg data-ok-illustration="name">` and load `owlky-illustrations.js` after `owlky.js`. The script draws the shapes with DOM methods. Use this option when you show the same picture on many pages.
sections.html:
<!-- Load once per page -->
<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@owlky/html@0/dist/owlky.css">
<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@owlky/html@0/dist/owlky.js" defer></script>
<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@owlky/html@0/dist/owlky-illustrations.js" defer></script>

<!-- The script draws the "error-404" illustration inside this element -->
<svg data-ok-illustration="error-404" data-ok-color="primary" aria-hidden="true"></svg>
sections.title: Add an illustration

sections.body:
Every scene is drawn on the same 480 × 360 canvas, so pictures line up on a page. An illustration is 480px wide by default and never wider than its container, so it shrinks on small screens. The height follows the 4:3 canvas.

Set `size` to a number in pixels or to a CSS length, such as `"20rem"`. In HTML, `data-ok-size` needs the illustrations script. Without the script, set a `width` attribute or a CSS `width` instead.
sections.html:
<svg data-ok-illustration="empty-content" data-ok-color="primary" data-ok-size="240" aria-hidden="true"></svg>

<!-- Without the illustrations script -->
<svg data-ok-illustration="empty-content" data-ok-color="primary" width="240" aria-hidden="true" viewBox="0 0 480 360">…</svg>
sections.title: Choose a size

sections.body:
Each shape has a `data-ok-tone` attribute:

- **Brand tones:** `lighter`, `light`, `main`, `dark` and `darker` take the palette that `color` names. The default is `primary`, so they also follow the theme's preset.
- **Accent tones:** `accent-light`, `accent-main` and `accent-dark` use the warning palette for stars and highlights.
- **Neutral tones:** `paper`, `neutral`, `outline`, `line`, `shadow`, `shade` and `ink` follow the color scheme, so paper stays paper in dark mode.
- **Fixed tones:** `white`, `grey-300`, `grey-500`, `grey-600` and the skin tones `skin-light`, `skin-medium` and `skin-deep`.

To recolor one illustration, set `color` to `secondary`, `info`, `success`, `warning` or `error`. To recolor every illustration, change the palette with your theme, or set the skin tones `--ok-illustration-skin-light`, `--ok-illustration-skin-medium` and `--ok-illustration-skin-deep`. Inside a `data-ok-theme` or `data-ok-preset` scope, an illustration takes that scope's colors.
sections.html:
<svg data-ok-illustration="sign-in" data-ok-color="info" aria-hidden="true"></svg>

<!-- A dark section of a light page -->
<section data-ok-theme="dark">
  <svg data-ok-illustration="sign-in" data-ok-color="primary" aria-hidden="true"></svg>
</section>
sections.title: Change colors and themes

sections.body: In React, options are props of `Illustration`. In HTML, they are attributes of the `svg` element.
sections.title: Options

sections.body:
In React and in bundled HTML apps, import the illustrations you use from `@owlky/core/illustrations`. Each one adds about 0.7 to 1.6 kB gzip to your bundle. Pictures that share parts, such as people and sparkles, share that code. The `illustrations` export lists the whole set: import it only for a catalog.

`owlky-illustrations.js` and `@owlky/html/illustrations` register every illustration, about 10 kB gzip. To ship fewer, register your own set with `createIllustration`.
sections.html:
<script type="module">
  import { createIllustration, getRuntime } from "@owlky/html";
  import { error404, error500 } from "@owlky/core/illustrations";

  // Only these two pictures are bundled.
  getRuntime().register(createIllustration([error404, error500])).start();
</script>
sections.title: Load only the illustrations you need

sections.body: Components that show an illustration accept your own content. For example, the upload's drop zone shows the `upload` illustration. Its `placeholder` replaces the illustration and the texts. To keep your own art theme-aware, draw it as inline SVG with `data-ok-tone` on each shape inside an `svg[data-ok-illustration]` root, or describe it as data for `Illustration`. To match the style of the set, compose your data from the parts that `@owlky/core/illustrations` exports, such as `backdrop()`, `groundShadow()`, `sparkle()` and `person()`. They draw the same backdrop, shadow, sparkles and people as the built-in pictures. A picture in an `` element, such as a file from an illustration library kept in your app, works too, but it keeps its own colors in every theme.
sections.html: …
sections.title: Replace an illustration with your own

sections.body:
- **Decorative by default:** most illustrations repeat what the text next to them says. They render `aria-hidden="true"`, so screen readers skip them.
- **Meaningful pictures** need a name. In React, set `title`. In HTML, set `role="img"` and `aria-label`.
- **No focus stop:** illustrations render `focusable="false"` and never take keyboard focus.
- **No text in pictures:** the illustrations contain no words. Put headings and messages in real text next to them.
- **Contrast:** decorative art has no contrast requirement. If a picture carries meaning, check that its key shapes reach a contrast ratio of at least 3:1 with the background (WCAG 2.2, success criterion 1.4.11).
sections.html: Page not found
sections.title: Accessibility

sections.body: The illustrations are original artwork drawn for Owlky in the flat style of the Minimal dashboard. They are released under the MIT license, like the rest of the library.
sections.title: Credits

sections.body:
Theme settings let your users personalize the interface. There are four settings:

- **Mode:** `light`, `dark` and `system`. The `system` mode follows the operating system.
- **Primary color preset:** `default`, `cyan`, `purple`, `blue`, `orange` and `red`.
- **Font family:** `public-sans`, `inter`, `dm-sans` and `nunito-sans`.
- **Font size:** the root font size, from 12px to 20px. The default is 16px.

Each setting is an attribute or a style on an element, so it works without JavaScript. The **Theme**, **Preset**, **Font** and **Font size** menus in the toolbar change the same settings for every story.
sections.title: Theme settings

sections.body: Set `data-ok-preset` to replace the primary color everywhere it's used, such as filled buttons, selected states and colored shadows. The other palette colors don't change.
sections.html:
<html data-ok-preset="purple">
  …
</html>
sections.react:
import { applyThemeSettings } from "@owlky/react";

applyThemeSettings({ preset: "purple" });
sections.title: Change the primary color

sections.body: Set `data-ok-font` to switch the main font. Owlky doesn't bundle fonts, so load the one you choose. Fontsource packages work well: for example, `@fontsource-variable/inter` for Inter. Display headings keep the Barlow font.
sections.html:
<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@fontsource-variable/inter/index.css">

<html data-ok-font="inter">
  …
</html>
sections.title: Change the font family

sections.body: Every size in Owlky is in `rem`, so the root font size scales the whole interface: text, spacing and components. Set it on the `<html>` element, between 12px and 20px.
sections.html:
<html style="font-size: 18px">
  …
</html>
sections.react:
import { applyThemeSettings } from "@owlky/react";

applyThemeSettings({ fontSize: 18 });
sections.title: Change the text size

sections.body:
`applyThemeSettings()` sets any of the four settings and returns the result. Settings you leave out keep their current value, and invalid values fall back to the default.

To remember the choice, pass a storage such as `localStorage`. On the next visit, read it back with `readThemeSettings()` and apply it. Call `resetThemeSettings()` to go back to the defaults.
sections.html:
<script type="module">
  import { applyThemeSettings, readThemeSettings } from "@owlky/html";

  // On page load: restore the saved settings
  applyThemeSettings(readThemeSettings({ storage: localStorage }));

  // In a settings menu: change and save
  applyThemeSettings({ mode: "dark", preset: "blue" }, { storage: localStorage });
</script>
sections.title: Save the user's choice

sections.body: The attributes work on any element, not only `<html>`, and they nest. Use this to preview a theme inside a settings panel, or to give one section of a page its own look. With `applyThemeSettings()`, pass the element as the `target` option.
sections.html:
<section data-ok-theme="dark" data-ok-preset="orange" data-ok-font="dm-sans">
  <!-- This section uses its own settings -->
</section>
sections.title: Apply settings to part of a page

sections.body:
- Offer the `system` mode, so people who set a dark theme in their operating system get it automatically.
- Larger text sizes help people with low vision. Because everything is in `rem`, the browser's own font size setting works too.
- Every preset keeps neutral text at WCAG 2.2 AA contrast. Colored text uses each preset's accessible `text` tone.
- Save the user's choice, so they don't have to set it again on every visit.
sections.title: Accessibility

sections.body:
Shadows show how far a surface sits above the page. Owlky has three kinds:

- **Elevation:** 24 levels, from `--ok-elevation-1` (almost flat) to `--ok-elevation-24` (floating).
- **Named shadows:** shadows for common surfaces. Use `--ok-shadow-card` for cards, `--ok-shadow-dropdown` for menus and popovers, `--ok-shadow-dialog` for dialogs and `--ok-shadow-dialog-start` for drawers. The scale `--ok-shadow-z1` to `--ok-shadow-z24` covers everything in between.
- **Colored shadows:** one per palette color, such as `--ok-shadow-primary`, for filled buttons and highlighted elements.
- **Drop shadows:** `--ok-drop-shadow-z1`, `--ok-drop-shadow-z4` and `--ok-drop-shadow-z8` repeat `--ok-shadow-z1`, `--ok-shadow-z4` and `--ok-shadow-z8` as `filter` values, for shapes such as map pins and icons.

The stories in the sidebar show every shadow.
sections.title: Shadow levels

sections.body: Load the Owlky stylesheet once, then set `box-shadow` to a shadow variable. Pick the shadow by the role of the surface, not by how it looks: a card always uses the card shadow.
sections.html:
<!-- Load once per page -->
<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@owlky/html@0/dist/owlky.css">

<style>
  .card {
    padding: 24px;
    border-radius: 16px;
    background-color: var(--ok-bg-paper);
    box-shadow: var(--ok-shadow-card);
  }
</style>

<article class="card">Weekly sales</article>
sections.title: Add a shadow with CSS

sections.body: With the Owlky theme for Tailwind CSS v4, every shadow is a utility: `shadow-card`, `shadow-dropdown`, `shadow-dialog`, `shadow-dialog-start`, `shadow-z1` to `shadow-z24` and `shadow-elevation-1` to `shadow-elevation-24`.
sections.title: Use Tailwind CSS utilities

sections.body: Colored shadows are tinted with a palette color: `--ok-shadow-primary`, `--ok-shadow-secondary`, `--ok-shadow-info`, `--ok-shadow-success`, `--ok-shadow-warning` and `--ok-shadow-error`. Contained buttons already use them on hover. Use one for your own highlighted element, such as a featured plan.
sections.html:
<style>
  .featured {
    padding: 24px;
    border-radius: 16px;
    background-color: var(--ok-bg-paper);
    box-shadow: var(--ok-shadow-primary);
  }
</style>

<article class="featured">Pro plan</article>
sections.title: Use a colored shadow

sections.body: A `box-shadow` follows the element's box, so an icon or a pin gets a rectangular shadow. Set `filter` to a drop shadow variable instead: the shadow then follows the shape. Drop shadows use the same offsets, blur and color as the shadow levels, so a pin and a card at the same level look alike.
sections.html:
<style>
  .pin {
    width: 26px;
    height: 26px;
    color: var(--ok-palette-primary-main);
    filter: var(--ok-drop-shadow-z4);
  }
</style>

<svg class="pin" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="currentColor" aria-hidden="true">
  <path d="M12 2a7 7 0 0 0-7 7c0 5 7 13 7 13s7-8 7-13a7 7 0 0 0-7-7Z" />
</svg>
sections.title: Shadow a shape with a filter

sections.body: Shadows follow the theme. In the light theme they use a soft grey; in the dark theme they use black, so surfaces still stand out from a dark page. `--ok-shadow-primary` follows the active preset. You don't need any extra code.
sections.title: Shadows in dark mode

sections.body:
- A shadow alone isn't a strong enough boundary for everyone. When a surface must stand out clearly, such as an input or a selected card, add a border with `--ok-divider` or a stronger color.
- Don't use a shadow as the only sign of focus or selection: use an outline or a color change as well.
sections.title: Accessibility

sections.body:
Owlky has 13 text styles, called variants: `h1`, `h2`, `h3`, `h4`, `h5`, `h6`, `subtitle1`, `subtitle2`, `body1`, `body2`, `caption`, `overline` and `button`. Each variant sets a font family, size, weight, line height and text transform.

The `h1`, `h2` and `h3` headings use the display font, Barlow. All other variants use the main font, Public Sans by default. Sizes are in `rem`, so text scales with the root font size.

The stories in the sidebar show each variant in detail. To set a variant on an element without writing CSS, use the **Typography** component, described in **Components › Typography**.
sections.title: Type scale

sections.body:
- **Variants:** `--ok-typography-<variant>-<property>`, where the property is `font-family`, `font-size`, `font-weight`, `line-height` or `text-transform`. For example, `--ok-typography-h3-font-size`.
- **Font families:** `--ok-font-family` for text, `--ok-font-family-secondary` for display headings and `--ok-font-family-mono` for code.
- **Font weights:** `--ok-font-weight-regular`, `--ok-font-weight-medium`, `--ok-font-weight-semibold`, `--ok-font-weight-bold` and `--ok-font-weight-extrabold`.
- **Small sizes for components:** `--ok-font-size-xs` to `--ok-font-size-xl`.
sections.title: Token reference

sections.body: Load the Owlky stylesheet once, then apply the variables of a variant to your own elements. Using all of a variant's properties keeps the text consistent with Owlky components.
sections.html: Monthly report
sections.title: Style text with CSS

sections.body: With the Owlky theme for Tailwind CSS v4, each variant from `h1` to `caption` is a `text-<variant>` utility that sets the size, weight and line height. Add `font-display` for the display font. The `overline` and `button` variants have no utility: use their CSS variables instead.
sections.title: Use Tailwind CSS utilities

sections.body: Headings grow on larger screens, at `600px`, `900px` and `1200px`. For example, `h1` goes from 2.5rem (40px) on phones to 4rem (64px) on desktops. The variables change by themselves, so you don't need media queries. Resize the window to see the current `h1` size below.
sections.title: Responsive headings

sections.body: To use another font, set `data-ok-font` to `public-sans`, `inter`, `dm-sans` and `nunito-sans`. To make all text larger or smaller, change the root font size: every size is in `rem`. Load the fonts yourself, for example from Fontsource. The **Settings** page explains both options.
sections.html:
<html data-ok-font="inter" style="font-size: 18px">
  …
</html>
sections.title: Change the font and text size

sections.body:
- Choose the heading element by the page structure, and the variant by the look you need. For example, a section title can be an `<h2>` styled as `h4`.
- Sizes are in `rem`, so text follows the user's browser font size and zoom.
- Body text has a line height of at least 1.5, as WCAG 2.2 recommends for readability.
- Don't set text in all capitals for long content: the `overline` and `button` variants are meant for short labels.
sections.title: Accessibility

sections.body: An icon button is an action shown as an icon only, such as in a toolbar, a table row or a card. Because there is no visible label, use it for actions people recognize from the icon alone, and always give it a name. For actions that need words, use a **Button**.
sections.html:
<!-- Load once per page -->
<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@owlky/html@0/dist/owlky.css">

<button type="button" data-ok-icon-button data-ok-color="default" data-ok-size="md" aria-label="Delete">
  <svg aria-hidden="true" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><path d="M4 7h16" /><path d="M10 11v6" /><path d="M14 11v6" /><path d="M6 7l1 12a2 2 0 0 0 2 2h6a2 2 0 0 0 2-2l1-12" /><path d="M9 7V4h6v3" /></svg>
</button>
sections.title: Overview

sections.body: The default color is a soft grey that suits most toolbars. Use `inherit` to take the surrounding text color, or a palette color to give the action meaning, such as `error` for a destructive one.
sections.html:
<button type="button" data-ok-icon-button data-ok-color="error" data-ok-size="md" aria-label="Delete">
  <svg aria-hidden="true" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><path d="M4 7h16" /><path d="M10 11v6" /><path d="M14 11v6" /><path d="M6 7l1 12a2 2 0 0 0 2 2h6a2 2 0 0 0 2-2l1-12" /><path d="M9 7V4h6v3" /></svg>
</button>
sections.title: Pick a color

sections.body: Three sizes are available: `sm`, `md` (the default) and `lg`. Every size keeps a touch target of at least 24 × 24px. Inside a row of content, set `edge` to `start` or `end` so the icon lines up with the content edge instead of the button's padding.
sections.html:
<button type="button" data-ok-icon-button data-ok-color="default" data-ok-size="sm" data-ok-edge="end" aria-label="Delete">
  <svg aria-hidden="true" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><path d="M4 7h16" /><path d="M10 11v6" /><path d="M14 11v6" /><path d="M6 7l1 12a2 2 0 0 0 2 2h6a2 2 0 0 0 2-2l1-12" /><path d="M9 7V4h6v3" /></svg>
</button>
sections.title: Set the size

sections.body: Set `loading` while the action runs. The icon is replaced by a spinner, the button is disabled and it tells assistive technology that it's busy.
sections.title: Show that an action is in progress

sections.body: Set `animate` to scale the button slightly when it's pressed. The animation is plain CSS and turns off when the user prefers reduced motion.
sections.html:
<button type="button" data-ok-icon-button data-ok-color="primary" data-ok-size="md" data-ok-animate aria-label="Add">
  <svg aria-hidden="true" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><path d="M12 5v14" /><path d="M5 12h14" /></svg>
</button>
sections.title: Add a press animation

sections.body: Every option works the same way in both versions: a prop in React, an attribute in HTML. Values that aren't listed fall back to the default.
sections.title: Options

sections.body: These props set the content and behavior. They aren't options, because HTML writes them as markup.
sections.title: Content and behavior

sections.body: Icon buttons are native buttons, so the browser provides the keyboard behavior.
sections.title: Keyboard

sections.body:
- An icon button has no visible label, so it **must** have a name: set `aria-label`, or `aria-labelledby` to point to visible text. Describe the action ("Delete"), not the icon ("Trash can").
- The icon is decorative and hidden from assistive technology.
- While loading, the button is disabled and marked busy (`aria-busy="true"`).
- Every size is at least 24 × 24px, and focus is shown with a 2px outline.
sections.title: Accessibility

sections.body: Image shows a picture that the browser loads only when it nears the screen. A placeholder fills the space until the picture arrives, then the picture appears with a short blur effect. You can crop the picture to an aspect ratio and paint an overlay on it. Image is a native `img` in a `span`, so it works inside links and buttons. Without JavaScript every picture shows at once.
sections.title: Overview

sections.body: Set `ratio` to give the image a fixed shape, such as `16/9` for a cover or `1/1` for a tile. The image takes the full width of its container and the height that the ratio gives. The picture covers that box and is cropped to it. Use `fit` to show the whole picture instead (`contain`), and `position` to choose which part stays in view, such as `top` for portraits. Without `ratio`, the picture keeps its own shape: set `width` and `height` to the picture's size, so the page reserves the space before it loads and doesn't shift.
sections.title: Crop to an aspect ratio

sections.body: Images load lazily by default (`loading="lazy"`), which saves data on long pages. Set `visibleByDefault` for pictures in the first screen, such as a hero: they load at once, with no placeholder and no effect. `effect` chooses how the picture appears: `blur` (the default), `opacity`, `black-and-white` or `none`. Set `placeholderSrc` to a small preview of the picture, which shows blurred while the full picture loads, or `disablePlaceholder` to show nothing. Pass `srcSet` and `sizes` so the browser picks the file that fits the screen. When people prefer reduced motion, the picture appears without the effect.
sections.title: Control loading

sections.body: Set `overlay` to paint a layer over the picture, for example to keep white text on it readable. `dark` is a 48% dark grey. A palette color, such as `primary`, is a gradient from transparent at the top to the color at 80% at the bottom. Add `overlayFrom` for a gradient between two colors: from `overlayFrom` at the bottom to `overlay` at the top. In HTML, the overlay is a `span` that you add before the `img`.
sections.title: Add an overlay

sections.body: When a picture fails to load, the placeholder stays and shows a broken-image icon. The picture's text alternative stays available to screen readers. Use `onError` in React, or the `ok:image:error` event in HTML, to log the failure or to try another source. Setting a new `src` loads the picture again.
sections.html:
<script>
  document.addEventListener("ok:image:error", (event) => {
    const img = event.target.querySelector(":scope > img");
    img.src = "fallback.jpg";
  });
</script>
sections.title: Handle errors

sections.body: Every option works the same way in both versions: a prop in React, an attribute in HTML. Values that aren't listed fall back to the default.
sections.title: Options

sections.body: The picture's own attributes go to the `img`. In React they are props of `Image`, and `imgProps` passes any other attribute.
sections.title: Content and behavior

sections.body:
- **`ok:image:load`** fires when the picture loads. `detail.src` is the file the browser picked.
- **`ok:image:error`** fires when the picture fails to load. `detail.src` is the file that failed.
- **Instance:** `runtime.get(element, "image")` returns `{ state }`: `loading`, `loaded` or `error`.
- **React:** `onLoad(event)` and `onError(event)`, the image's events.
- **State:** the root's `data-ok-state` attribute holds the same state. Don't write it in your markup.
sections.title: Events and methods

sections.body: An image isn't interactive and takes no focus. To make it a link or a button, put it inside an `a` or a `button` element.
sections.title: Keyboard

sections.body:
- `alt` is required. Describe what the picture shows, in a short sentence. Use `alt=""` for decorative pictures, so screen readers skip them.
- Inside a link or a button, the `alt` text names it: describe where the link goes or what the button does.
- The placeholder, the overlay and the error icon are hidden from assistive technology.
- A broken picture keeps its `alt` text for screen readers. Sighted users see the icon.
- White text on a picture needs a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1: add a `dark` overlay under it.
- When people prefer reduced motion, pictures appear without the transition.
sections.title: Accessibility

sections.body:
Owlky is a UI component library for dashboards and web apps. It gives your product a polished, consistent interface without locking you into one way of building it.

- **One design system everywhere.** Every component has a single markup structure, a single stylesheet and a single set of design tokens. Use it in plain HTML or through a framework package, and it looks and behaves the same.
- **Accessible by default.** Components follow the WAI-ARIA patterns, work with the keyboard and meet WCAG 2.2 level AA.
- **Easy to theme.** Every color, size and shadow is a CSS variable. Switch to dark mode, change the primary color or bring your own brand with a few lines of CSS.
- **Built on the platform.** Components use native elements, such as `<button>` and `<dialog>`, so browser features like form submission, find-in-page and focus handling keep working.
- **Small.** The complete stylesheet is about 46 kB, gzipped. The script for every interactive component is about 155 kB, and the npm packages let you load only what you use.
sections.title: Why Owlky?

sections.body:
Owlky is built in layers, so the same component can be used in many environments:

- **Markup and styles.** Each component is HTML with `data-ok-*` attributes, styled by one prebuilt stylesheet. This layer works on any page.
- **Behavior.** Interactive components, such as dialogs and tables, share one behavior core. On a plain HTML page, a small script connects it to your markup.
- **Framework packages.** A framework package renders the same markup and uses the same behavior core, with the API you expect from your framework.

Because every layer is shared, you can move between environments, or mix them on one page, without visual differences.
sections.title: How it works

sections.body:
- **`@owlky/styles`:** the prebuilt stylesheet, which needs no build step, and a theme for Tailwind CSS v4.
- **`@owlky/tokens`:** the design tokens, as CSS variables and as JavaScript values.
- **`@owlky/html`:** HTML snippets and the script that adds behavior to them. Also available from a CDN.
- **Framework packages:** components for a specific framework, such as `@owlky/react`. Support for more frameworks will follow.
- **`@owlky/core`:** the shared behavior core. Framework packages include it, so you rarely install it yourself.
- **`@owlky/mcp`:** a Model Context Protocol server for coding agents. It answers with the exact components, options, examples and tokens of your Owlky version, without a network connection.
sections.title: Packages

sections.body: Choose how you build your app. For a plain HTML page, add the stylesheet and the script from the CDN. For a framework, install its package and the stylesheet from npm.
sections.html:
<!-- In the <head> of every page -->
<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@owlky/html@0/dist/owlky.css">
<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@owlky/html@0/dist/owlky.js" defer></script>
sections.title: Install Owlky

sections.body: Copy an example from any story's **Code** panel, or write it yourself. Whichever way you build, the result is the same button.
sections.title: Add your first component

sections.body:
Every design value is a CSS variable that starts with `--ok-`. To change one, set it in your own CSS, for the whole page or for one part of it. Your values always win, because Owlky's own rules have zero specificity.

For dark mode, set `data-ok-theme="dark"` on the `<html>` element or on any container. Use `system` to follow the operating system. The **Foundations** pages describe every token.
sections.html:
<style>
  :root {
    --ok-palette-primary-main: #2065d1;
    --ok-palette-primary-dark: #103996;
    --ok-palette-primary-contrast-text: #ffffff;
    --ok-radius-md: 10px;
  }
</style>

<html data-ok-theme="dark">…</html>
sections.title: Make it yours

sections.body:
- **Foundations** explains the design tokens: colors, typography, shadows, spacing, icons and theme settings. Each page is a guide with live examples.
- **Components** lists every component. Each story shows one example. Choose plain HTML or a framework with the **Framework** menu in the toolbar: the example and its source switch together.
- Open the **Code** panel to copy an example's source, with the imports you need.
- Use the **Controls** panel to change a component's options, and the toolbar to switch the theme, primary color, font and text size for every story.
sections.title: Find your way around

sections.body: Owlky supports Chrome and Edge 114 and later, Firefox 128 and later, and Safari 17 and later. When a browser lacks a newer feature, Owlky detects it and uses a fallback that still works.
sections.title: Browser support

sections.body:
- Every component is tested with axe, in light and dark mode, and with the keyboard.
- Focus is always visible, and dialogs and drawers return focus to where it was.
- Neutral text meets a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 in every theme.
- Some things depend on your content: give icon-only buttons and scrollable regions a name, as each component's examples show.
sections.title: Accessibility

sections.body: A label is a small tag that shows a status or a category, such as Paid, Pending or Draft, in tables, cards and lists. Labels are text, not controls, and need no JavaScript. For something people can click or remove, use a **Chip**.
sections.html: Paid
sections.title: Overview

sections.body: A lightbox shows images and videos over the page, one at a time. People open it from a gallery, swipe or use the arrow keys to move between slides, zoom into details, start a slideshow, go fullscreen and close it with Escape. A toolbar, a counter, captions and a row of thumbnails come built in. The lightbox is a modal dialog, so the page behind it is inert and focus returns to the picture that opened it.
sections.html:
Mountain lake

…
…
…
sections.title: Overview

sections.body: In React, pass the slides as data. An image slide has a `src`, an `alt` text and, ideally, its natural `width` and `height`, so the lightbox knows how far it can zoom before the image gets blurry. Add `srcSet` for other sizes of the same image. A video slide has `type: "video"`, its `sources` and a `poster`, plus the usual video settings such as `muted` or `autoPlay` (the video plays when its slide becomes current). `title` and `description` become the captions. `thumbnail` sets another picture for the thumbnail. In HTML, write the same markup the React version renders: one slide per item, with the image or video inside `data-ok-lightbox-zoom`.
sections.html:
Color bands

A short clip.
sections.title: Describe the slides

sections.body: Put a `LightboxTrigger` per picture inside `Lightbox`: it opens the lightbox at its `index`. In HTML, give the dialog an `id` and point each trigger at it with `data-ok-lightbox-open` and `data-ok-index`. To control the lightbox yourself, pass `open` with `onOpenChange`, and `index` with `onIndexChange`. `onOpenChange` receives the reason for closing: `escape`, `backdrop`, `pull` or `close` (the close button).
sections.title: Open the lightbox

sections.body: The zoom buttons, the slideshow button, the fullscreen button, the counter and the close button are on by default, like the thumbnails and the captions. Turn each one off with `disableZoom`, `disableSlideshow`, `disableFullscreen`, `disableTotal`, `disableThumbnails` and `disableCaptions`. Turn on more buttons with `download`, `share` and `rotate`, and add toggles for the captions and the thumbnails with `captionsShowToggle` and `thumbnailsShowToggle`. The share button uses the browser's share sheet and only shows where the browser offers one, and the fullscreen button only shows where fullscreen is available. In React, add your own buttons with `toolbarButtons`.
sections.html:
<dialog id="photos" data-ok-lightbox data-ok-theme="dark" aria-label="Lightbox"
  data-ok-download data-ok-share data-ok-rotate data-ok-disable-slideshow
  data-ok-captions-show-toggle data-ok-thumbnails-show-toggle>…</dialog>
sections.react:
<Lightbox
  slides={slides}
  download
  share
  rotate
  disableSlideshow
  captionsShowToggle
  thumbnailsShowToggle
/>
sections.title: Choose the toolbar buttons

sections.body: Zoom in with the toolbar, the plus and minus keys, a double click or double tap, a pinch, or Ctrl and the mouse wheel. Then drag, use the arrow keys or the wheel to move around the image. An image zooms until one image pixel covers one screen pixel (`maxZoomPixelRatio`), so give images their natural `width` and `height`. `zoomInMultiplier` sets the size of each step, `doubleClickMaxStops` how many steps a double click goes through, and `scrollToZoom` lets the wheel zoom without Ctrl. Images that are no larger than the screen don't zoom.
sections.html:
<dialog id="photos" data-ok-lightbox … data-ok-max-zoom-pixel-ratio="2"
  data-ok-zoom-in-multiplier="1.5" data-ok-scroll-to-zoom>…</dialog>
sections.react: <Lightbox slides={slides} maxZoomPixelRatio={2} zoomInMultiplier={1.5} scrollToZoom />
sections.title: Zoom and pan

sections.body: Thumbnails sit at the `bottom` by default. Set `thumbnailsPosition` to `top`, `start` or `end` to move them, and change their size with `thumbnailsWidth`, `thumbnailsHeight`, `thumbnailsBorder`, `thumbnailsBorderRadius`, `thumbnailsPadding` and `thumbnailsGap` (in pixels). `thumbnailsImageFit` crops them to fill (`cover`) or shows the whole picture (`contain`). The row fades out at its edges unless `thumbnailsVignette` is `false`.
sections.html:
<dialog id="photos" data-ok-lightbox … data-ok-thumbnails-position="end"
  data-ok-thumbnails-width="96" data-ok-thumbnails-height="64">…</dialog>
sections.react: <Lightbox slides={slides} thumbnailsPosition="end" thumbnailsWidth={96} thumbnailsHeight={64} />
sections.title: Place the thumbnails

sections.body: Set `inline` to place the lightbox in the page as a carousel, with the same toolbar, captions and thumbnails but no close button. In HTML, use a `div` with `data-ok-inline` instead of the dialog. It is 3:2 by default: change the size with your own CSS.
sections.html: …
sections.react: <Lightbox slides={slides} inline />
sections.title: Show it inline

sections.body: Escape and the close button always close the lightbox, unless you set `closeOnEscape` to `false`. Set `closeOnBackdropClick` to close it with a click beside the image, and `closeOnPullDown` or `closeOnPullUp` to close it when people pull the slide down or up. `finite` stops the slides at both ends instead of looping, and `disableSwipeNavigation` keeps swipes from changing slides.
sections.html:
<dialog id="photos" data-ok-lightbox … data-ok-close-on-backdrop-click
  data-ok-close-on-pull-down data-ok-finite>…</dialog>
sections.react: <Lightbox slides={slides} closeOnBackdropClick closeOnPullDown finite />
sections.title: Close the lightbox

sections.body: Every option works the same way in both versions: a prop in React, an attribute in HTML. Values that aren't listed fall back to the default.
sections.title: Options

sections.body: These props set content and callbacks. They aren't options, because HTML writes them as markup or listens to events.
sections.title: Content and behavior

sections.body:
- **`ok:lightbox:open`** and **`ok:lightbox:close`** fire on the dialog, with `detail.reason` when it closes. **`beforeopen`** and **`beforeclose`** come first and can be canceled.
- **Other events:** `view` (`detail.index`), `click` (`detail.index`), `zoom` (`detail.zoom`), `rotate` (`detail.index`, `detail.rotation`), `fullscreen`, `slideshow` (`detail.playing`), `captions` and `thumbnails` (`detail.visible`). **`download`** and **`share`** can be canceled to replace the default action.
- **Instance:** `runtime.get(dialog, "lightbox")` returns `open(index)`, `close()`, `prev()`, `next()`, `goTo(index)`, `zoomIn()`, `zoomOut()`, `changeZoom(zoom)`, `rotateClockwise()`, `rotateCounterClockwise()`, `enterFullscreen()`, `exitFullscreen()`, `play()`, `pause()`, `showCaptions()`, `hideCaptions()`, `showThumbnails()`, `hideThumbnails()`, `download()` and `share()`, and the current `index`, `zoom`, `maxZoom`, `rotation` and `fullscreen`.
- **React:** `apiRef` receives the same methods. Callbacks are `onOpenChange(open, reason)`, `onIndexChange(index)`, `onSlideClick(index)`, `onZoomChange(zoom)`, `onRotate(index, rotation)`, `onFullscreenChange(fullscreen)`, `onSlideshowChange(playing)`, `onCaptionsChange(visible)`, `onThumbnailsChange(visible)`, `onDownload(index)` and `onShare(index)`.
sections.title: Events and methods

sections.body: Keys work anywhere in the lightbox, except inside a video, whose own controls keep their keys.
sections.title: Keyboard

sections.body:
- The lightbox is a modal dialog named "Lightbox": the page behind it is inert, Tab stays inside, and focus returns to the trigger when it closes.
- Give every image an `alt` text. Triggers take their name from the picture inside them.
- Only the current slide is reachable: the others are inert, and a polite live region announces the slide people move to.
- Every toolbar button has a name, and toggles change their name with their state, such as **Enter Fullscreen** and **Exit Fullscreen**. Buttons that can't act, such as zooming past the limit, stay focusable and say they're unavailable.
- The slideshow never starts on its own when the system asks for reduced motion, and it has a pause button.
- Zoom levels and failures (a download that didn't work) are read out in a polite live region.
sections.title: Accessibility

sections.body:
A linear progress indicator is a thin bar that shows that something is happening. It fills the width of its container, so it fits at the top of a card, a table or a page.

Use the **indeterminate** or **query** variant while you can't tell how long a task takes. Use the **determinate** or **buffer** variant when you know how far it has got. Each indicator is a `progressbar` for assistive technology: give it a name.
sections.title: Overview

sections.body: Set `variant` to `determinate` and pass `value`, from `min` (default 0) to `max` (default 100). The determinate bar has one part. In HTML, the value is the `aria-valuenow` attribute: change it, and the runtime moves the bar. Values outside the range are clamped.
sections.title: Show how far a task has got

sections.body: The `buffer` variant shows two values: `value` (how far playback or processing has got) and `valueBuffer` (how far loading has got). Dots move along the rest of the bar. In HTML, the buffer is the `data-ok-value-buffer` attribute, and the markup starts with a `data-ok-linear-progress-dashed` part.
sections.react: <LinearProgress variant="buffer" value={30} valueBuffer={45} aria-label="Video" />
sections.title: Show what is buffered

sections.body: The `query` variant moves from the end to the start. Use it while a request waits for an answer, then switch to `determinate` once the progress is known.
sections.react: <LinearProgress variant="query" aria-label="Searching" />
sections.title: Show a request before loading starts

sections.body: The default color is `primary`. Use another palette color, such as `success` or `error`, to match the context. Use `inherit` to take the text color of the surrounding element. The track behind the bar is the same color at 24% opacity.
sections.react: <LinearProgress color="inherit" aria-label="Loading" />
sections.title: Choose a color

sections.body: Put the value next to the bar when people need the exact number. For values that aren't percentages, such as floors or steps, set `aria-valuetext` so assistive technology reads the same text.
sections.html: Step 3 of 5
sections.react: Step 3 of 5
sections.title: Show the value as text

sections.body: Every option works the same way in both versions: a prop in React, an attribute in HTML. Values that aren't listed or aren't valid numbers fall back to the default.
sections.title: Options

sections.body: These props name the indicator. They aren't options, because HTML writes them as markup.
sections.title: Content and behavior

sections.body:
- **HTML:** there are no events or instance methods. Change `aria-valuenow`, `aria-valuemin`, `aria-valuemax` or `data-ok-value-buffer`, and the runtime moves the bars. It writes private CSS custom properties through the CSS object model, so it works under a strict Content Security Policy.
- **React:** render with a new `value`. The bar positions are set with the `style` prop. On server-rendered pages with a Content Security Policy that blocks inline styles, the bars move to their values once the page hydrates.
- The bar eases to a new value in 300ms. If the value changes many times per second, the bar trails behind it.
sections.title: Events and methods

sections.body: Progress indicators don't take focus and have no keyboard interaction.
sections.title: Keyboard

sections.body:
- Each indicator has `role="progressbar"`. Name it with `aria-label` or `aria-labelledby`.
- Determinate and buffer indicators report their value with `aria-valuenow`, `aria-valuemin` and `aria-valuemax`. The buffer value is visual only.
- When an indicator stands for a region that is loading, set `aria-busy="true"` on that region until it's ready, and point the region's `aria-describedby` at the indicator.
- With reduced motion turned on, the bars sweep at half speed, the dots stop and values change without easing.
- Brand colors follow the design. Light colors such as `warning` have a contrast ratio below 3:1 on white, so don't rely on the bar alone to tell people something important.
- The bar fills from left to right in every language.
sections.title: Accessibility

sections.body: A link takes the reader to another page or to another place on the same page. It is a Typography element with link styles: by default it keeps the font of the text around it, uses the primary color and is always underlined, so readers can tell it apart from the text without relying on color. It needs no JavaScript.
sections.html: Read the setup guide before you start.
sections.title: Overview

sections.body:
Set `color` to a palette color, such as `primary` (the default) or `error`, to a text tone such as `textSecondary`, or to `inherit` to use the color of the text around the link. Set `variant` to a step of the type scale, such as `body2`. The default, `inherit`, keeps the surrounding font.

Set `underline` to `always` (the default), `hover` or `none`. Keep `always` for links inside running text: without an underline, a link in a sentence is told apart by its color only, which some readers can't see. Use `hover` or `none` where the context already shows that the text is a link, such as navigation menus and breadcrumbs.
sections.html: Privacy Terms
sections.title: Set the color, style and underline

sections.body:
Add `target="_blank"` only when readers need to keep the current page, such as a form in progress. In React, the link then always gets `rel="noopener noreferrer"`, so the new page can't control the current one through `window.opener` and gets no referrer. Tokens that you pass in `rel` are kept. In HTML, write `rel="noopener noreferrer"` yourself. Tell screen reader users that the link opens a new tab, for example in its `aria-label`.

Owlky passes `href` to the element as you write it: validate addresses that come from users before you render them.
sections.html: WCAG overview
sections.title: Open a link in a new tab

sections.body: When the text runs an action instead of going to an address, render a button: screen readers announce it as a button, and Space activates it. In React, a `Link` without `href` and without `component` renders `<button type="button">`. You can also pass `component="button"`. In HTML, write a `button` with the same attributes.
sections.html: <button type="button" data-ok-typography data-ok-link data-ok-variant="body2" data-ok-color="primary" data-ok-underline="always">Show more details</button>
sections.title: Use a link style for an action

sections.body: To navigate on the client without a full page load, pass your router's link component in `component`, with the props it needs, such as `to`. Link adds its attributes to that component, which must pass them, and its `ref`, to the element it renders. In HTML, the router renders the `a` element: add the attributes to it.
sections.html: Settings
sections.title: Use a routing library

sections.body: Every option works the same way in both versions: a prop in React, an attribute in HTML. A link also takes the Typography options `align`, `gutterBottom` and `noWrap`. In HTML, write every attribute, including `data-ok-typography`: values that aren't listed get no link styles.
sections.title: Options

sections.body: These props set the content, the element and the destination. They aren't options, because HTML writes them as markup.
sections.title: Content and behavior

sections.body: Link has no events or methods of its own. Use the element's native events, such as `click`.
sections.title: Events and methods

sections.body: Links and link buttons are native elements, so they keep the browser's keyboard behavior.
sections.title: Keyboard

sections.body:
- Write link text that says where the link goes, such as "Download the 2025 report". Avoid "click here" and "read more".
- Keep `underline="always"` for links inside text. Color alone doesn't tell a link apart from the text around it.
- Palette colors use their main tone, which can be below a contrast ratio of 4.5:1 for small text. Use `textPrimary`, `textSecondary` or `inherit` on neutral text when you need that ratio.
- A focused link shows a 2px focus ring in the primary text color.
- Use a button, not a link without `href`, for actions: a link without `href` can't take focus.
sections.title: Accessibility

sections.body: A list shows rows of text, icons, avatars and controls, one below the other. It is a native `<ul>`, so assistive technology announces the number of items. Rows are plain list items, or buttons and links when people can choose them. Lists need no JavaScript, except to open and close nested lists in HTML.
sections.title: Overview

sections.body:
A row is a list item with up to four parts, in this order:

- **Icon or avatar:** `ListItemIcon` or `ListItemAvatar`, 16px before the text.
- **Text:** `ListItemText` with a `primary` line and an optional `secondary` line in the secondary text color.
- **Control:** a switch or another control at the end of the row.
- **End action:** `secondaryAction`, such as an icon button, placed 16px from the end.

Set `alignItems` to `flex-start` when the text wraps to several lines, so the icon or avatar stays next to the first line.
sections.html: • … Photos Jan 9, 2014
sections.react:
<ListItem>
  <ListItemAvatar>
    <Avatar>
      <ImageIcon />
    </Avatar>
  </ListItemAvatar>
  <ListItemText primary="Photos" secondary="Jan 9, 2014" />
</ListItem>
sections.title: Build a row

sections.body: Put a `ListItemButton` in a list item with `disablePadding`: the button then fills the row. It is a native `<button type="button">`, or an `<a>` when you set `href`. Use `selected` to highlight the current choice with a primary tint. Because the tint is color only, also set `aria-current`: `"page"` in navigation, `"true"` otherwise.
sections.html: • Drafts
sections.react:
<ListItem disablePadding>
  <ListItemButton href="/drafts" selected aria-current="page">
    <ListItemText primary="Drafts" />
  </ListItemButton>
</ListItem>
sections.title: Make rows clickable

sections.body: A subheader names the list. It is the first list item and sticks to the top while the list scrolls. Give it an `id` and point the list's `aria-labelledby` at it. Set `disableSticky` to let it scroll away.
sections.html:
• Settings
    • …
sections.react:
<List
  aria-labelledby="settings-title"
  subheader={<ListSubheader id="settings-title">Settings</ListSubheader>}
>
  …
</List>
sections.title: Add a subheader

sections.body:
Put a list inside a list item, after the item's button. Its rows start 32px in. To open and close it, give the button `aria-expanded` and `aria-controls` with the nested list's `id`, and add a `ListItemExpandIcon`: its chevron points down while the list is closed and up while it is open.

To animate the height as it opens and closes, make the nested list a Collapse.

- **HTML:** the runtime toggles `aria-expanded` on the button and `hidden` on the nested list when the button is clicked. Add `data-ok-collapse` to the nested list to animate it.
- **React:** keep the open state in your component and set `aria-expanded` from it. Render the nested list with `<Collapse component={List} in={open}>`: it sets `hidden` while the list is closed.
sections.html: • …
sections.title: Nest lists

sections.body: A row can hold a checkbox or a switch. Don't put a control inside a `ListItemButton`: a control inside a button can't be reached or announced reliably. Instead, label the control with the row's text: a `<label>` around the text for a checkbox at the start, or `aria-labelledby` with the text's `id` for a switch at the end.
sections.html: • … Wi-Fi
sections.react:
<ListItem>
  <ListItemIcon>
    <WifiIcon />
  </ListItemIcon>
  <ListItemText id="wifi-label" primary="Wi-Fi" />
  <Switch edge="end" aria-labelledby="wifi-label" defaultChecked />
</ListItem>
sections.title: Add controls to rows

sections.body: Every option works the same way in both versions: a prop in React, an attribute in HTML. `dense` on the list makes every row compact. Values that aren't listed fall back to the default.
sections.title: Options

sections.body: These props set the content. They aren't options, because HTML writes them as markup.
sections.title: Content and behavior

sections.body:
- **`ok:list:toggle`** (cancelable) fires on the list before a nested list opens or closes. `event.detail` is `{ open, list }`: the new state and the nested list.
- **Instance:** `runtime.get(element, "list")` returns `{ toggle(button, open?) }`.
- **React:** handle `onClick` on the `ListItemButton` and update your state.
sections.title: Events and methods

sections.body: List item buttons and links are native, so they follow the browser's keyboard behavior.
sections.title: Keyboard

sections.body:
- Wrap navigation lists in a `<nav>` with an `aria-label`, and mark the current page with `aria-current="page"`.
- Icons in rows are decorative (`aria-hidden="true"`): the text names the row.
- Secondary text uses the secondary text color, with a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1, also on a selected row.
- Disabled buttons are native `disabled`. Disabled links lose their `href` and get `aria-disabled="true"`.
sections.title: Accessibility

sections.body:
A map shows places and data that people can pan, zoom, tilt and turn. It is drawn by MapLibre GL JS, an open-source map engine, so both versions share the same behavior and markup. Around the map, Owlky draws its own controls, markers, popups and panels, which follow your theme and work with the keyboard.

The map is a separate script so that pages without one don't download the map engine. Load `owlky-map.js` after `owlky.js`. It finds its worker, `owlky-map-worker.js`, next to itself. With npm, import `@owlky/html/map` (HTML) or use the map components of `@owlky/react`, and point `setMapWorkerUrl()` at `@owlky/core/map-worker.js`.

Owlky includes no map tiles. Pass the URL of a MapLibre style, for example one of OpenFreeMap's free styles, and keep the credits that the style requires.
sections.html: …
sections.title: Overview

sections.body:
`mapStyle` sets the style: a URL of a MapLibre style JSON, or the style object itself. Add `mapStyleDark` to switch styles when the map sits in a dark theme, such as the **Theme** menu's dark mode or a `data-ok-theme="dark"` area. Without it, the map keeps one style in both themes.

In HTML, change `data-ok-map-style` to switch the style later. In React, pass a new `mapStyle`, and keep style objects in a constant or `useMemo`, because a new object reloads the style.

Layer colors can use Owlky tokens: write `"var(--ok-palette-info-main)"` as a paint value. The map reads the token's value, and reads it again when the theme changes.
sections.html: …
sections.react: <MapView mapStyle="https://tiles.openfreemap.org/styles/positron" mapStyleDark="https://tiles.openfreemap.org/styles/dark" />
sections.title: Choose the map style

sections.body:
A marker sits on a point given by `longitude` and `latitude`. By default it is a pin in the `color` you choose. Set `anchor` to `bottom` for pins, so the tip touches the point. Give interactive markers a name with `aria-label`: a marker with a click handler or `draggable` is a button that people reach with Tab.

A popup is a dialog that points at a place. It picks the side where it fits unless you set `anchor`, and `offset` moves it away from its marker. Escape, the close button and a click on the map close it. In React, a popup shows while you render it, and `onClose` asks you to remove it. In HTML, write popups with `hidden` and open them from a marker with `data-ok-map-popup-open`.

With `draggable`, people drag a marker or move it with the arrow keys. In HTML the marker stores its new position in its attributes. In React, update `longitude` and `latitude` in `onDragEnd`. Also let people place a marker with a click, because dragging is hard for some people.
sections.html: Capital of France
sections.title: Add markers and popups

sections.body:
A source holds data, such as GeoJSON points or polygons, and its layers draw it as circles, fills, lines, labels or a heatmap. The `paint`, `layout` and `filter` values follow the MapLibre style specification. A GeoJSON source can group nearby points in clusters with `cluster`.

In HTML, sources and layers are hidden elements inside the map. Write their `paint`, `layout` and `filter` as JSON in single-quoted attributes. Change an attribute, for example `data-ok-filter`, and the map updates the layer. For data that changes every frame, call `setSourceData(id, data)` on the instance instead.
sections.title: Show data on the map

sections.body: List the layers people can point at in `interactiveLayerIds` (HTML: `data-ok-interactive-layer-ids`, separated by spaces). Mouse events then report the features under the pointer in `features`, and the cursor turns into a pointer over them. `onMouseEnter` and `onMouseLeave` fire when the pointer enters or leaves those features. Use them for highlights and hover popups. Give a hover popup `closeButton={false}`, `closeOnClick={false}` and `focusAfterOpen={false}`.
sections.html: …
sections.react:
<MapView
  interactiveLayerIds={["states-fill"]}
  onMouseMove={(event) => console.log(event.features?.[0]?.properties.name)}
/>
sections.title: Respond to the pointer

sections.body:
`initialViewState` sets where the map starts: `longitude`, `latitude`, `zoom`, `pitch` and `bearing`, or `bounds` to fit. To control the view, pass `viewState` and update it from `onMove`. The map ref has `flyTo`, `easeTo`, `jumpTo` and `fitBounds`, and `getMap()` returns the MapLibre map for anything else.

In HTML, the root's `data-ok-longitude`, `data-ok-latitude` and `data-ok-zoom` set the view, and the map moves when you change them. Any element with `data-ok-map-fly-to="<map id>"` and `data-ok-view="longitude,latitude,zoom"` flies the map there when it is clicked, or when a radio button is selected. With reduced motion, the map jumps instead of flying.
sections.html:
<button type="button" data-ok-map-fly-to="world" data-ok-view="139.69,35.69,10">
  Tokyo
</button>
sections.react:
const mapRef = useRef(null);
// …
<MapView ref={mapRef} … />
<button type="button"
  onClick={() => mapRef.current?.flyTo({ center: [139.69, 35.69], zoom: 10 })}>
  Tokyo
</button>
sections.title: Move the map

sections.body:
Controls sit in the corners of the map: `NavigationControl` (zoom and a compass you can drag to turn the map), `GeolocateControl`, `FullscreenControl`, `ScaleControl`, `GlobeControl`, `TerrainControl` and `AttributionControl`, which every map shows unless you turn it off with `attributionControl={false}`. Place them with `position`, and add your own buttons in a `MapControl`. In HTML, write the controls inside the four corner elements.

Put settings and readouts in a `MapPanel`: a dark, translucent card in a corner of the map.
sections.react:
<MapView …>
  <NavigationControl position="bottom-left" />
  <ScaleControl position="bottom-left" />
  <FullscreenControl position="top-left" />
</MapView>
sections.title: Add controls

sections.body: The map accepts only `http` and `https` URLs for styles, data and tiles, and shows the credits of a style as text and links, never as HTML. Its engine draws in a Web Worker. With a Content Security Policy, allow the worker with `worker-src 'self'`, and add `blob:` when the worker comes from another origin, such as a CDN. Pages that enforce Trusted Types need a policy for the worker's URL.
sections.title: Use the map on a strict page

sections.body: Every option works the same way in both versions: a prop in React, an attribute in HTML. The map's options come first, then the marker, popup and control options.
sections.title: Options

sections.body: These props set the style, the content and the callbacks. They aren't options, because HTML writes them as markup or listens to events.
sections.title: Content and behavior

sections.body:
- **`ok:map:load`**, **`ok:map:move`**, **`ok:map:moveend`**, **`ok:map:click`**, **`ok:map:mousemove`**, **`ok:map:mouseenter`**, **`ok:map:mouseleave`** and the other map events fire on the map with `detail.viewState`, and for pointer events `lngLat`, `point` and `features`.
- **`ok:map:popupopen`** and **`ok:map:popupclose`** fire on a popup. `popupclose` has `detail.reason` and can be canceled to keep it open.
- **`ok:map:markerdragstart`**, **`ok:map:markerdrag`** and **`ok:map:markerdragend`** fire on a marker with `detail.lngLat`.
- **`ok:map:fullscreen`**, **`ok:map:geolocate`**, **`ok:map:geolocateerror`**, **`ok:map:trackuserlocation`** and **`ok:map:fallback`** report the controls and a map that can't draw.
- **Instance:** `runtime.get(element, "map")` returns `{ map, controller, viewState, flyTo, easeTo, jumpTo, fitBounds, setSourceData(id, data), getClusterExpansionZoom(source, id), openPopup(popup), closePopup(popup), fullscreen, setFullscreen(on) }`.
- **React:** event props such as `onLoad`, `onMove`, `onClick`, `onMouseMove` and `onMouseEnter`; a ref with `getMap()`, `flyTo`, `easeTo`, `jumpTo` and `fitBounds`; and `useMap()` inside a map or a `MapProvider`.
sections.title: Events and methods

sections.body: The map itself is one stop in the Tab order. With focus on the map, the keys below move it. Markers that people can click or drag, popups and controls are buttons in the Tab order.
sections.title: Keyboard

sections.body:
- Name each map with `aria-label` (HTML: `data-ok-label`). Without a name, it is called "Map".
- Describe what the map shows with `description` (HTML: a `p[data-ok-map-description]` with an `id`). Screen readers read it with the map, and it replaces the map when the browser can't draw it.
- Give every interactive marker a name. People can open its popup with Enter or Space, and move a draggable marker with the arrow keys.
- A popup takes focus when it opens and gives it back when it closes, unless you turn off `focusAfterOpen`.
- Controls have names and states: fullscreen and globe report `aria-pressed`, and the location result is announced.
- Moving content needs a way to pause it, and animations respect reduced motion.
sections.title: Accessibility

sections.body:
Markdown turns Markdown text into styled content: headings, paragraphs, links, lists, task lists, tables, code, images and quotes. It reads GitHub Flavored Markdown by default. Both versions run the same parser, built on unified, and build the content with DOM methods or React elements, never from an HTML string.

Markdown is a separate script so that pages without it don't download the parser. Load `owlky-markdown.js` after `owlky.js`, or import `@owlky/html/markdown` after `@owlky/html/auto`. In HTML, write the Markdown inside a `pre[data-ok-markdown-source]` element. Escape `&` and `<` as `&` and `<`, as for any text in HTML. Without JavaScript, the page shows the Markdown text itself.
sections.html:
## Release notes

- [x] Faster start-up
- [ ] Offline mode

Read the [changelog](https://example.com/changelog).
sections.title: Overview

sections.body:
By default, HTML in the Markdown shows as text, so content from people can't add elements to your page. Turn on `rawHtml` to render it. The HTML then goes through an allow list, the same one GitHub uses, plus `u`, `mark` and the `text-align` and `text-transform` styles. Scripts, event handler attributes, forms, frames and unknown elements are removed. Turn on `skipHtml` to drop the HTML instead.

To allow more, pass your own `sanitizeSchema`. Extend `markdownSanitizeSchema` rather than writing one from scratch, because a missing rule can let unsafe markup through.
sections.html: Press <kbd>Ctrl</kbd> + <kbd>S</kbd> to save.
sections.title: Render HTML in Markdown

sections.body:
Every URL in `href`, `src` and similar attributes goes through `urlTransform`. The default, `defaultUrlTransform`, keeps relative URLs and the `http`, `https`, `mailto`, `irc`, `ircs` and `xmpp` protocols, and empties anything else, such as `javascript:` or `data:` URLs. Pass your own function to rewrite URLs, for example to send images through a proxy. Keep the default checks in it, because an unchecked URL can run script when it is clicked.

Turn on `externalLinks` to open absolute `http` and `https` links in a new tab. Links that open a new tab always get `rel="noopener noreferrer"`.
sections.html: See the [documentation](https://example.com/docs).
sections.title: Control links and URLs

sections.body: Pass `allowedElements` to keep only those tag names, or `disallowedElements` to remove some. You can't use both. A removed element disappears with its content, unless `unwrapDisallowed` is on: then its content stays in place. In JavaScript, `allowElement(element, index, parent)` decides element by element after those lists.
sections.html:
# Title

Some **bold** text.
sections.title: Allow only some elements

sections.body: Set `images` to `image` to render every picture as an Image component: it loads lazily, shows a placeholder until it arrives and appears with a short blur effect. Add `imageRatio`, such as `16/9`, to crop every picture to the same shape. By default, pictures are plain `img` elements that keep their own size. In HTML, the Image needs the script, which also renders the Markdown. In React, a `components.img` replacement takes precedence.
sections.html: ![A quiet beach at sunrise](beach.jpg)
sections.title: Show pictures as Image

sections.body:
In React, `components` replaces elements by tag name, with a component or another tag name. Each component receives the element's props and `node`, its syntax tree node. Both versions take remark plugins (`remarkPlugins`, for Markdown syntax) and rehype plugins (`rehypePlugins`, for the HTML tree), and `remarkRehypeOptions`. In HTML, pass them to `createMarkdown()` and register the result. Plugins run with the same rights as your code: use only plugins you trust.

`Markdown` processes the text synchronously. For asynchronous plugins, use `MarkdownAsync` on a server or `MarkdownHooks` in the browser, which shows `fallback` while it works. In HTML, pass `async: true` to `createMarkdown()`.
sections.html:
<script type="module">
  import { createMarkdown, getRuntime } from "@owlky/html";
  import remarkMath from "remark-math";

  // Register this definition instead of loading owlky-markdown.js
  getRuntime().register(createMarkdown({ remarkPlugins: [remarkMath] })).start();
</script>
sections.title: Replace elements and add plugins

sections.body: Fenced code with a language, such as ` ```js `, shows plain text unless you give Markdown a highlighter, because syntax grammars are large. Pass a lowlight instance, which uses the highlight.js grammars. Code without a language, or in a language the highlighter doesn't know, stays plain.
sections.html:
<script type="module">
  import { createMarkdown, getRuntime } from "@owlky/html";
  import { common, createLowlight } from "lowlight";

  getRuntime().register(createMarkdown({ highlighter: createLowlight(common) })).start();
</script>
sections.title: Highlight code

sections.body: Every option works the same way in both versions: a prop in React, an attribute in HTML.
sections.title: Options

sections.body: These props set the content and the pipeline. Lists are attributes in HTML; functions and plugins go to `createMarkdown()`.
sections.title: Content and behavior

sections.body:
- **`ok:markdown:render`** fires on the root after every render, with the Markdown in `detail.value`.
- **`ok:markdown:error`** fires when the Markdown can't be rendered, for example with both `allowedElements` and `disallowedElements`, with `detail.error`. The Markdown text stays visible.
- **Instance:** `runtime.get(element, "markdown")` returns `{ value, setValue(markdown), render() }`. Changing the source element's text or an option attribute renders again by itself.
- **React:** the content follows `children`. `MarkdownHooks` reports failures through `onError`.

sections.body: Markdown adds no keys of its own. Links in the content are in the Tab order and open with Enter, like any link.
sections.title: Keyboard

sections.body:
- Headings keep their level, so the content joins the page outline. Use `components` (React) or plugins to shift levels when the content sits under a page heading.
- Images need alternative text: write it between the brackets, as in `![A chart of sales](chart.png)`.
- Task list boxes are read-only checkboxes, announced as checked or not checked.
- Code blocks wrap long lines instead of scrolling, so they stay readable at 320 pixels wide without a keyboard trap.
- The footnotes' heading is visually hidden but read by screen readers.

sections.body: A menu shows a list of choices on a popover. Opening it moves focus to the selected item, or the first one. Choosing an item closes the menu, and focus returns to the button that opened it.

sections.title: Overview

sections.body: Mark the current choice with `selected`: it is bold and tinted, and the menu focuses it when it opens. Use `disabled` for a choice that isn't available: the keyboard skips it and clicks are ignored.
sections.html:

sections.react:
<MenuItem disabled>Choose an option</MenuItem>
<MenuItem selected>Show all</MenuItem>
