sections.body: In React, handle `onClick` on each `MenuItem`. The menu then asks to close with the reason `select`; call `event.preventDefault()` in the handler to keep it open. In HTML, listen for `ok:menu:select` on the menu: `event.detail.item` is the item, and `preventDefault()` keeps the menu open.
sections.html:
<script type="module">
  document.querySelector("#account-menu [data-ok-menu]").addEventListener("ok:menu:select", (event) => {
    console.log(event.detail.item.textContent);
  });
</script>
sections.react: <MenuItem onClick={() => setSort("name")}>Sort by name</MenuItem>

sections.body: The menu's popover takes the Popover options, such as `placement` (default `bottom-start` for menus). Every option works the same way in both versions.
sections.title: Options

sections.body: These props set the content and the state. They aren't options, because HTML writes them as markup or triggers.
sections.title: Content and behavior

sections.body:
- **`ok:menu:select`** (cancelable, `detail.item`) fires on the menu when an item is chosen. Then the popover closes with the reason `select`.
- The popover's events fire too: `ok:popover:open`, `ok:popover:close` (`detail.reason`: `escape`, `backdrop`, `select`, `tab`, `trigger`).
- **Instance:** `runtime.get(list, "menu")` returns `{ select(item) }`.
- **React:** `onOpenChange(false, reason)` with `escape`, `backdrop`, `select` or `tab`.
sections.title: Events and methods

sections.body: Menus follow the WAI-ARIA menu pattern.
sections.title: Keyboard

sections.body:
- The trigger has `aria-haspopup="menu"` and `aria-expanded`, and the list names itself with `aria-labelledby` pointing at the trigger.
- Focus moves into the menu when it opens and back to the trigger when it closes.
- Disabled items have `aria-disabled="true"`: they stay visible but can't be chosen.
- The selected item is bold and tinted. The tint alone isn't the only cue.

sections.body: Motion animates its content in or out. By default, it plays when the content scrolls into view, so long pages reveal their sections as you read. The animation comes from the stylesheet. The script only decides when it plays. Without the script, the content shows as usual, so nothing stays hidden. Users who ask for reduced motion see the content appear at once.
sections.html: Plans for every team
sections.title: Overview

sections.body:
`variant` names the animation. Entrances end with the content in place, and exits end with it hidden.
- **Slide, fade, zoom and bounce:** `slideInUp`, `fadeIn`, `zoomOutLeft`, `bounceInDown` and more. `Up` and `Down` name the movement, `Left` and `Right` the side it comes from or goes to.
- **Flip, scale and rotate:** `flipInX`, `flipOutY`, `scaleInX`, `scaleOutY`, `rotateIn` and `rotateOut`.
- **Backgrounds:** `kenburnsTop` and the other Ken Burns directions zoom slowly into an image. `panTop` and the other pan directions move a gradient background. `color2x` to `color5x` paint text with a moving gradient. These loop until you pause them.

`duration` sets the length of an entrance in milliseconds (640 by default), `delay` waits before it starts, and `distance` sets how far directional animations travel in pixels.
sections.html: …
sections.react: <Motion variant="zoomInLeft" duration={800} distance={80}>…</Motion>
sections.title: Choose an animation

sections.body:
`trigger` decides when the animation plays:
- **`inView` (default):** when at least `amount` of the content is visible (0.3 by default). It plays once. Set `once` to `false` to play the exit when the content leaves the view and the entrance again when it comes back.
- **`mount`:** as soon as the page loads, for content that is visible from the start.
- **`manual`:** when you set `in`. Turning `in` off plays the animation backwards. In HTML, add or remove the `data-ok-in` attribute.

Changing `variant`, `duration` or `distance` plays an entered animation again. In HTML, `replay()` plays it again too. In React, change the `key`.
sections.html: Saved
sections.title: Decide when it plays

sections.body: MotionGroup plays the Motions inside it together, one direct child after the other. `stagger` sets the time between two children, 50 milliseconds by default. The group's trigger replaces the trigger of its Motions.
sections.html:
• Design
  • Develop
  • Release
sections.title: Animate several items

sections.body: MotionText animates each letter of a short text, 25 milliseconds apart by default. Screen readers read a hidden copy of the whole text, because separate letters would be read one by one. Put MotionText inside a heading or a paragraph. In HTML, you can write the text alone: the script adds the letters.
sections.html: Owlky moves
sections.title: Animate text letter by letter

sections.body: Set `transition` on a Dialog to open its paper with a Motion entrance, such as `slideInUp` or `zoomIn`. Without it, the paper fades and scales in briefly.
sections.html:
Share your location?

…
sections.react: <Dialog open={open} onOpenChange={setOpen} transition="slideInUp">…</Dialog>
sections.title: Animate a dialog

sections.body: Ken Burns, pan and color animations keep moving. Give your users a way to pause them, because moving content that lasts more than five seconds distracts many people. Set `paused` from your own control, such as a switch or a button.
sections.title: Pause looping animations

sections.body:
Two variants aren't entrances:
- **`draw`:** traces the strokes of an SVG, then fades its fill in. Give every shape `pathLength="1"`, so the stroke length is known.
- **`interactive`:** scales the content up on hover and down while it's pressed, such as a card or a button. The element shrinks to its content. Icon buttons and floating action buttons have their own `animate` option for the same effect.
sections.title: Draw an icon or react to the pointer

sections.body: CountUp counts from `start` (0 by default) to `end` when it scrolls into view, in 2 seconds by default. Set `decimals` for digits after the decimal point, and `prefix` or `suffix` for units. Screen readers read the end value from the start, because the changing digits are hidden from them. Digits keep the same width, so the text doesn't shake.
sections.html: 200k 0k
sections.title: Count up to a number

sections.body:
MotionBorder draws a moving border around its content, such as a logo, an avatar or a button.

- **Color:** `multi` (the default) turns several brand colors all around. `inherit` (the text color) or a palette color runs one light along a faint track of the same color.
- **Second light:** `secondaryColor` adds a light in another color that starts on the opposite side. It has no effect with `multi`.
- **Shape and size:** set `shape` to `circle` for round content, `width` for the border width in pixels and `duration` for one turn.
- **Edges and corners:** the border follows the element's CSS. Set `border-width` to `0` on a side to leave it out, and set `border-radius` per corner. Your rules win over the library's, because its selectors have zero specificity.

The inside is painted with the paper color, so put the border on a paper or a page background.
sections.title: Turn a border around content

sections.body: Every option works the same way in both versions: a prop in React, an attribute in HTML. Values that aren't listed fall back to the default.
sections.title: Options

sections.body: These props aren't options, because HTML writes them as markup or reads them from the page.
sections.title: Content and behavior

sections.body:
- **`ok:motion:end`** fires on a Motion when its animation ends, with the state in `detail.state`: `enter` or `exit`.
- **Instance:** `runtime.get(element, "motion")` returns `{ state, replay() }`. MotionGroup (`"motion-group"`) and MotionText (`"motion-text"`) have the same instance. `replay()` plays the entrance again.
- **React:** use `onAnimationEnd`, and change the `key` to play the entrance again.
sections.title: Events and methods

sections.body: Motion isn't interactive. Links and buttons inside it work as usual, also while they move.
sections.title: Keyboard

sections.body:
- Content never depends on the animation: without the script, it shows, and with reduced motion it appears at once.
- Looping animations and turning borders stop with reduced motion. Provide a pause control for them anyway (WCAG 2.2.2).
- CountUp exposes its end value to assistive technologies, and hides the changing digits.
- MotionText keeps the text readable: assistive technologies read a visually hidden copy, and the letters are hidden from them.
- Avoid animations on content that people need to read right away, such as errors.
- Directional animations start outside the content's box. Clip the container (`overflow: clip`) if they would widen the page on small screens.

sections.body: An organization chart shows a hierarchy as a tree, such as the people of a company or the parts of a product. Each node holds any content you choose, such as a card with a name and a role. Lines join every node to its parent. The chart is a set of nested lists (`ul` and `li`), so screen readers announce each level and how many nodes it has. It needs no JavaScript.
sections.html:
• Maya Lindqvist, CEO
    • Jonah Pereira, design
    • Priya Raman, development
sections.title: Overview

sections.body: `OrganizationChart` is the root: its `label` is the top node and its children are the next level. Each `OrganizationChartNode` has a `label` and may hold more nodes, at any depth. In HTML, a node is an `li` with a label `div` and, when it has children, a `ul` of child nodes. Leave out the children list on nodes without children, so no line hangs below them. Labels take any content, such as cards with an avatar, a name, a role and a menu button.
sections.html:
• Priya Raman
    • Elias Novak
sections.react:
<OrganizationChartNode label="Priya Raman">
  <OrganizationChartNode label="Elias Novak" />
</OrganizationChartNode>
sections.title: Build the tree

sections.body: The line options are set on the root and apply to the whole chart. `lineColor` is `divider` by default. Set it to a palette color for its light tone, or to `inherit` to use the chart's text color, which you can set with the `color` property. `lineStyle` draws `solid`, `dashed` or `dotted` lines. Lengths are numbers in pixels, or strings with a unit such as `"1.5rem"`: `lineHeight` (40 by default) is the height of the lines between two levels, `lineWidth` (1) their thickness, `lineBorderRadius` (24) the corner radius where they turn and `nodePadding` (4) the space on each side of every node. In HTML, the lengths need the script: it turns the attributes into private CSS properties, because CSS can't read lengths from attributes. Without the script, the default lengths apply.
sections.html: …
sections.react:
<OrganizationChart
  aria-label="Company"
  label="Maya Lindqvist"
  lineColor="primary"
  lineStyle="dashed"
  lineHeight={20}
  lineBorderRadius={8}
>
  …
</OrganizationChart>
sections.title: Style the lines

sections.body: A chart is as wide as its widest level and is centered when it fits. Put it in a `Scrollbar` so that a wide chart scrolls sideways inside the page, from its first node, instead of widening the page on small screens. Name the scroll area: it takes keyboard focus so that keyboard users can scroll it.

sections.title: Scroll wide charts

sections.body: Every option works the same way in both versions: a prop in React, an attribute in HTML. Values that aren't listed, and lengths that aren't valid, fall back to the default.
sections.title: Options

sections.body: These parts hold the content. They aren't options, because HTML writes them as markup.
sections.title: Content and behavior

sections.body: A chart isn't interactive. Buttons and links in its labels work as usual, in reading order: each node, then its children. **Tab** reaches the scroll area of a wide chart, and the arrow keys scroll it.
sections.title: Keyboard

sections.body:
- The chart is a set of nested lists. Screen readers announce each level, the number of nodes in it and the position of each node.
- Name the chart with `aria-label` or `aria-labelledby`, such as the name of the team it shows.
- Lines are decorative: the list structure carries the hierarchy. Don't rely on a line color alone to convey meaning.
- Text in labels needs a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1, like any other text.
- In right-to-left pages, the chart mirrors: the first child is on the right.

sections.body:
Pagination lets people move through content that is split into pages, such as search results or a long table. It shows the current page, nearby pages, the first and last pages, and previous and next buttons. Long ranges are shortened with an ellipsis.

In HTML, write the previous and next buttons; the script builds the page buttons from `data-ok-count` and `data-ok-page`.
sections.title: Overview

sections.body: Choose how the current page stands out with `variant` (`text`, `outlined` or `soft`) and `color`. Set `shape` to `rounded` for square corners, and `size` to `sm`, `md` or `lg`.
sections.react: <Pagination count={10} variant="outlined" color="primary" shape="rounded" />
sections.title: Style the pages

sections.body: `siblingCount` sets how many pages appear on each side of the current page, and `boundaryCount` how many appear at each end. Both default to 1. Add first and last buttons with `showFirstButton` and `showLastButton` in React, or by writing those buttons in the HTML.
sections.react: <Pagination count={20} defaultPage={10} siblingCount={2} showFirstButton showLastButton />
sections.title: Control which pages are shown

sections.body: In React, slice your rows for the current page. In HTML, point the pagination at a table with `data-ok-pagination="<table id>"` and set `data-ok-rows-per-page`: the script shows only that page's rows and counts the pages for you. For a rows-per-page menu and a "1–5 of 12" label, use the table's own `TablePagination` instead.

sections.title: Options

sections.body: These props set the range, the labels and the buttons.
sections.title: Content and behavior

sections.body:
- **`ok:pagination:change`** (cancelable) fires when a page is requested, with `detail.page` (1-based).
- **Instance:** `runtime.get(element, "pagination")` returns `{ page, count, setPage(page), refresh() }`. Call `refresh()` after you change `data-ok-count`.
- **React:** `onChange(page)`. A controlled pagination refuses a change by keeping `page`.

sections.body: Every item is a native button, so the browser provides the keyboard behavior. Focus stays on the button you pressed while the pages update.

- The pagination is a `<nav>` landmark: give it an `aria-label` that says what it pages, such as "Orders pages". The default is "pagination navigation".
- The current page has `aria-current="page"`, and every button has a name such as "Go to page 3".
- Ellipses are hidden from assistive technology.
- Translate the labels with `getItemAriaLabel` in React, or `data-ok-label-page` and `data-ok-label-current` in HTML.

sections.body: Paper is a surface for content. It paints the paper background and the primary text color of the current theme, rounds its corners and raises itself with a shadow. Other surfaces, such as cards, are built on it. Paper needs no JavaScript, and it has no size or padding of its own: your layout decides them.

sections.body: Set `elevation` to a level from 0 to 24. The default is 1. A higher level casts a larger shadow, so the surface looks further away from the page. Level 0 has no shadow. Each level uses the matching `--ok-elevation-<level>` shadow, and the shadows follow the light and dark themes.

Pick the element that describes the content, such as `section`, `article` or `li`: in React with the `component` prop, in HTML by writing the attributes on that element. Paper adds no role, so the element's own meaning is what assistive technology announces.

sections.body: Paper doesn't take focus. Interactive content inside it keeps its own keyboard behavior.

sections.body:
- Paper is a visual surface only. To make it a landmark or a group, use an element with that meaning, such as `section` with a heading.
- Text on paper uses the primary text color, with a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 in the light and dark themes.

sections.body: A popover shows content next to the element that opened it, its anchor. It sits in the browser's top layer, so no container clips it, and it flips to the other side of the anchor when there is no room. A press outside or Escape asks it to close, and focus moves into it and back to the anchor.
sections.html: …
sections.title: Overview

sections.body: Set `placement` to a side of the anchor (`top`, `bottom`, `left` or `right`) and, optionally, an alignment (`-start` or `-end`). The default is `bottom`, centered. Add `arrow` to point at the anchor. The arrow sits on the side that faces the anchor and follows the anchor's center, even after a flip. For example, `bottom-start` opens the popover below its anchor with the arrow at the top left, and `top-end` opens it above with the arrow at the bottom right.
sections.html: …
sections.react:
<Popover open={open} anchorEl={anchor} placement="right-start" arrow>
  …
</Popover>
sections.title: Place the popover

sections.body: In HTML, point `data-ok-popover-hover` at the popover instead of `data-ok-popover-open`: it opens while the pointer or keyboard focus is on the trigger, and focus stays on the trigger. In React, set the anchor from the pointer and focus events, and add `disableAutoFocus` and `disableRestoreFocus`.
sections.html: …
sections.react:
<Button
  variant="outlined"
  onPointerEnter={(event) => setAnchor(event.currentTarget)}
  onPointerLeave={() => setAnchor(null)}
  onFocus={(event) => setAnchor(event.currentTarget)}
  onBlur={() => setAnchor(null)}
>
  Hover me
</Button>
<Popover open={anchor !== null} anchorEl={anchor} disableAutoFocus disableRestoreFocus>
  …
</Popover>
sections.title: Show a popover on hover

sections.body: Every option works the same way in both versions: a prop in React, an attribute in HTML. Values that aren't listed fall back to the default.
sections.title: Options

sections.body: These props set the content and the state. They aren't options, because HTML writes them as markup or triggers.
sections.title: Content and behavior

sections.body:
- **`ok:popover:beforeopen`** (cancelable) and **`ok:popover:open`** fire on the popover, with `detail.anchor`.
- **`ok:popover:beforeclose`** (cancelable) and **`ok:popover:close`** fire with `detail.reason`: `escape`, `backdrop` (a press outside), `trigger`, `select` (a menu item), `tab` or `api`.
- **Instance:** `runtime.get(element, "popover")` returns `{ isOpen, open(anchor), close(reason?), toggle(anchor) }`.
- **React:** `onOpenChange(false, reason)` reports `escape` or `backdrop`. Set `open` to close it.
sections.title: Events and methods

sections.body: The trigger is a native button. Inside the popover, Tab moves between its controls.
sections.title: Keyboard

sections.body:
- Give an interactive popover `role="dialog"` and a name (`aria-label` or `aria-labelledby`), and its trigger `aria-haspopup="dialog"`. The HTML runtime keeps the trigger's `aria-expanded` up to date.
- Focus moves into the popover when it opens and back to the trigger when it closes. Hover popovers leave focus on the trigger.
- Escape closes the top popover first, so nested popovers close one at a time.
- Popovers that only appear on hover also open on keyboard focus.
sections.title: Accessibility

sections.body:
Radio buttons let people pick exactly one option from a short list, such as a delivery method. Show every option at once; for long lists, use a text field with `select`. For a single on/off choice, use a **Checkbox** or a **Switch**.

Radios are native `<input type="radio">` elements in a `radiogroup`. The browser keeps one of them checked and moves between them with the arrow keys. They need no JavaScript.
sections.title: Overview

sections.body: A group stacks its radios in a column. Set `row` to place them side by side; they wrap on narrow screens. Use `labelPlacement` on each form control label to move the text to the `start`, `top` or `bottom`.
sections.title: Lay out the group

sections.body: The color shows on the selected radio. The default is `primary`; `default` uses the text color. The `small` size has a 36px target and a 20px circle.
sections.title: Choose a color and size

sections.body: Every option works the same way in both versions: a prop in React, an attribute in HTML. Values that aren't listed fall back to the default. The form control label has its own options.
sections.title: Options

sections.body: These props set the content and behavior. They aren't options, because HTML writes them as markup.
sections.title: Content and behavior

sections.body:
- **HTML:** the newly checked input fires the native `change` event. Read the group's value with `form.elements.delivery.value` or `querySelector("input:checked")`.
- **React:** `RadioGroup` calls `onChange(value)` with the selected radio's value. Use `value` to control it, or `defaultValue`. A `Radio` outside a group calls `onChange(checked)`.
sections.title: Events and methods

sections.body: Radios are native inputs, so the browser provides the keyboard behavior.
sections.title: Keyboard

sections.body:
- Name the group with `aria-label` or `aria-labelledby`, and each radio with a form control label (or `aria-label`).
- Only the checked radio is in the tab order; the arrow keys move the selection.
- Focus is shown with a 2px ring inside the target. The target is at least 36 × 36px.
- Unselected radios use the secondary text color, with a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1. Brand colors of selected radios follow the design.
sections.title: Accessibility

sections.body: A rating lets people give a score, such as stars for a product, and shows a score as a row of icons. It is a group of native radio buttons drawn as icons: each value has a radio with a label such as "3 Stars", so the keyboard, screen readers and forms work as they do for any radio group. A last, hidden radio means no rating.
sections.title: Overview

sections.body: Clicking an icon chooses its value. Clicking the chosen icon again clears the rating, so `onChange` receives `null`. `max` sets the number of icons (5 by default). Set `precision` to `0.5` (or `0.25`) for half values: each icon then holds two radios, and the left half of the icon is its own target.
sections.title: Choose and clear a value

sections.body: Set `readOnly` to show a score without radios. The rating is then one image named by its value, for example "2.5 Stars". `disabled` keeps the radios but dims them and ignores input.
sections.title: Show a score

sections.body: `icon` replaces the star and `emptyIcon` the empty one. `renderIcon` returns a different icon per value, for example faces from unhappy to happy, and works well with `highlightSelectedOnly`, which fills only the chosen icon. `color` picks the palette color of filled icons (`warning` by default). Name the values with `getLabelText`.
sections.title: Change the icons and the color

sections.body: While the pointer is over the icons, they show the value under it, and that icon grows slightly. `onChangeActive` reports that value, or `null` when the pointer leaves, so you can show a label such as "Good". In HTML, listen to `ok:rating:active`.
sections.title: Give feedback on hover

sections.body: `size` sets the icon size: `xxSmall` (12px), `xSmall` (16px), `small` (20px), `medium` (24px, the default) or `large` (28px).
sections.title: Size

sections.body: Every option works the same way in both versions: a prop in React, an attribute in HTML. Values that aren't listed fall back to the default.
sections.title: Options

sections.body: These props set the value and the content. They aren't options, because HTML writes them as markup.
sections.title: Content and behavior

sections.body:
- **`ok:rating:change`** (cancelable) fires on the rating with `detail.value` and `detail.previous`. Call `preventDefault()` to keep the previous value.
- **`ok:rating:active`** fires with `detail.value`: the value under the pointer, or `null`.
- **Instance:** `runtime.get(element, "rating")` returns `{ value, setValue(value) }`. `setValue` doesn't fire events.
- **React:** `onChange(value)` and `onChangeActive(value)`; controlled with `value`, uncontrolled with `defaultValue`.
sections.title: Events and methods

sections.body: The rating is one radio group: Tab reaches the chosen value, and the arrow keys change it.
sections.title: Keyboard

sections.body:
- Every value has a label, such as "3 Stars". Pass `getLabelText` when your icons mean something else, or to translate it.
- The focused value shows a focus ring around its icon.
- Read-only ratings are one image with the value as its name.
- Icons are 24px by default, the minimum target size for pointers. Use the smaller sizes for read-only scores.
sections.title: Accessibility

sections.body: A scrollbar area keeps long content inside a fixed frame, with a thin scrollbar that matches the theme. Use it for any region that scrolls on its own: a panel, a list, a table or the content of a drawer. The browser does the scrolling, so touch momentum, wheel scrolling and find-in-page keep working.
sections.html:
<!-- Load once per page -->
<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@owlky/html@0/dist/owlky.css">

<section data-ok-scrollbar aria-label="Release notes" tabindex="0" style="max-height: 320px">
  …
</section>
sections.title: Overview

sections.body: By default, the scrollbar appears when the pointer rests on the area or when focus is inside it. On touch screens it's always visible. Set `autoHide` to `false` to always show it, for example when people might not notice that the area scrolls.
sections.html:
<section data-ok-scrollbar data-ok-auto-hide="false" aria-label="Release notes" tabindex="0">
  …
</section>
sections.react: <Scrollbar autoHide={false} aria-label="Release notes">…</Scrollbar>
sections.title: Keep the scrollbar visible

sections.body: Other components scroll by wrapping their content in a scrollbar area. Put a **Table** inside one within its `TableContainer`, place one inside a **Drawer**'s content, or wrap a **Sortable** list. The component around it stops scrolling by itself, and the scrollbar area takes over.

sections.title: Scroll other components

sections.body: Every option works the same way in both versions: a prop in React, an attribute in HTML.
sections.title: Options

sections.body: These props name the area and make it reachable with the keyboard.
sections.title: Content and behavior

sections.body: The area takes focus, then the browser scrolls it with the usual keys.
sections.title: Keyboard

sections.body:
- The area is a named region that keyboard users can reach with Tab and scroll. Give it a name that says what's inside, such as "Release notes"; the default is "scrollable content".
- The scrollbar shows while focus is inside, so keyboard users can see where they are.
- On Windows and Linux, the scrollbar takes a little space next to the content; on macOS, iOS and Android, the system's overlay scrollbars are used.
sections.title: Accessibility

sections.body:
A select lets people choose one or more options from a list. The field shows the current value. A press, or a key such as Arrow Down, opens a menu of options under it. It is made of these parts:

- **FormControl:** the root. It shares the variant, the size and the states with the select, its label and its helper text.
- **InputLabel:** the label. It rests inside the field and moves above it when the field has focus or a value.
- **Select:** the field. Its options are **MenuItem**s, shown in a menu on the page's top layer.
- **FormHelperText:** a hint or an error message under the field.

In HTML, the select needs the JavaScript runtime: it opens the menu, moves focus through the options and writes the value. The value also sits in a hidden input, so the select works in a `<form>`. With `native`, the field is the browser's own `<select>` and needs no JavaScript.
sections.html:
Twenty
Age
  • Ten
  • Twenty
  • Thirty
sections.title: Overview

sections.body: Put the select in a form control with an **InputLabel**. Give the label an `id` and pass it to the select's `labelId`: the field and its menu are named by it. Repeat the label text in `label`, so the outlined field leaves a gap in its outline for the floating label. Without a visible label, name the field with `aria-label`.
sections.html:
City
  • Paris
  • Rome
sections.title: Label a select

sections.body: Set `variant` and `size` on the form control: the select, the label and the helper text follow it. The **Outlined** variant is the default. **Filled** tints the field and **Standard** draws a line under it. The `small` size is 40px high instead of 56px (outlined). A prop on the select itself overrides the form control's.
sections.html:
• Ten
  • Twenty
  • Thirty
  • Ten
  • Twenty
  • Thirty
sections.react:
import { FormControl, InputLabel, MenuItem, Select } from "@owlky/react";

export function Variants() {
  return (
    <>
      <FormControl variant="filled">
        <InputLabel id="age-filled-label">Age</InputLabel>
        <Select labelId="age-filled-label" id="age-filled" defaultValue="">
          <MenuItem value={10}>Ten</MenuItem>
          <MenuItem value={20}>Twenty</MenuItem>
        </Select>
      </FormControl>
      <FormControl variant="standard" size="small">
        <InputLabel id="age-standard-label">Age</InputLabel>
        <Select labelId="age-standard-label" id="age-standard" defaultValue="">
          <MenuItem value={10}>Ten</MenuItem>
          <MenuItem value={20}>Twenty</MenuItem>
        </Select>
      </FormControl>
    </>
  );
}
sections.title: Choose a variant and a size

sections.body: Add a **FormHelperText** under the select and reference its `id` with `aria-describedby`. Set `error`, `disabled` or `required` on the form control: the field, the label and the helper text change together. `readOnly` keeps the value visible but the menu doesn't open. A disabled select is skipped by Tab.

Plan
  • Free

Choose a plan to continue
sections.title: Show help, errors and states

sections.body: Set `multiple`: the value is a list, each option toggles, and the menu stays open while people pick. The field shows the chosen options' text, separated by commas. To show chips instead, return **Chip**s from `renderValue`. In HTML, add a `<template data-ok-select-chip>` with one chip as the field box's first child: the runtime fills a copy for each value.

  • April Tucker
sections.title: Choose several values

sections.body: An empty select shows nothing. With `displayEmpty`, it shows the option whose value is `""`, or what `renderValue` returns for the empty value, such as a placeholder. In HTML, a `<template data-ok-select-placeholder>` holds what an empty value shows. A select without an InputLabel needs an `aria-label`.
sections.html:
Choose people
  • Oliver Hansen
  • Van Henry
  • April Tucker
sections.title: Show a placeholder

sections.body: Put a **ListSubheader** before each group of options. Subheaders aren't options: the keyboard skips them and assistive technology reads them as text.

Grouping

  • Category 2

sections.title: Group options

sections.body: Set `native` and pass `<option>` elements: the field is the browser's `<select>`, with the platform's own menu, and it needs no JavaScript. It suits long lists on touch devices. With `multiple`, the options show as a list in the field. The InputLabel then names the select with `htmlFor`.
sections.html: Fruit
sections.title: Use the native select

sections.body: A **Text field** with `select` has the select inside its own field, label and helper text. Its select is native by default. Set `selectProps` to `{ native: false }` and pass **MenuItem**s for the listbox select. In HTML, the text field's control carries `data-ok-select` around the same parts.

€
Currency
  • $

sections.title: Use a select in a text field

sections.body: In React, keep the value in state with `value` and `onChange`, and the menu with `open` and `onOpenChange`. `onOpenChange` receives the reason of a close: `escape`, `backdrop` (a press outside), `select`, `tab` or `toggle` (a press on the field). In HTML, a button with `data-ok-select-open` set to the field's `id` opens the select.
sections.html:
Size
  • Small
  • Large
sections.title: Control the value and the open state

sections.body: Every option works the same way in both versions: a prop in React, an attribute in HTML. Values that aren't listed fall back to the default. In React, the select takes `variant`, `size`, `color`, `error`, `disabled`, `required` and `fullWidth` from its form control when it doesn't set them.
sections.title: Options

sections.body: These props set the content and the menu. They aren't options, because HTML writes them as markup.
sections.title: Content and behavior

sections.body: In HTML, the select emits `ok:select:change` with `{ value }` before the value changes: call `preventDefault()` to refuse it. `ok:select:open` and `ok:select:close` (with `{ reason }`) follow the menu. The instance from `Owlky.runtime.get(element, "select")` has `value`, `setValue(value)`, `isOpen`, `open()` and `close()`. In React, use `onChange(value)` and `onOpenChange(open, reason)`.
sections.html:
<script>
  document.addEventListener("ok:select:change", (event) => {
    console.log("New value:", event.detail.value);
  });
</script>
sections.title: Events and methods

sections.body: The field takes focus with Tab. When the menu opens, focus moves to the selected option, or to the first one. It goes back to the field when the menu closes.
sections.title: Keyboard

sections.body:
- The field is a `combobox` with `aria-haspopup="listbox"` and `aria-expanded`. The menu is a `listbox` of `option`s with `aria-selected`. A multiple select's list has `aria-multiselectable`.
- Name the field with an InputLabel and `labelId`, or with `aria-label`. Reference the helper text with `aria-describedby`.
- `error`, `required`, `disabled` and `readOnly` set `aria-invalid`, `aria-required`, `aria-disabled` and `aria-readonly` on the field: the colors and the asterisk are visual only.
- The label, the value and the helper text keep a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 in the light and dark themes. A disabled field is dimmed.
- A checkbox in an option only shows its state: mark it `inert`, so the option stays the one control.
sections.title: Accessibility

sections.body: A slider picks a value, or a range of two values, along a track, such as a volume or a price range. Each thumb holds a native range input: the keyboard, screen readers and forms work as they do for `<input type="range">`. People drag a thumb, or press the track to move the nearest thumb there, with a mouse, a finger or a pen.
sections.title: Overview

sections.body: `min`, `max` and `step` set the values (0, 100 and 1 by default). `marks` draws a tick at every step (`true`), or at the values you list, each with an optional label below the track. Set `step` to `null` to allow only the marked values. In HTML, write one `data-ok-slider-mark` per mark and set `data-ok-step="0"` for marks only.
sections.html: 0°C 20°C 100°C
sections.title: Set steps and marks

sections.body: `valueLabelDisplay` shows the value in a bubble above the thumb: `auto` while the thumb is hovered, focused or dragged, `on` always. `valueLabelFormat` sets its text, and `getAriaValueText` what screen readers announce, such as "30°C". In HTML, `data-ok-label-value="{value}°C"` sets both.
sections.html: 30°C
sections.title: Show the value

sections.body: Pass two values to get two thumbs. Name each one with `getAriaLabel`, for example "Minimum price". A thumb that passes the other one swaps places with it, unless you set `disableSwap`. `onChange` fires while the value changes, and `onChangeCommitted` once a drag or a key press ends: use it for costly work such as a search.
sections.title: Pick a range

sections.body: `size` is `medium` (a 10px track) or `small` (6px). `color` is a palette color or `inherit`. `track` is `normal`, `inverted` (filled from the value to the end) or `false`. Set `orientation` to `vertical` for a slider that fills its container's height: give that container a height.
sections.title: Change the look

sections.body: Every option works the same way in both versions: a prop in React, an attribute in HTML. Values that aren't valid fall back to the default.
sections.title: Options

sections.body: These props set the value and the content. They aren't options, because HTML writes them as markup.
sections.title: Content and behavior

sections.body:
- **`ok:slider:change`** (cancelable) fires while a thumb moves, with `detail.value` (one value per thumb) and `detail.activeThumb`.
- **`ok:slider:commit`** fires when a drag or a key press ends, with `detail.value`.
- **Instance:** `runtime.get(element, "slider")` returns `{ value, setValue(value) }`. `setValue` doesn't fire events.
- **React:** `onChange(value, activeThumb)` and `onChangeCommitted(value)`; controlled with `value`, uncontrolled with `defaultValue`.
sections.title: Events and methods

sections.body: Each thumb is in the tab order. With `step` set to `null`, the arrow keys move from mark to mark.
sections.title: Keyboard

sections.body:
- Name every thumb with `aria-label`, `aria-labelledby` or `getAriaLabel`.
- Give values a unit with `getAriaValueText` when the number alone isn't clear.
- Vertical sliders set `aria-orientation="vertical"` on their inputs.
- The focused thumb shows a ring and a halo. Mark labels use the secondary text color, with a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1.
- Pressing anywhere on the track moves a thumb, so people don't need to hit the 20px thumb exactly.
sections.title: Accessibility

sections.body: A snackbar, or toast, shows a brief message at the edge of the screen and closes by itself after 4 seconds. Render one toaster per page. Then show toasts from anywhere: with the `toast()` function in React, or with a `<template>` and a button in HTML. Toasts pause while you hover over or focus the toaster.
sections.title: Overview

sections.body: Use `toast.info`, `toast.success`, `toast.warning` or `toast.error` for a toast with a colored icon. `toast.promise` shows a loading toast and replaces it with the result. In HTML, set `data-ok-type` on the toast; a loading toast with `data-ok-then` is replaced by another template when its time (`data-ok-duration`) runs out, and the instance's `promise()` method follows a real promise.
sections.html:
<script type="module">
  const toaster = window.Owlky.get(document.querySelector("[data-ok-toaster]"), "toaster");
  toaster.show({ type: "success", title: "Event created", description: "Monday at 6:00 PM" });
  toaster.promise(fetch("/api/save"), { loading: "Saving…", success: "Saved", error: "Not saved" });
</script>
sections.react:
toast.success("Event created", { description: "Monday at 6:00 PM" });
toast.promise(save(), { loading: "Saving…", success: "Saved", error: "Not saved" });
sections.title: Show the status

sections.body: Pass `action: { label, onClick }` to add a button, such as **Undo**. The toast closes when it is clicked, unless the handler calls `preventDefault()`. Pass your own nodes as `action` for several buttons. Toasts with an action have no close button.
sections.react: toast("Message deleted", { action: { label: "Undo", onClick: restore } });
sections.title: Add an action

sections.body: Set `position` to a corner or the center of the top or bottom edge. At the bottom, the newest toast sits nearest to the edge. In HTML, a trigger with `data-ok-toaster-position` moves the toaster before it shows its toast.
sections.html: <section data-ok-toaster data-ok-position="bottom-center" aria-label="Notifications">…</section>
sections.react: <Toaster position="bottom-center" />
sections.title: Move the toaster

sections.body: Every option works the same way in both versions: a prop of `Toaster` in React, an attribute of the toaster in HTML.
sections.title: Options

sections.body: These are the `toast()` options. In HTML they are the toast's markup and attributes.
sections.title: Content and behavior

sections.body:
- **`ok:toaster:show`** (`detail.toast`) and **`ok:toaster:dismiss`** (`detail.toast`, `detail.reason`: `close`, `dismiss`, `action`, `cancel`, `timeout`, `escape`, `api` or `overflow`) fire on the toaster.
- **`ok:toaster:action`** (cancelable) fires before an action or cancel button closes its toast.
- **Instance:** `runtime.get(toaster, "toaster")` returns `{ show(options), showTemplate(template), promise(promise, messages), dismiss(id?) }`. `show()` builds the toast from text, never from HTML.
- **React:** `toast()` returns the toast's id; `toast.dismiss(id?)` closes one toast or all of them. `onDismiss` and `onAutoClose` report how it closed.
sections.title: Events and methods

sections.body: Toasts don't take focus when they appear, so they never interrupt typing.
sections.title: Keyboard

sections.body:
- The toast list is a polite live region: screen readers announce new toasts without interrupting.
- Time pauses while the pointer or focus is in the toaster, so people can read and act.
- Don't rely on a toast for anything that must be done: it closes by itself. Use a Dialog instead.
- Icons are decorative; the title carries the message. Typed toasts keep their text at a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1.
sections.title: Accessibility

sections.body:
A sortable list lets people put items in their own order, such as tasks by priority or widgets on a dashboard. Each item has a handle: drag it with a mouse, finger or pen, move it with the keyboard, or tap two handles to swap places. Items can also have a remove button.

Every move is announced to screen reader users, such as "Moved to position 2 of 4".
sections.html:
• Design
  • Build
sections.title: Overview

sections.body: `grid` (the default) arranges items in columns that fit the width, `vertical` stacks them in one column and `horizontal` puts them in one row. Wrap a vertical or horizontal list in a **Scrollbar**: it scrolls the list and draws its frame.
sections.html: …
sections.react:
<Scrollbar aria-label="Widgets list">
  <Sortable layout="horizontal" aria-label="Widgets" … />
</Scrollbar>
sections.title: Choose a layout

sections.body: In React, pass `onRemove`: every item gets a remove button, and you update your data. In HTML, add a `data-ok-sortable-remove` button to each item; the script removes the item. Remove buttons appear when the pointer rests on an item or focus is inside it, and are always visible on touch screens.
sections.html: • Design
sections.react:
<Sortable
  …
  onRemove={(task) => setTasks((all) => all.filter((t) => t !== task))}
/>
sections.title: Let people remove items

sections.body: Adding is up to you. In React, add to your data. In HTML, put a `<template data-ok-sortable-template>` with the new item's markup in the list, and a button with `data-ok-sortable-add="<list id>"`. The script clones the template and fires `ok:sortable:add`, where you fill in the new item.
sections.html: …
sections.react:
<Button onClick={() => setTasks((all) => [...all, `Task ${all.length + 1}`])}>
  Add task
</Button>
sections.title: Add items

sections.body: Every option works the same way in both versions: a prop in React, an attribute in HTML.
sections.title: Options

sections.body: In React, the list is driven by your data; in HTML, by the markup.
sections.title: Content and behavior

sections.body:
- **`ok:sortable:move`** (cancelable) fires before an item moves, with `detail: { from, to, item }`.
- **`ok:sortable:remove`** (cancelable) fires before an item is removed, with `detail: { index, item }`.
- **`ok:sortable:add`** fires after a new item is added from the template, with `detail: { item, index }`. Fill in its content here.
- **Instance:** `runtime.get(element, "sortable")` returns `{ move(from, to), remove(index) }`.
- **React:** `onReorder(items)` and `onRemove(item, index)`. The `arrayMove(items, from, to)` helper is exported too.
sections.title: Events and methods

sections.body: Focus a handle, grab the item, move it, then drop it. Focus stays on the handle while the item moves.
sections.title: Keyboard

sections.body:
- Every drag has a keyboard and a tap alternative, so people who can't drag can still reorder (WCAG 2.2, success criteria 2.1.1 and 2.5.7).
- Name the list with `aria-label`. Handles and remove buttons are named from each item, such as "Reorder Design"; set the item's label with `getItemLabel` in React or the buttons' `aria-label` in HTML.
- The handle has `aria-pressed="true"` while its item is grabbed.
- Moves are announced in a polite live region. Translate the messages with `messages` in React.
sections.title: Accessibility

sections.body: A stepper shows progress through a sequence of steps, such as a checkout or a setup wizard. Each step has a numbered icon and a title. Steps before the active one are completed and show a check, steps after it are not reached yet. The stepper only shows progress: your app owns the active step and changes it from its Back and Next buttons. For views that people visit in any order, use **Tabs** instead.
sections.html:
1. 1 Choose a plan
  2. …
sections.title: Overview

sections.body: In React, pass `activeStep` (0-based) and change it from your buttons. Each `Step` gets its state from it: the active step, completed steps before it, not reached steps after it. Set `active`, `completed` or `disabled` on a `Step` to override the state, for example to leave a skipped step uncompleted. Once `activeStep` equals the number of steps, every step is completed. In HTML, the runtime keeps every step's state in line with `data-ok-active-step`. Buttons with `data-ok-stepper-next`, `data-ok-stepper-back` or `data-ok-stepper-reset` move the stepper they name. Back buttons are disabled on the first step.
sections.html:
Pick the plan that suits your team.

Invite the people who will work on it.

Set `position` to `top`, or to `static` to keep it in the page. In HTML, Back and Next buttons inside the bar move it, and the runtime disables them at the ends.

sections.body:
- **`ok:stepper:change`** (cancelable) fires on the stepper before it moves, with `detail.activeStep` and `detail.previous`.
- **`ok:mobile-stepper:change`** (cancelable) fires the same way on a mobile stepper.

sections.body:

- The active step carries `aria-current="step"`.
- Step icons are decorative. The title says what the step is, so keep it meaningful without the number.
- The dots and the bar of a mobile stepper are named "Step 2 of 3". Pass `getStepLabel` (React) or `data-ok-label-step` (HTML, with `{step}` and `{steps}`) to translate it.

A switch is a native checkbox with `role="switch"`, so forms submit it and assistive technology announces "on" or "off". It needs no JavaScript. Put it in a **form control label**, so the text names it.

sections.body: In React, the table is made of parts that render the matching native elements.
sections.title: Content and behavior

sections.body:
- **`ok:table:sort`** (cancelable) fires before the rows are sorted, with `detail: { column, direction }`.
- **`ok:table:select`** fires after the selection changes, with `detail.rows`, the selected rows.
- **`ok:table:expand`** (cancelable) fires before a detail row opens or closes, with `detail: { row, expanded }`.
- **`ok:table-pagination:change`** (cancelable) fires before the page or rows per page change, with `detail: { page, rowsPerPage }`.
- **Instances:** `runtime.get(table, "table")` returns `{ sort(column, direction?), expand(row, open?), groups() }`. `runtime.get(element, "table-pagination")` returns `{ page, rowsPerPage, lastPage, setPage(page), setRowsPerPage(rows), refresh() }`.
- **React:** `onClick` on `TableSortLabel` and `TableExpandButton`, and `onPageChange` and `onRowsPerPageChange` on `TablePagination`.

sections.body: Sort labels, checkboxes, expand buttons and page buttons are native controls.
sections.title: Keyboard

sections.body:
- Name the scrollbar area around the table with `aria-label`, such as "Orders". Header cells use `scope="col"`, and the sorted column has `aria-sort`.
- Give every checkbox and expand button a name that includes the row, such as "Select Eclair".
- The expand button has `aria-expanded` and `aria-controls`, which point to its detail row.
- The "1–5 of 12" label is a polite live region, so page changes are announced.
- Header text meets a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 in light and dark mode.

sections.body: Tabs switch between related views on the same page. Each tab names one panel, and only the selected tab's panel shows. A line under the selected tab marks it and slides to the next tab you pick. Use tabs for content at the same level, such as the sections of a profile. For steps that follow each other, use a **Stepper** instead.

sections.title: Overview

sections.body: Give each tab an `id` and an `aria-controls` that names its panel. Give each panel the matching `id` and an `aria-labelledby` that names its tab. Screen readers then announce which tab a panel belongs to. In HTML, the runtime shows the panel of the tab you select and hides the others with `hidden`. In React, the app owns the selection: pass `value` and `onChange`, and set `hidden` on the panels yourself. `defaultValue` keeps the selection inside `Tabs` when you don't need it.

sections.body: Pass an icon with `icon`. With a label, `iconPosition` puts the icon above (`top`, the default), below (`bottom`), before (`start`) or after (`end`) the label. Tabs with an icon above or below are 72px tall. Icon-only tabs have no visible text, so give each one an `aria-label`.

Use `primary` or `secondary` to match your brand. Tabs that aren't selected keep the secondary text color, which has a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 in both themes.

By default (`scrollButtons="auto"`) they show only when the tabs overflow, and only from 600px up: on phones, people swipe. Set `allowScrollButtonsMobile` to show them on phones too, `scrollButtons` to `false` to hide them, or `visibleScrollbar` to keep the scrollbar. In HTML, add the scroll buttons to the markup as the stories show.

Set `orientation` to `vertical` to stack the tabs in a column, with the line on their right. Vertical tabs answer the Up and Down arrow keys. sections.title: Options

sections.body: These props set the content and the selection. They aren't options, because HTML writes them as markup.
sections.title: Content and behavior

sections.body:
- **`ok:tabs:change`** (cancelable) fires on the tabs root before a selection, with `detail.value`, `detail.previous` and `detail.tab`. Call `preventDefault()` to keep the current tab.
- **Instance:** `runtime.get(element, "tabs")` returns `{ value, setValue(value), select(tab) }`. `setValue` doesn't fire the event.
- **React:** `onChange(value)` receives the value of the tab the user picks. A tab's value is its `value` prop, or its position (`"0"`, `"1"`, …) when it has none.
sections.title: Events and methods

sections.body: Only the selected tab is in the tab order. The arrow keys move focus between the tabs and skip disabled ones. By default, focus moves without selecting, and Enter or Space selects. Set `selectionFollowsFocus` to select a tab as soon as focus reaches it, which suits panels that render instantly.
sections.title: Keyboard

sections.body:
- Name the tab list with `aria-label` or `aria-labelledby`, for example after the heading above it.
- Connect every tab and panel through `aria-controls` and `aria-labelledby`, as shown above.
- Panels are in the tab order (`tabindex="0"`), so keyboard users reach panels that hold only text. Remove it when the panel starts with a focusable element.
- Every tab and the selected panel show a focus ring for keyboard users.
- Disabled tabs are skipped by the arrow keys and announced as unavailable.
sections.title: Accessibility

sections.body:
A text field lets people enter and edit text: one line in an `<input>`, several lines in a `<textarea>`, or a choice in a `<select>`. The label sits inside the field and moves up when the field gets focus or a value. Helper text under the field gives a hint or an error message.

The field is built from native elements, so forms, autofill, the keyboard and assistive technology work as usual. It needs no JavaScript, except for growing textareas and the show-password button.
sections.html: Email
sections.title: Overview

sections.body: The variant sets the field's frame. `outlined` (the default) draws a border with a gap for the label, `filled` tints the background, and `standard` draws a line under the input. Use one variant throughout a form. In HTML, only the outlined variant has the `fieldset` with the label repeated in its `legend`: that is what leaves the gap in the border.
sections.title: Choose a variant

sections.body: Pass `helperText` for a hint under the field. Set `error` to show an error: the field turns red, the input gets `aria-invalid`, and the helper text should say how to fix it. In HTML, give the helper text an `id` and point the input's `aria-describedby` at it, so screen readers read it with the field. The script sets `aria-invalid` from `data-ok-error`. Without the script, write `aria-invalid="true"` yourself.

Enter at least 8 digits
sections.title: Show hints and errors

sections.body: Put an `InputAdornment` at the start or the end of the input for an icon, a unit such as kg, or a button. A start adornment keeps the label above the field. In React, show or hide a password by keeping `type` in state; in HTML, give the end button `data-ok-text-field-reveal`, and the script switches the type and `aria-pressed`.

sections.title: Add icons, units and buttons

sections.body: Set `select` and pass `<option>` elements to get a native `<select>` in the field's frame. The label always stays above it. A native select uses the system's list on every device, which works well on touch screens and with assistive technology. For a list in the page's own style, set `selectProps` to `{ native: false }` and pass **MenuItem**s: the field then holds a **Select** (see its page).

sections.body: Set `multiline` for a textarea. With `rows`, it has a fixed height. Without `rows`, it grows with the text, from `minRows` (default 1) up to `maxRows`, and then scrolls. Growing needs a browser with `field-sizing` support; other browsers show `minRows` rows and scroll.

sections.body: These props set the content and behavior. They aren't options, because HTML writes them as markup.
sections.title: Content and behavior

sections.body:
- **HTML:** the input fires the native `input` and `change` events. There are no instance methods.
- **React:** `onChange(value)` is called with the new value. Use `value` to control the field, or `defaultValue` to let it keep its own state. The `ref` and every other prop, such as `name`, `type` or `autoComplete`, go to the input.

sections.body: The field is a native input, textarea or select, so the browser provides the keyboard behavior: Tab moves focus, and a select opens with Space, Enter or the arrow keys.
sections.title: Keyboard

sections.body:
- The label is a `<label for>`, so it names the input. A field without a label needs `aria-label`. Don't use the placeholder as the only label: it disappears when people type.
- Helper text is linked with `aria-describedby`; an error also sets `aria-invalid`.
- Required fields show an asterisk. The asterisk is hidden from screen readers, which announce the input's `required` state instead.
- The resting label and the helper text use the secondary text color, and error text uses the error text tone: each has a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1. The error border uses the brand error color.
- Focus shows as a 2px border, line or ring in the text color.
- Set `autoComplete` (such as `email` or `current-password`) so browsers and password managers can fill the field.

sections.body: A timeline lists events in order along a vertical line, such as the steps of an order or the history of a project. Each event has a dot on the line and its content beside it. The timeline is a list (`ul`), so screen readers announce how many events it has. It needs no JavaScript.

      </TimelineItem>
      <TimelineItem>
        <TimelineSeparator>
          <TimelineDot />
        </TimelineSeparator>
        <TimelineContent>Shipped</TimelineContent>
      </TimelineItem>
    </Timeline>
  );
}

sections.body: A timeline isn't interactive. Links and buttons in its content work as usual.

sections.body: A toggle button stays pressed until it's pressed again, such as a bold button in a text editor. Group related toggle buttons to let people pick one option, such as a view, or several options, such as text formats. For a one-time action, use a **Button**.

sections.body: Put the buttons in a group and set `exclusive`: pressing a button releases the others, and pressing the pressed button clears the choice. Give each button a `value`; the group's value is the pressed button's value, or `null`.
sections.title: Let people pick one option

sections.body: Without `exclusive`, each button toggles on its own and the group's value is the list of pressed values.
sections.title: Let people pick several options

sections.body: In React, handle `onChange`: it receives the requested value, and a controlled component keeps its value until you update it. In HTML, listen to `ok:toggle-group:change` (or `ok:toggle-button:change` for a standalone button) and call `preventDefault()` to keep the current state.
sections.title: React to changes

sections.body: The first table lists the options of a toggle button, the second those of a group. In React, the group's `color`, `size` and `disabled` pass to every child button. Values that aren't listed fall back to the default.
sections.title: Options

sections.body: These props set the content and behavior. They aren't options, because HTML writes them as markup.
sections.title: Content and behavior

sections.body:
HTML events are cancelable: call `preventDefault()` to keep the current state.

- **`ok:toggle-button:change`** on a standalone button, with `detail: { pressed }`, the new state.
- **`ok:toggle-group:change`** on a group, with `detail: { value, previous, button }`.
- **Instances:** `runtime.get(element, "toggle-button")` returns `{ pressed, setPressed(pressed) }`, and `runtime.get(element, "toggle-group")` returns `{ value, setValue(value) }`. The setters don't emit events.
- **React:** `onChange(selected)` on a standalone `ToggleButton` and `onChange(value)` on a `ToggleButtonGroup`. Both work controlled and uncontrolled.
sections.title: Events and methods

sections.body: Toggle buttons are native buttons, so the browser provides the keyboard behavior.
sections.title: Keyboard

sections.body:
- `aria-pressed` tells assistive technology whether a button is pressed.
- A group has `role="group"`: give it an `aria-label` that names the choice, such as "Text format".
- Buttons that show only an icon need `aria-label`.
- Disabled buttons never change their state.
sections.title: Accessibility

sections.body: A tooltip shows a short text label when you hover over, focus or long-press an element. Use it to name icon-only buttons or to add a short description. Keep the text brief and never put controls in it.

sections.body: A tooltip opens 100 ms after the pointer enters its trigger (`enterDelay`) and closes when it leaves (`leaveDelay`, 0 ms). Keyboard focus opens it at once. On touch screens, a press held for 700 ms opens it, and it closes 1.5 seconds after you lift your finger. The pointer can move onto the tooltip without closing it.

sections.body:
- The tooltip has `role="tooltip"`, and its trigger points at it with `aria-labelledby` or `aria-describedby`.
- It appears on keyboard focus, not only on hover, and Escape closes it without moving focus.
- You can move the pointer onto the tooltip to read it: it stays open while hovered.
- The text is white on dark grey, with a contrast ratio well above 4.5:1.
- Don't put links or buttons in a tooltip: it closes when focus moves. Use a Popover instead.

sections.body: A transfer list moves items between two lists, such as the columns you can add to a report and the ones you chose. People check items and press a move button. It is built from components you already know: each list is a **List** in a **Scrollbar**, each row a **Checkbox** with its label, and the move buttons are outlined **Buttons**. On screens under 600px the lists stack and the arrows turn to point at them.
sections.title: Overview

sections.body: In React, pass every item in `items` and the values that start on the left in `defaultLeft`. The rest start on the right. To control both sides, pass `left` and `right` and update them from `onChange(left, right)`. Moved items go to the end of the other list and are unchecked. In HTML, listen to `ok:transfer-list:change`, or read `value` on the instance.
sections.title: Read and control the sides

sections.body: Set `variant` to `enhanced` to give each list a title, a select-all checkbox and a count such as "1/4 selected". The select-all checkbox shows a mixed state when some items are checked. `titles` names the two lists ("Choices" and "Chosen" by default) and `getCountLabel` writes the count. In HTML, `data-ok-label-count` takes a template such as `{checked} of {total}`.

- Move buttons have names such as "Move selected right". Pass `buttonLabels` to translate them.

sections.body: A tree view shows nested items that people expand and select, such as folders and files. It follows the WAI-ARIA tree pattern: one tab stop for the whole tree, and the arrow keys to move, open and close. `SimpleTreeView` takes `TreeItem` children. `RichTreeView` builds the same tree from data.

sections.title: Overview

sections.body: A click on an item's row opens or closes it. Set `expansionTrigger` to `iconContainer` so only the icon does, for example when a click on the row opens a page. `defaultExpandedItems` sets the items open at first. To control them, pass `expandedItems` and `onExpandedItemsChange`. `onItemExpansionToggle` reports each toggle. Each group of child items is a Collapse: its height animates as it opens and closes, and it opens at once when the user prefers reduced motion. In HTML, keep `data-ok-collapse` on the groups.

sections.body: A click selects the item. Set `multiSelect` to select several: Ctrl or ⌘ click adds or removes one, and Shift click selects a range. `checkboxSelection` shows a checkbox on each item and implies `multiSelect`. Use `selectedItems` and `onSelectedItemsChange` to control the selection, or `disableSelection` when items are only for browsing.

sections.body: By default, items with children show a chevron that turns when they open. Pass `expandIcon` and `collapseIcon` for your own pair, and `endIcon` for items without children. Set `variant` to `lines` for dashed guides beside nested items, round tinted expand icons and compact rows.

sections.body: Typography sets text in one step of the type scale, such as a page heading, body text or a caption. Each variant reads its font, size, weight and line height from the typography tokens, so the text follows the theme, the **Font** menu in the toolbar and the responsive heading sizes. It needs no JavaScript. The type scale itself is described in **Foundations › Typography**.
sections.html:
Monthly report

Sales grew in every region this month.
sections.title: Overview

sections.body:
Set `variant` to a step of the type scale: `h1` to `h6` for headings, `subtitle1` and `subtitle2` for short emphasized lines, `body1` (the default) and `body2` for running text, `caption` and `overline` for small labels, and `button` for text that looks like a button label. Use `inherit` to keep the parent's font, for example inside a link.

Add `gutterBottom` for a bottom margin of 0.35em. The margin scales with the variant, so headings get more space than captions.

sections.body: The style and the element are separate, so the heading levels of your page can follow its outline. In React, each variant renders a default element: `h1` to `h6` for headings, `h6` for subtitles, `p` for body text and `span` for the rest. Pass `component` to render another element once, or `variantMapping` to change the element of some variants. In HTML, write the element you need and add the attributes.

sections.body:
- Pick the element for the page outline and the variant for the look: don't skip heading levels to get a smaller heading.
- Font sizes are in `rem`, so text scales with the browser's font size setting.
- The text tones `textPrimary` and `textSecondary` reach a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 on the theme's backgrounds. Palette colors use their main tone, which can be lower for small text, such as `warning` on white: keep them for large or short text.

sections.body: An upload lets people choose files by dropping them on a zone, by pressing the zone to open the file dialog, or by pasting them. It checks each file against the types, sizes and counts you allow, lists the files it keeps with a preview, a name and a size, and lists the rejected files with the reasons. The zone is built around a native file input, so it works with the keyboard and screen readers, and a form submits the files it holds. The upload never sends files anywhere: you decide when and how to send them.
sections.html: Drop or select a file Drag a file here, or browse your device.
sections.title: Overview

sections.body: Turn on `multiple` to keep adding files: each drop or pick adds its files to the list. Without it, a new file replaces the current one. In HTML, put `multiple` on the input and add the list, its item `<template>` and, if you want them, the **Remove all** and **Upload** buttons. In React, `onRemoveAll` and `onUpload` show those buttons. Pass `value` with `onChange` to control the files yourself; `onChange` receives every file the upload holds.
sections.html: …
sections.title: Accept several files

sections.body: `accept` takes the same values as the input's `accept` attribute, such as `image/*,.pdf`, or, in React, a map of MIME types to extensions such as `{ "image/*": [".png", ".jpg"] }`. The file dialog shows those types, and dropped or pasted files are checked against them too. `maxSize` and `minSize` are in bytes. `maxFiles` caps how many files a multiple upload holds. Add your own check with `validator`: it receives each file and returns `null`, an error `{ code, message }` or a list of errors, and it may return a promise. Rejected files appear under the zone with their reasons. Rewrite the messages, for example to translate them, with `getErrorMessage`.
sections.html:
…
PNG or JPEG, up to 1 MB each.
…
sections.react:
<Upload
  multiple
  accept={{ "image/*": [".png", ".jpg", ".jpeg"] }}
  maxFiles={3}
  maxSize={1048576}
  helperText="PNG or JPEG, up to 1 MB each."
  validator={(file) =>
    file.name.length > 60 ? { code: "name-too-long", message: "Use a shorter name" } : null
  }
  onDropRejected={(rejections) => console.warn(rejections)}
/>
sections.title: Limit types, sizes and counts

sections.body: The list shows a row per file with a preview, the name and the size. Set `layout` to `horizontal` for a wrapping row of tiles instead: the names stay available to screen readers. Image files show a preview made from a temporary object URL, which the upload releases when the file leaves. Turn previews off with `thumbnail={false}` (HTML: `data-ok-thumbnail="false"`) to show a colored file type icon for every file.

sections.react: <Upload multiple layout="horizontal" thumbnail={false} />
sections.title: Show the files

sections.body: `UploadAvatar` is a round photo picker: the photo fills the circle and **Update photo** shows on hover and focus. It accepts images by default. `UploadBox` is a small box for toolbars and forms: it shows a cloud icon, or the `placeholder` you give it, and keeps the files without a list. In HTML, set `data-ok-variant` to `avatar` or `box`.
sections.html: Upload photo
sections.title: Pick an avatar or a small box

sections.body: With `noClick`, pressing the zone no longer opens the file dialog, and with `noKeyboard` the input leaves the tab order. Give people a button instead: any element with `data-ok-upload-open` inside the upload opens the dialog, in HTML and in React. You can also call `open()` from a click handler: on the HTML instance, or on the `apiRef` in React. Browsers only open the dialog right after a user action. `noDrag` turns dropping off and `noPaste` turns pasting off.
sections.html:
Drag files here
…
sections.react:
import { Button, Upload } from "@owlky/react";

<Upload
  multiple
  noClick
  noKeyboard
  aria-label="Files"
  placeholder={
    <Button variant="outlined" color="inherit" data-ok-upload-open="">
      Open file dialog
    </Button>
  }
/>
sections.title: Open the file dialog yourself

sections.body: The upload copies the files it holds into its input, so a form with the input's `name` submits them, including dropped and pasted files. To send them yourself, read `files` from the HTML instance or the `onChange` value in React, and post them with `fetch()` and `FormData`. The **Upload** button gives you the files in `onUpload` (HTML: the `ok:upload:upload` event). Files a user chose before, such as a saved avatar, can be URL strings in `value`: the upload shows them but can't put them in the input.
sections.html: …
sections.react:
<Upload
  multiple
  onUpload={async (files) => {
    const body = new FormData();
    for (const file of files) if (file instanceof File) body.append("attachments", file);
    await fetch("/attachments", { method: "POST", body });
  }}
/>

sections.body: Props and attributes that aren't styling options: files, texts, callbacks and the input's own attributes.
sections.title: Content and behavior

sections.body: In HTML, the runtime fires these events on the upload root and adds methods to its instance (`window.Owlky.get(root, "upload")`). `ok:upload:drop` is cancelable: cancel it to keep the files as they are. `ok:upload:change` reports the files after every change, with the reason: `add`, `remove`, `clear` or `reset` (the form was reset). `ok:upload:remove` is cancelable too. `ok:upload:drag` reports the drag state, and the root carries it as `data-ok-drag` (`accept`, `reject` or `unknown`) and `data-ok-drag-global`, which you can style. Instance methods: `open()`, `setFiles(files)`, `removeFile(file)`, `clearFiles()`, `setValidator(fn)`, `setErrorMessage(fn)` and `setFilesFromEvent(fn)`; properties `files`, `rejections`, `dragState`, `isFileDialogActive` and `isProcessing`.
sections.title: Events and methods

sections.body: The input is the zone's focus target, so the zone shows a focus ring.
sections.title: Keyboard

sections.body:
- **Native control:** the zone holds a real file input, named by the zone's title (or `aria-label`) and described by the helper text. Screen readers announce it as a file button, and it works without JavaScript.
- **Errors:** with `error`, the input gets `aria-invalid`. Rejected files appear in an alert, so screen readers announce them.
- **New files:** the list is a polite live region, so added files are announced.
- **Remove buttons:** each one is named after its file, such as "Remove report.pdf". When a removed button had the focus, the focus moves to the next remove button, or back to the input.
- **Text and contrast:** the texts meet a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1, including the zone's description and the helper text. File names are always shown as text, never as markup.

sections.body: A walktour guides people through a page, one step at a time. Each step is a small dialog next to the element it explains. An overlay dims the rest of the page and leaves a spotlight on that element. People move on with **Next**, go back with **Back**, end the tour with **Skip**, and close a step with the close button or Escape. A progress bar and a step count show how far they are. Instead of opening a step at once, a tour can show a pulsing beacon on the element, which people select when they are ready.
sections.html:
…

Your inbox

New messages arrive here.
…
sections.title: Overview

sections.body: In React, pass the steps as data. Each step has a `target`, which is a CSS selector, an element, a ref or a function that returns the element. It also has its `content` and, usually, a `title` that names the dialog. `placement` puts the step on a side of the target, such as `bottom` or `left-start`. Use `auto` to pick the side with the most room, or `center` for a step in the middle of the screen with no target. A step can override most options of the tour, such as `disableBeacon`, `spotlightClicks` or `showSkipButton`. In HTML, write one step element per step. `data-ok-target` holds the selector, and an option attribute on a step overrides the tour's. The value `false` turns a tour option off for that step.
sections.html: …
sections.title: Describe the steps

sections.body: The tour runs while `run` is `true`. Setting it to `false` pauses the tour, and setting it back resumes it. A tour that finished or was skipped starts over. `apiRef` gives you `start`, `stop`, `reset`, `next`, `prev`, `go`, `close`, `skip` and `open`. To control the current step yourself, pass `stepIndex` and update it from `onStepChange`. In HTML, `data-ok-run` runs the tour, a button with `data-ok-walktour-start` starts it over, and the instance has the same methods.
sections.html:
<button type="button" data-ok-button data-ok-walktour-start="tour" data-ok-index="0">Start the tour</button>

<script type="module">
  // Or from code, once the runtime has started.
  const tour = window.Owlky.get(document.getElementById("tour"), "walktour");
  tour.start();
  tour.go(2);
</script>
sections.title: Run and control the tour

sections.body: Without `continuous`, the primary button reads **Close**: it closes the step and shows a beacon on the next target. People select the beacon to open that step. In a continuous tour, **Next** and **Back** go from step to step without beacons, and closing a step with the close button, Escape or the overlay shows the next step's beacon. `disableBeacon` opens steps at once, for the whole tour or for one step.
sections.html: …
sections.react: <Walktour steps={steps} run showSkipButton />
sections.title: Use beacons

sections.body: The overlay blocks the page while a step is open, so the step is a modal dialog. `spotlightClicks` lets people use the element in the spotlight, and `disableOverlay` removes the overlay: in both cases the step is no longer modal. `disableOverlayClose` keeps a click on the overlay from closing the step. `spotlightPadding` sets the space around the target and `spotlightRadius` the spotlight's corners, in pixels. When a target is out of view, the tour scrolls it into view and keeps `scrollOffset` pixels above it. `disableScrolling` turns that off, and `scrollToFirstStep` scrolls for the first step too.
sections.html: …
sections.react: <Walktour steps={steps} spotlightClicks spotlightPadding={12} spotlightRadius={16} scrollOffset={80} />
sections.title: Configure the overlay and the spotlight

sections.body: Options of the tour. In React, pass them as props. In HTML, write the attributes on the `data-ok-walktour` element. Every boolean option can also go on a step.
sections.title: Options

sections.body: Options of one step: React step fields, HTML attributes on the step element.
sections.title: Step options

sections.body: Steps, texts and the tour's state.
sections.title: Content and behavior

sections.body: React reports changes with `onStepChange(index, details)`, `onStatusChange(status, details)` and `onEvent(type, data)`. `onEvent` receives every event of the tour in order: `tour:start`, `step:before`, `beacon`, `tooltip`, `step:after`, `tour:end`, `tour:status` and `error:target-not-found`. Each comes with the action, the control that asked for it, the step, the status and the number of steps. In HTML, listen for `ok:walktour:change` (the new state), `ok:walktour:event` (the same events as `onEvent`) and `ok:walktour:beforechange`, which you can cancel to keep the current step. A step whose target isn't in the page is skipped.
sections.html:
<script type="module">
  const root = document.getElementById("tour");
  root.addEventListener("ok:walktour:event", (event) => {
    if (event.detail.type === "tour:end") console.log("Tour ended:", event.detail.status);
  });
</script>
sections.react:
<Walktour
  steps={steps}
  run
  onEvent={(type, data) => {
    if (type === "tour:end") console.log("Tour ended:", data.status);
  }}
/>
sections.title: Events and methods

sections.body: Keys while a step is open.
sections.title: Keyboard

sections.body:
- Each step is a dialog named by its title (or "Step 2 of 5" without one) and described by its content. While the overlay blocks the page, the step is modal: Tab stays inside it and the rest of the page is inert.
- Focus moves to the step's primary button when a step opens, to the beacon when a step closes to one, and back to where it was when the tour ends.
- A polite live region announces "Step 2 of 5" when a step opens.
- The beacon is a button named "Open the dialog". Change the text with `locale.open`.
- Escape closes a step unless `disableCloseOnEsc` is set. Keep it on: it is the quickest way out for keyboard users.
- The beacon's pulse stops when the system asks for reduced motion, and scrolling to a target is instant then.
